Bedrocks.Name: Crystalline shield
Bedrocks.Description: Mostly under flat land, lowland and hills. Gives granite, banded iron, lode gold in the hills, diamonds and kaolin.
Bedrocks.Lore: The oldest rock, the floor of the world. Dwarves say it was laid down before the Dawn and that nothing has happened to it since, which is why they trust it.

Bedrocks.Name: Fold belt
Bedrocks.Description: Mostly under hills and mountains. Gives slate, marble, silver, lode gold, garnet and emerald.
Bedrocks.Lore: The earth here was pushed up like a rucked carpet, and seashells lie on the peaks. The priests say it was a flood, and the Dwarves say it was a quarrel.

Bedrocks.Name: Granite intrusion
Bedrocks.Description: Mostly under hills and mountains. Gives granite, tin lodes, skarn iron, topaz and beryl, and kaolin.
Bedrocks.Lore: Rock that rose molten and cooled in the dark. The Dwarves cut their oldest holds in it and say the fire left its wealth along the edges.

Bedrocks.Name: Volcanic arc
Bedrocks.Description: Mostly under mountains. Gives basalt, obsidian, pumice, porphyry copper, gold, rock crystal, alum, sulphur and quicksilver.
Bedrocks.Lore: Young rock that is not yet finished. The ground steams and shakes, and those who mine it grow rich quickly and do not build in stone.

Bedrocks.Name: Flood basalt
Bedrocks.Description: Mostly under flat land, lowland and hills. Gives basalt, native copper, agate and black sands.
Bedrocks.Lore: Black rock that once ran like water over the whole land, layer on layer. The steps of it climb the horizon, and the soil on top is dark and deep.

Bedrocks.Name: Ophiolite
Bedrocks.Description: Mostly under hills and mountains. Gives soapstone, massive-sulfide copper and jade.
Bedrocks.Lore: Green rock from the floor of a vanished sea, pushed up among the mountains. Little grows on it, and what does grows nowhere else.

Bedrocks.Name: Carbonate platform
Bedrocks.Description: Mostly under lowland and hills. Gives limestone, chalk, flint, lead and zinc, skarn iron and cave saltpetre.
Bedrocks.Lore: Rock built of shells, which water hollows out. The rivers go underground, the hills are full of caves, and every cave has its tale of what was put there.

Bedrocks.Name: Clastic basin
Bedrocks.Description: Mostly under flat land and lowland. Gives sandstone, coal, lignite, red-bed copper, rock salt, amber, gypsum and alum shale.
Bedrocks.Lore: Sand and mud laid down by old rivers and turned to stone, with the forests of another age pressed black between the beds. The bones of dragons weather out of it.

Bedrocks.Name: Unconsolidated cover
Bedrocks.Description: Mostly under flat land and lowland. Gives field stone and clay only.
Bedrocks.Lore: No rock at all, the Dwarves say: only what the rivers and the ice left lying. The farmers call it the best land there is and do not ask what is under it.

Races.Name: Northmen
Races.Description: Tall, long in the leg and heavy in the shoulder. The skin is fair and burns before it browns. Hair runs from flaxen through red to light brown and is worn long and combed daily. Men braid their beards. Eyes are blue, grey or green. They dress in wool and linen under a fur-lined cloak pinned at one shoulder, and wear their wealth as silver arm-rings that are cut up when a payment falls due.
Races.Lore:
Before the Ashen Years the Northmen were forest farmers and fishers at the cold edge of the ploughed world, living on rye, barley, cattle and herring. They call the Ashen Years the Great Winter: three winters with no summer between them, and four more years of bad hay. A farm that fed ten now fed four. The younger sons took the boats that had been built for fishing and went to find out who still had grain. Some traded furs, amber and walrus ivory for it. Some took it. Most did both on the same voyage, and the choice depended on how well the town was walled.

The hunger ended, and the sea-road did not. Their shallow clinker-built ships can cross open water, run up a river and be dragged over a watershed, so Northmen turned up far inland as traders, settlers of empty coasts, and hired guards of kings who trusted no one born nearby.

They hold that the world is the upturned hull of a ship, built by the first Shipwright: the sky is its planking and the stars are the rivets. One day it will be righted and launched, and those who died well will row it. A person who dies in bed can still earn a bench by being remembered, which is why they carve stones for kin who died abroad and why a good poet eats at the high table.

Races.Name: Midlanders
Races.Description: Middling in height and build, and mixed in colouring: skin from fair to olive, hair from blond to black, straight or curled, eyes of any colour. A crowd of Midlanders looks like several peoples, which it once was. Rank shows in the clothes. Peasants wear undyed wool and wooden shoes. Townsfolk wear dyed cloth cut to the fashion of their guild. The nobility wear fur trim, long sleeves and a coat of arms.
Races.Lore:
The Midlanders are the people of the old provinces. When an Old Realm ruled the temperate plains, their ancestors were its farmers, soldiers and clerks, drawn from many conquered tribes and taught one script and one law. When the Realm broke in the Ashen Years they stayed where they were. The roads were still there, and the bridges, the boundary stones and the habit of writing things down. The sorcery was gone. What grew over the ruins was smaller and tougher: a lord with a wooden tower and a dozen horsemen, who protected the villages in his sight and took a share of their harvest for it.

Everything since has been built up from that bargain. Lords swore to greater lords, and the greatest called themselves kings. Each Midlander kingdom claims to be the true successor of the Realm and keeps a little of its ceremony: a crown, an anointing, a court language no peasant speaks. Their histories are full of the wish to put the Realm back together and the wars fought over who would hold it.

The Midlanders are also the people of the heavy plough. Eight oxen and an iron share turn the wet clay that lighter ploughs cannot, and that opened the forest lowlands to grain. Their saying is that land unploughed is land unfinished. The Elves have another word for it.

Races.Name: Saltroad folk
Races.Description: Lean, fine-boned and long in the limb, built to shed heat. The skin runs from light brown at the cooler coasts to a deep red-brown in the far desert and the highlands. Hair is black or dark brown, wavy to tightly curled. Eyes are dark brown, now and then green or amber. They wear loose robes in layers and a long cloth wound as turban and veil. Among the desert clans it is the men who veil their faces, and a man of standing is never seen without it.
Races.Lore:
The Saltroad folk say their cities are older than the Old Realms, and the ruins bear them out. Along the one great river of a desert country their ancestors built in stone before anyone else did, and counted years by the river's flood. When the sorcerer-kings rose elsewhere, the desert was too wide to be worth conquering and too hard to cross without a guide. That has been the fortune of the Saltroad folk ever since: they live on land nobody else can use, and they own the way across it.

The way is the salt road. South of the desert lie the gold fields of the Sunlanders, where salt is scarce enough to be weighed against gold. North of it are the coasts that want gold. Between them are forty days of sand and a chain of wells that only the desert clans can find. A caravan of a thousand camels carries slabs of salt south and comes back with gold, ivory and kola nuts, and every oasis on the route takes its fee.

In the Ashen Years the desert suffered least, since it had no harvest to lose. Scholars fled to the oasis towns with their books, and the towns have been places of learning since. A Saltroad library is a family's treasure, walled into the house and passed down. They follow one unseen god, whose law is written, and whose judges are the scholars. In the dry highlands an older rite survives, with priest-kings and temples cut down into the living rock.

Races.Name: Sunlanders
Races.Description: The Sunlanders vary more in build than any other human race. The cattle herders of the open grass are among the tallest people in the world, slender and long-legged. The farmers of the forest edge are of middling height and strongly built, and the hunters of the deep forest are short and light. The skin runs from dark brown to a black with a blue sheen. Hair is black and tightly coiled, and is braided, shaved in patterns or built up with clay and beads to show age, rank and home. Dress is wrapped cotton in strong dyes, indigo first among them.
Races.Lore:
The Sunlanders hold that they were the first to draw iron from stone, and nobody has proof against it. Their smiths smelted in tall clay furnaces while the Old Realms were still working bronze. A Sunlander smith is more than a craftsman: he commands fire, makes the hoe and the spear, and is feared and honoured like a priest. In many of their kingdoms the first king is remembered as a smith.

Iron cleared the forest edge and armed the grassland, and gold paid for the rest. The gold fields lie in Sunlander country, washed from river gravel and dug from shallow pits. The kings who held them grew rich enough that one, on a journey, gave away so much gold that its price fell for a generation. That is the tale the Saltroad folk tell, and the Sunlanders do not deny it.

The Old Realms never ruled them. A fly of the wet forest kills horses and cattle with a sleeping sickness, and no mounted army could pass it. So the grassland built empires on cavalry, and the forest built walled city-states that no cavalry could reach. In the Ashen Years the rains failed, the herders moved south and east, and the kingdoms they met or founded on the way make up the Sunlander lands today.

Little of this is written down. It is kept by the praise-singers, a hereditary class who hold the genealogy and deeds of every great family in memory and sing them on demand. A king without a praise-singer has no past.

Races.Name: Grass riders
Races.Description: Compact, deep-chested and bow-legged from a life on horseback, with broad faces, high cheekbones and narrow dark eyes creased against wind and glare. The skin is tan to bronze and weathered early. Hair is straight and black, and men shave the crown and braid what is left behind the ears. Both sexes wear a long wrapped coat belted at the waist, felt boots and a fur hat, and carry a bow case and a knife.
Races.Lore:
The steppe cannot be ploughed. It has grass, and what turns grass into a living is the horse, the sheep and the will to move. The Grass riders have lived that way since the Dawn: a few families and their herds, shifting camp four or five times a year, each clan at feud or at marriage with the next.

Their history has one shape, which repeats. For generations the clans raid each other and the farmers at the steppe's edge, and no one outside pays them much attention. Then a leader appears who can make the clans obey. He breaks up the old clans and sorts the fighting men into tens, hundreds and thousands under officers chosen for merit. He gives one written law for everyone. In a few years he has an army in which every man has three remounts and can shoot from the saddle at a gallop, and no farming kingdom can stand against it. The Old Realms paid tribute to such khans. The Ashen Years, which killed the herds and drove the clans outward together, broke the realms that still stood.

Then the khan dies, his heirs divide the conquests, and within a few generations each is ruling farmers from a palace and is a steppe lord in name only. The clans at home begin again. Every Grass rider knows the shape and believes the next khan will be the one whose realm holds.

They worship the Sky, which is everywhere and needs no temple. A shaman speaks to the lesser spirits for a fee. They care little what conquered people believe, tax every faith alike and enjoy setting priests to argue before the khan.

Races.Name: Rainkeepers
Races.Description: Slight to middling in height and fine-featured. The skin runs from a light wheat-brown to very dark brown, often within one town. Hair is black, straight or wavy, oiled, and worn long by both sexes. Eyes are large and dark. Dress is unsewn cotton: a length of cloth wrapped and pleated at the waist for a man, a longer one drawn over the shoulder for a woman, in colours that tell the wearer's community. A mark of coloured paste on the brow shows which god the wearer follows.
Races.Lore:
The monsoon lands get a year's rain in three months and none in the other nine. The Rainkeepers became a people when they learned to hold on to it. They dammed a shallow valley with an earth bank to make a reservoir, then another below it to catch the overflow, and another below that. A chain of reservoirs feeds rice fields through the dry season, and the kingdom that builds the chains can feed cities. Their kings are judged by their dams, and the proudest boast in their inscriptions is that not one drop reaches the sea without first serving the people.

The Old Realms traded with them and did not conquer them. Their own empires rose and fell on the rain: a run of bad monsoons broke more dynasties than any enemy. The Ashen Years stopped the rain for three seasons. The cities emptied and the forest took the canals. What the Rainkeepers rebuilt afterwards was a land of many middling kingdoms, each around a temple town.

Their thought runs to great spans of time. They hold that the world is made, destroyed and made again in cycles of millions of years, and that a soul is reborn through many lives, higher or lower by its deeds, until it wins release. They have a thousand gods, whom their teachers call so many faces of one. Their epics are the longest poems in the world. Their scholars gave the world its numerals, the zero and the game of kings.

Races.Name: Canal folk
Races.Description: Middling in height, slender in the south and sturdier in the north. The skin runs from pale tan to golden-brown. Hair is straight and black, never cut, and worn in a topknot under a cap. Eyes are dark and narrow-lidded. Dress is a robe crossed left over right and tied with a sash. Farmers wear hemp or cotton and a wide straw hat. Officials wear silk in the colour of their grade, with a square badge on the chest that shows their rank to anyone who can read it.
Races.Lore:
The Canal folk live on river plains that flood. Their first hero was an engineer who tamed the flood by digging channels to lead the water away, after his father had failed with dams. The lesson shaped everything after: water is managed by many people working to one plan for many years, and that needs someone to keep the plan. So they have the oldest continuous state in the world, built to maintain dikes, canals and granaries.

They call that state the Realm, and they hold that there is only one. Heaven grants its mandate to a ruling house for as long as the house rules well. Floods, famines and rebellions are signs that the mandate has been withdrawn, and whoever then wins the throne has received it. So a dynasty may fall, and the Realm goes on. The Canal folk alone among peoples say that their Old Realm never ended. It lost its sorcery in the Ashen Years and kept its files.

In the Scattered Age the throne is disputed or empty, and each Canal folk state is ruled by a governor or king who holds it, by his own account, in trust for the emperor to come. All of them keep the same calendar, script, weights and ritual, so that the pieces will fit when they are put back together.

Their teaching is about conduct, not gods: the duty of child to parent, subject to ruler, younger to elder, and the duty of the ruler to deserve it. Ancestors are fed and informed at the family altar. Other faiths are welcome so long as they do not question the order.

Races.Name: Elves
Races.Description: A head taller than most humans and lighter in build, with long hands and a way of standing entirely still. The ears rise to a point. The face is fine-boned and shows no age after the thirtieth year: an Elf of four hundred has a smooth brow and old eyes. Colouring follows the forest. Elves of the cold woods are pale and silver-haired, those of the oak woods brown-haired and green-eyed, those of the warm forests dark and gold-eyed. They dress in greens, greys and browns that are hard to see between trees.
Races.Lore:
The Elves say the temperate world was once forest from shore to shore and that they planted a good part of it. It may be so. An Elf thinks nothing of setting an acorn where a hall will be wanted in two hundred years. In the Dawn they tended the woods as a farmer tends a field, but on a rotation of centuries. They thinned and coppiced, moved saplings, bred trees for nuts and fruit, and grew their halls from living trunks.

Then humans came with fire and the plough. The Elves did not at first understand that a people could clear land and never let it grow back. By the time of the Old Realms they understood it well. The Realms cut whole forests for fleets and furnaces, and the Elves fought them in a string of wars that each lasted one human generation and that the Elves count as a single war, not yet over. They also taught the first sorcerer-kings. Elves do not like to be reminded of it.

In the Ashen Years the old forest lived on its stored strength while the grain fields died. Some elven houses opened their stores of nuts and dried fruit to the starving farmers at the forest edge. Others closed the paths. That choice still divides them into the Open houses and the Closed, and it still decides how each forest is regarded by its neighbours.

They are few and grow fewer. A couple may have two children in five centuries, and a war that kills fifty is a disaster that takes three hundred years to mend.

Races.Name: Dwarves
Races.Description: Four to four and a half feet tall and nearly as broad, with thick wrists, big hands and a heavy brow. The skin is ruddy or brown and seamed like worked leather. Both men and women grow beards, which are braided and ringed to show clan, craft and standing, so outsiders often cannot tell the sexes apart and Dwarves see no reason to help them. They see well in very little light. They dress in leather and thick wool and are rarely without a tool on the belt.
Races.Lore:
The Dwarves hold that the first of them were not born. They woke inside the rock and dug their way out, and the urge to dig is the memory of it. They have a sense no other race has: a Dwarf feels the depth, the direction and the grain of the stone around him, and is never lost underground.

Through the Dawn and the Old Realms they went deeper. A hold begins as a mine and becomes a city: halls, forges, cisterns and tombs cut into a mountain behind one gate. The sorcerer-kings never ruled them, since a hold cannot be taken except by starving it, and the Realms wanted dwarven steel more than dwarven obedience. They paid in grain. For a thousand years the holds grew rich and stopped keeping fields.

Then the Ashen Years came and the grain carts did not. The Dwarves call this the Hungry Gate. Holds that had never been breached starved behind their own doors. Others opened the gate and sent their people out as smiths, masons and soldiers to anyone who could feed them. The holds that came through drew two lessons, which are now law in all of them. Every hold keeps seven years of grain in sealed halls. And every hold keeps treaties with the farmers below it, and honours them to the grain.

Races.Name: Halflings
Races.Description: Three to three and a half feet tall, built like small adults, not like children: sturdy, round in the face and inclined to be stout. The hair is thick and curly, brown or sandy. The eyes are bright and the hands are deft. They walk very quietly without trying. They have a sense of taste and smell far finer than a human's and can name the field a cheese came from. They dress in bright waistcoats, wide hats and good boots, and wear their prosperity on their backs.
Races.Lore:
The small folk have always lived in the gaps the big folk left: river meadows, the hedged corners of the lowlands, the sunny slopes too steep for the heavy plough. They have no tale of where they came from and no interest in one. Their history is family history, kept in genealogies that every Halfling can recite to the seventh cousin.

Their name is a tax record. The registers of an Old Realm entered each of them at half a head, since they ate half a ration and could carry half a load. The clerks wrote "halfling" in the margin and the word stuck. Their own word for themselves just means the Folk.

A Halfling household has always kept a deep cellar, and custom says it should hold enough to feed the family for seven years, though no one remembers who set the number. In the Ashen Years the custom paid. Small bodies need little, the cellars were full, and the Halflings were the one people of the farmland who did not starve. Most of them fed their human neighbours as well. The neighbours have not forgotten. The charters that give Halfling districts their own law inside human kingdoms nearly all date from the first years after the ash.

Races.Name: Gnomes
Races.Description: About three feet tall and lightly built, with a large head, a long nose, big ears and very large eyes of a clear grey or brown. Hair goes white early and is worn in tufts or under a pointed cap. The fingers are long and thin. A Gnome sees close detail as a human sees through a lens: the facets of a seed, the scratches on a gear. At thirty paces the same Gnome sees a blur and wears ground glass spectacles to correct it. They dress in many pockets.
Races.Lore:
The Gnomes are hill folk. Where the Dwarves went into the mountain, the Gnomes dug warrens under the roots of the oak and beech woods in the foothills, shallow, dry and warm. They were never numerous and never fought anyone if there was a back door.

Their close sight made them the makers of everything fine. In the Old Realms the sorcerer-kings prized them above gold. Gnomes ground the lenses, cut the crystals, engraved the measuring rings and built the clockwork that the sorcery needed, and they were kept in comfortable workshops that had locks on the outside. Being Gnomes, they kept a copy of every design.

When the Realms broke, the Gnomes walked out with the drawings and without the masters. They drew one conclusion from the whole age and made it a rule. No workshop takes more than a third of its work from one patron. A Gnome will sell to a king, and will not belong to one.

They went into their warrens in the Ashen Years with mushroom beds and with something nobody else had thought to save in good order: seed. Sorted, labelled and sealed, the seed vaults of the warrens resowed a good many fields when the sun came back. Farmers still buy their seed from Gnomes when they want it true to kind.

Races.Name: Orcs
Races.Description: Six to seven feet tall and heavy in the bone, with long arms, a thick neck, a low brow and two tusks rising from the lower jaw. The skin is grey-green, olive or dun brown. Hair is coarse and black and is worn in a crest or a knot. The eyes are small, yellow or red-brown, and see well at dusk. Scars are left to show and are sometimes rubbed with ash so that they stand out: an Orc's skin is a record. Dress is leather, hide and whatever armour was won.
Races.Lore:
In the Dawn the Orcs lived on good land too. Humans with ploughs fed ten on the ground that fed one Orc hunter, and over the generations the Orcs were pushed outward to the dry plains, the scrub and the badlands, which is where they are now. The land made them what they are. An Orc can eat carrion, bone, bark and meat a week dead and take no harm, heals from wounds that would kill a human, and is full grown at twelve.

The Old Realms saw a use for that. They raised orc legions, the heavy infantry of the sorcerer-kings, paid them in loot and settled the veterans in forts along the frontiers. When the Realms fell the garrisons did not go home, because the forts were home. Many orc holds today stand on the walls of an old frontier fort, and their chiefs keep the standard of a legion that no state has paid for a thousand years.

They have a name for the Ashen Years, and it is the Lean Feast. When the harvests failed, the Orcs lived on what the others could not eat. They came out of the poor land into country emptied by famine and took a good deal of it. The stories that make them monsters date from then: they arrived when everyone was starving, and they were not.

Races.Name: Hoarkin
Races.Description: Stocky and short-limbed, with skin as pale as skimmed milk that shades to blue-grey at the lips, the nails, the eyelids and the tips of the ears. Hair is white or ash-grey, fine and dense. The eyes are pale grey with a dark rim. A Hoarkin never shivers and moves slowly and exactly. Their breath makes no cloud in the frost, and their hand is as cold as a stone from the beach. They wear one layer of sealskin, against wind and wet. They do not need it against cold.
Races.Lore:
The Hoarkin are cousins of the humans who followed the seals out onto the ice in the Dawn and stayed, for more generations than human history has. A warm body on the ice burns food all day to stay alive. Over that long time the Hoarkin body stopped trying. Something in their blood keeps it liquid far below freezing. At rest the heart beats twenty times a minute. A Hoarkin can sit by a seal's breathing hole from one tide to the next without moving and without harm, and needs a third of the food a human does. That is how the ice can feed a people at all.

Their own account is a bargain. The First Mother met Cold on the ice, and Cold was killing her children. She gave him their fire, and he agreed to stop. So the Hoarkin have no fire inside them, and they call every other people the Burning: folk who are alight within, eat without end to feed the flame, and die of it young.

In the Ashen Years the ice spread south and the Hoarkin came with it, further than they had ever been, onto coasts emptied by famine. They call that time the Wide Years. When the sun returned the ice drew back and most of them followed it home. A few bands were stranded on high glaciers, where they still are.

Races.Name: Hearthbloods
Races.Description: Broad, deep-chested and well fleshed, with skin of a flushed copper red, like someone just in from a hard run. Hair is black or dark red and cropped short. The eyes are dark with a ruddy light in them. In frost a Hearthblood walks in a cloud of their own breath, steam rises from the bare shoulders, and snow melts where they sit. They wear a kilt and an open vest in weather that kills. Their touch is as hot as a brow in a fever.
Races.Lore:
The Hearthbloods are the youngest of the races, and they remember their making. They were a human people of the high valleys. When the Ashen Years came, the snow in the passes did not melt for three summers, and they were shut in. They burned the firewood, then the furniture, then the roof beams. In the third winter the hearth-keeper of the last hall that still had a fire stood over the last coals. The hall stood by a warm spring, in a place where the world is thin and things asked for are sometimes given. She asked that the fire should not go out. Then she stirred the coals into the last broth, and everyone drank.

Nobody in that hall was ever cold again, and neither were their children. No Hearthblood hall has had a hearth since. The people are the hearth.

The price showed within the week. A fire has to be fed. A Hearthblood eats twice what a human eats and is in danger after two days without food. On the fifth day they are dead. They also burn out early, and forty-five is old.

Races.Name: Widegaze
Races.Description: Tall, lean and long-necked, with tawny skin and sand-coloured or brown hair tied back hard, so that it never crosses the eyes. The eyes are set wide, almost at the corners of the face. The iris is pale gold, and the pupil is a dark bar that stays level with the ground however the head is tilted. A Widegaze never seems to look at the person they are talking to, because they have no need to turn towards what they watch. They wear long plain coats and a brimmed hat cut away at the sides.
Races.Lore:
The Widegaze say plainly that their mothers were hunted. In the Dawn their ancestors lived on open grassland among great cats and running wolves, with no trees to climb and no caves. Those who saw the grass move lived. After enough generations of that, they were a people who could not be surprised: able to see in front, to both sides and most of the way behind in a single glance, and to pick out a rider at the edge of sight.

They never built a wall. Their safety was to see first and to be gone.

The Old Realms gave them a second trade. A sorcerer-king's frontier was too long to garrison, so the Realm raised a line of earth mounds across the plain, each within sight of the next, and set a Widegaze family on every one. A message passed by mirror flash and smoke from mound to mound crossed the Realm in an afternoon. The Realm fell, and the line remained. The mounds are now the Widegaze villages, the families still pass messages along them for a fee, and nobody else has ever learned the code. They call the line the Watch.

In the Ashen Years they were the first on the plain to see the ash coming, as a brown wall on the horizon, three days out. They moved their herds early and lost fewer than anyone.

Races.Name: Amberbloods
Races.Description: Sturdy and broad-handed, with brown-gold skin scattered with freckles the colour of clear resin. The eyes are amber and catch the light like a bead held to the sun. Hair is chestnut, copper or bark-brown. A faint grain, like that of planed wood, runs along the backs of the hands and down the spine, and deepens with age. A cut does not bleed. It wells one golden bead, which hardens in a breath. The old move stiffly, their skin is ridged, and their voices creak.
Races.Lore:
In the age of the Old Realms the loggers came north. The Realms wanted masts and charcoal, and they cut the great cold forests a valley at a time. The people who lived there were human then: woodcutters, trappers and charcoal burners, paid by the Realm to fell their own home. One winter they stopped.

Their story says that the forest itself made the offer, through whatever it is that lives in the oldest stands, where the world is thin. Trees cannot walk and cannot fight. The forest needed a people who could. It would give them its blood, so that steel could hardly kill them. In return they would give it their ending: when one of them could walk no longer, they would come back and stand. The people agreed, drove the loggers out over thirty years, and have kept the terms since.

The Elves say the compact was offered to them first and that they refused the price. The Amberbloods say nobody asked the Elves.

Later ages brought a worse enemy than loggers. Their blood, once set, is the finest varnish and glue there is, staunches any wound, and after some years in the ground becomes true amber. In the Tapping Wars, human slavers took Amberbloods alive to bleed them, a cup a week. They do not forgive it, and the trade in blood amber is not quite dead.

Races.Name: Brinefolk
Races.Description: Spare and smooth-skinned, with a grey-white skin that has the faint sheen of the inside of a shell. Hair is pale and stiff. The eyes are a very light grey or green. Beside each eye lies a gland that sheds the salt they take in, so a Brinefolk weeps brine all day without sorrow. It dries to a white crust on the lashes, in the corners of the eyes and along the brow, which they brush away or shape into ornament as fashion bids. They lick their lips often. They dress in pale wrapped linen, and both sexes line the eyes with dark paint against the glare of the flats.
Races.Lore:
The Brinefolk are not cousins of the humans, and their oldest carvings say so. The basins of the cold desert once held an inland sea. In its shallows lived a people the carvings show with fins along the arms, who gathered shellfish and never left the water for long. Over the Dawn the sea shrank. Each generation waded in shallower, saltier water than the last, and each stood a little straighter. When the last of the sea had gone into the sky, what was left on the white flats walked on two legs and looked, to a stranger, like a pale kind of human.

The clerks of the Old Realms listed them as human and taxed them in salt. The Realms needed salt in quantity, to keep meat for their armies and fish for their cities, and the Brinefolk had the pans and the patience. They grew rich on it. In the Ashen Years they grew richer. What little food the world had needed keeping, and for seven years a block of salt bought its weight in silver. Other peoples remember those years with grief, and remember who set the price.

They believe the sea will come back. The flats are its bed, kept in trust. So they do not plough there or build higher than one storey, and they bury their dead packed in salt, sitting up, so that the dead will be whole and ready when the water returns.

Races.Name: Duskreaders
Races.Description: Slight and narrow-built, with deep brown skin that has a grey undertone. The eyes are large and wholly black, without a visible white or iris, and glossy as wet stone. By day they wear a visor of smoked horn with a slit in it, or a veil of dark gauze. Among themselves they dress in thick quilted robes, gloves and often a mask of stiffened cloth. The robes are not for warmth. They hide the body's heat, and with it everything the body gives away.
Races.Lore:
In the Dawn their ancestors sheltered from the desert day in deep canyons and caves and came out to hunt at night. Over many generations in the dark, their eyes learned to see warmth: a hare under a bush, a snake on a rock, the ground a herd lay on an hour ago. A cool seep under sand shows dark to them, so they find water where others die.

The same sight shows them a blush, a fever, a quickened pulse in the throat and the heat of a hand that has just held a hidden knife. The sorcerer-kings of the Old Realms saw the use in it at once. They set Duskreaders beside their thrones as examiners. Subjects called them the King's Eyes, since nobody could stand in front of one and lie calmly. The kings were served, and their examiners were hated. When the Realms fell the mobs went for them first, and the survivors fled back into the deep desert.

Out of that they made the rule every Duskreader child learns: we read, we do not tell. A Duskreader says what they have been hired to see and nothing else, ever. An order of them, the Discreet, takes it as a formal vow.

The Ashen Years they remember differently from everyone else. The dimmed sun made the desert day mild, and for seven years they walked abroad at noon. They call it the Kind Time, and they have learned not to say so in company.

Races.Name: Noonfolk
Races.Description: Tall, slender and wide in the shoulder. The skin runs from copper-brown to deep olive and carries a tracery of green-bronze lines, most clearly across the shoulders, the back and the upper arms. The lines darken through the day and pale overnight. Noonfolk have no hair at all. The eyes are green or gold, with pupils that shrink to a point in full sun. They wear a wrap at the hips, and nothing that shades the back.
Races.Lore:
There was a kingdom of the Old Realms in the dry grassland that suffered one famine after another. Its sorcerer-king saw that most of every harvest went to feed the people who grew it. He set his makers to breed field hands who would not need feeding. They took debtors and convicts and worked on them, generation after generation, with a craft borrowed from the leaf. The result was the Noonfolk, who laboured from dawn to dusk on a bowl of gruel and a great deal of water.

The makers left two flaws. A Noonfolk falls asleep when the sun goes down, wherever they are standing, and nothing wakes them before dawn. So they were useless as soldiers, sentries or house servants. And nobody had planned for a sky without sun. When the Ashen Years came, the made people starved faster than anyone. Their stomachs were too small to live on food alone. Nine in ten died. They call it the Dark Hunger. The kingdom died in the same years, and the Noonfolk who were left walked off the estates and were not stopped.

They say of it: the king made us to eat light. Nobody asked the Sun. The Sun feeds us anyway.

Races.Name: Boughwalkers
Races.Description: Slender and very light, with arms that reach the knee, long hands, and feet that grip like a second pair of hands. The skin is dark brown to red-brown. Hair is black and braided flat to the skull, so that nothing can catch on it. The eyes are large and hazel-green. A Boughwalker has perfect balance and no fear of a drop. They wear belts, pouches and short wraps of cloth that looks plain brown or white to everyone else. To their own eyes it blazes with pattern.
Races.Lore:
In the Dawn their ancestors went up into the canopy of the wet forest and stayed. The fruit is there, with the light and the breeze. The forest floor is dark, flooded half the year, and full of fever and things with teeth. Countless generations aloft gave them their reach and grip. It also gave them eyes for the work that matters most up there: telling ripe fruit from unripe, and wholesome from poisonous, among a thousand shades of green. Flowers, fruit, feathers and some poisons show a colour beyond violet. Boughwalkers see it. They call it the high colour and cannot describe it to anyone else.

The Old Realms never reached them. The Ashen Years did. The canopy thinned, the fruit failed, and for the first time in memory the Boughwalkers came down to the ground to look for food. They call it the Year on the Floor. Many died of the fevers of the floor, and those who lived had met the ground peoples and started to trade with them. One custom has been kept from it. Every young Boughwalker spends a floor-year among the ground peoples before marrying.

Races.Name: Shoalfolk
Races.Description: Lean, sleek and very deep in the chest. The skin is brown with a grey or green cast, smooth and faintly oiled. Hair is black, cropped short or braided with shell. The eyes are large and dark. When a Shoalfolk blinks, a clear membrane flicks sideways across the eye, and it stays shut under water. The nostrils are slits that close at will. They wear a loincloth and a knife, and add a belt of lead weights when diving. Children swim before they walk.
Races.Lore:
Their ancestors were shore gatherers on the warm tidal coasts, where the mangroves leave no land to farm and the sea is full of food. Generations of diving for it remade them. The lungs and spleen grew and the eyes learned to focus in water. The skin came to need the sea.

The Old Realms found them useful. Officials set a quota of pearls on every Shoalfolk village and sent the divers deeper each year to fill it. Many came up bleeding from the ears, or did not come up. The Shoalfolk answer was to leave the land altogether. They rebuilt their villages on stilts in the shallows, or on rafts of boats, past the low-water mark where a king's law stops. No ground, no lord, they say, and they have kept to it. To this day a Shoalfolk village pays no land tax, because it stands on none.

In the Ashen Years the fields failed, and the tide still came in twice a day and brought fish with it. The Shoalfolk ate, and sold dried fish to the coast farmers who had looked down on them. They took the lesson that the land fails and the sea does not, and they do not let the farmers forget it.

Races.Name: Swiftborn
Races.Description: Small, wiry and quick, with warm olive or brown skin that is hot to the touch, and a pulse that can be seen in the throat. The eyes are bright and never still. The hair grows a hand's width in a year, dark in summer and pale in winter, so that it is ringed like a cut tree and an age can be counted off a braid. It is worn long for that reason. A Swiftborn of ten is a grown adult. One of twenty-five has the lined face and white brows of a human of seventy.
Races.Lore:
Late in the age of the Old Realms a plague emptied a warm and fertile province. The vineyards went wild, the olive harvest fell unpicked, and whole towns stood with their doors open. The sorcerer who governed the province wanted it full again in his own lifetime. His makers took settlers and quickened them. Their children were grown in seven years and had large families of their own, and in thirty years the province was full.

Nobody had asked what would happen in the thirty-first. The first quickened generation died of old age, all within a few years of each other, and the governor who had made them watched it. He lived to bury four generations of his people. They say it broke his mind, and that it was the fifth generation that pulled him down.

The Ashen Years lasted seven years. That is a quarter of a Swiftborn life. A whole generation was born, grew up and had children without once seeing a clear sun, and is remembered as the Ash-born. The Swiftborn came through by numbers alone. They died fast, and were born faster.

Races.Name: Flinchless
Races.Description: Tall, strong and upright. They were bred from prisoners of many peoples, so skin and hair are of every kind. The eyes are always the same, a pale silver-grey, which was the maker's mark. The skin is crossed with thin white scars, and a missing fingertip or a crooked, badly healed bone is common. What unsettles a stranger is what is absent. A Flinchless does not blink at a raised hand, does not favour a hurt leg and does not wince.
Races.Lore:
A war-wizard of an Old Realm, remembered only as the Marshal, wanted foot soldiers who would not break. He bred them from captives and took the pain out of them. The legion he raised never lost a battle line. It also lost a third of its strength every winter, to wounds nobody had noticed, frostbite nobody had felt, and broken feet that had been marched on for a week.

The makers could not put the pain back. They solved it with drill. Every soldier was paired with another, and at dawn and dusk each pair stripped and examined one another from scalp to sole. This was called the Looking-over. It worked, and it is the root of everything the Flinchless are.

When the Realm fell the legion was left without a master. Part of it marched into the farmland, took up empty holdings and married. Part stayed under arms as companies for hire. Both parts still exist. They divide on one question: whether the oath sworn to the Marshal passed to the kingdoms that claim to be the Realm's heirs. The Oathkept say yes and serve those crowns. The Released say the oath died with him.

Races.Name: Lanternkin
Races.Description: Slight and very pale, with skin so thin that it seems almost clear, and fine hair the colour of ash. The eyes are a light grey-blue. In daylight a Lanternkin looks only sickly. In shadow a blue-green tracery shows at the wrists, the throat and the temples, and it brightens and dims with the heartbeat. The sun burns them quickly, so out of doors they wear a hood, long sleeves and gloves.
Races.Lore:
Their ancestors lived on the floor of the deepest wet forest, where daylight never reaches, among fungi that glow. It was a place where the world is thin. In a famine in the Dawn they ate the glowing caps, having nothing else. Their children's blood shone. It has shone in every generation since.

For a long time it was only a way to find each other in the dark. Then a mother noticed that the drop she had kept in a glass bead from each of her children still glowed, year after year, until the one bead that went dark on the night her son drowned three valleys away. That is the lamp, and it changed what the Lanternkin were for.

The sorcerer-kings were quick to see the use of it. An Old Realm placed a Lanternkin on the staff of every governor and general, and kept the lamps together in a hall in the capital, so that the death of an officer's household was known at court the same hour. Other peoples' blood was tried and did not work.

In the Ashen Years, when the days were dark at noon, villages of every race took Lanternkin in as the light of the house. Many never went back to the forest. Most Lanternkin have lived in other peoples' towns ever since.

Races.Name: Stillfaces
Races.Description: Of middling height, sturdy and soft-footed, with tawny-grey skin and thick hair brindled in brown and grey. The eyes are dark, round and steady. The nose is broad, with wide nostrils that flare when they attend to something. The face is well made and entirely still. It does not smile, frown or lift a brow, and the mouth moves only to eat and to speak. A row of dark spots, like a string of moles, runs along each side of the jaw and behind the ear. Their voices are level. They stand close to a stranger and breathe in.
Races.Lore:
The Stillfaces say they were in the forest before the upright peoples came. In their own telling their ancestors went on four feet and spoke entirely by scent. When the first humans walked into the woods, they stood up to meet them, out of courtesy, and stayed standing. The face came last, they say, and they never learned to work it. Scholars who have examined them agree at least that the bones are arranged differently, and that nothing in them is cousin to a human.

The Old Realms listed them as the mask people and used them as trackers and as finders of poison at court. They left little mark on them.

The Ashen Years left a deep one. The ash that hid the sun also smothered scent. For seven years the forest smelled of nothing but cinders. To a Stillface that was like going deaf and dumb at once. They call those years the Silence. Villages that had talked across a valley on the wind fell out of touch, families broke, and many went mad. In that need they learned speech in the mouth, properly, from their human neighbours. Their spoken language to this day is a borrowed human one, used flatly, like a tool.

Races.Name: Twofold
Races.Description: Of middling height, graceful and even-featured. At any age an outsider finds it hard to say whether a given Twofold is a man or a woman, and the Twofold are amused by the effort. The skin is warm brown to dark brown. The hair is black and worn long by everyone. In the hollow of the throat lies a small patch of skin, pale gold in the young and deep indigo in the old, which changes during the year of the Turning. Everyone dresses alike, in wrapped cotton. Only the sash differs: saffron before the Turning, indigo after it.
Races.Lore:
The Twofold tell it like this. Once they were as other peoples are, and their men and women fell into a war with each other that lasted three generations. Each half held its own villages. Children were stolen back and forth across the line. At the end both sides were too few to go on. Both went to the shrine of the Pair, the god with two faces, and each asked for judgement against the other.

The Pair gave one judgement to both: each of you will be both, and will judge the other as yourself. Since then no Twofold has been only a man or only a woman, and there has been nothing left to have that war about.

The Old Realms had no column in their registers for them, and in the end taxed them by the hearth. In the Ashen Years many Twofold turned early, some at twenty, as if the body knew that mothers were needed. Their houses refilled within a generation.

Races.Name: Bitterbloods
Races.Description: Lean and smooth-skinned, with a dark olive-brown skin broken by patches of bright colour: sky blue, sulphur yellow, sometimes orange, across the throat, the shoulders and the outer arms. The patches are brightest in those whose blood is strongest, and are worn uncovered with pride at home. Hair is black and slicked back with oil. The eyes are dark with a yellow ring. Among other peoples a Bitterblood wears gloves and a coat of wax on the skin, and carries a cup of their own.
Races.Lore:
One of the Old Realms lay in the wet tropics, and its court ruled by poison. Every heir came to the throne over the bodies of the others. The dynasty wanted tasters who could not be killed at the table. Over forty generations the court alchemists raised a caste of servants on rising doses of every venom, root and mineral in the kingdom, and worked the tolerance into the blood, so that it was passed to the children.

They did it too well. The tasters became proof against poison, and then they became poison. A king died of a cup that a taster had sipped from first. A prince died of a kiss. The makers had given the caste its colours so that anyone at court could tell a taster at sight, as a livery worn in the skin. The court now read those colours as a threat, and ordered the caste destroyed.

The tasters fled into the swamp forest and the mangroves, where the fevers killed the soldiers sent after them and did not touch the fugitives. The dynasty starved in the Ashen Years. The Bitterbloods did not, because they can eat what poisons everyone else: bitter roots raw, toadstools, puffer fish, the frogs of the forest floor. No one has ever competed with them for their food.

Races.Name: Catfolk
Races.Description:
Apart from the ears, the tail and the eyes, a Catfolk looks like a human. The skin is human skin, bare and smooth, with no fur on the face or the body. There are no whiskers, no muzzle and no claws: the nose, the mouth, the teeth, the hands and the nails are human. They are lean, a little under middling height, and light on their feet.

The ears are a cat's ears: upright, pointed and furred, set high on the head. A Catfolk has no other ears, and the sides of the head are smooth under the hair. The ears turn toward a sound. The tail is as long as the leg, furred all over, and never quite still. Ears and tail show what the person feels, and a Catfolk cannot stop them.

The colouring follows the cat. The skin runs through the colours of a cat's coat: cream, sand, tawny gold, russet, warm brown, smoke grey and near black. The hair is human hair, worn at any length, in black, brown, sand, ginger, grey or white, and often in two of them, streaked or patched. The fur of the ears and the tail matches the hair, sometimes with a darker tip or with rings. The eyes are amber, gold, copper, green or pale blue, brighter than a human's, and now and then one of each. The pupil is a cat's: an upright slit in daylight, wide and round in the dark. They wear light, loose clothes cut to leave the tail free, and nothing that covers the ears.
Races.Lore:
The Catfolk were human once. They were the granary keepers of the Old Realms. Every city of that age lived on its stores, and a guild of wardens watched them, with cats to keep down the mice. Their patron was a small goddess of the storehouse, the Small Huntress, who has a cat's head in the old carvings.

In the Ashen Years the stores were all a city had. In the second year without a summer the mice and the rats bred in the granaries, and the wardens starved beside the grain they guarded. Their story is that they went to the Small Huntress and asked for two things: to keep the stores from the vermin, and to keep them from themselves. She gave both. The children born that winter had her ears and her tail. They heard a mouse through a wall, and they could not eat bread. The Catfolk call them the First Litter.

A warden who cannot eat grain can be trusted with it. By the Catfolk account, the cities that came through the Ashen Years with their stores whole were the ones that kept such wardens, and the charters date from then. A grain town gives its Catfolk meat and fish, and they keep the town's stores. This is the Warden's Portion, and many towns of the Scattered Age still pay it.

Not all of them stayed. When the Old Realms broke, most wardens had no city left to serve. They went out into the open grassland, where the game was, and became hunters. The two kinds, the wards of the towns and the bands of the grassland, still count themselves one people and marry between them.

Vocations.Name: Farmer

Variants.Name: ploughman
Variants.Description: Walks behind a heavy wooden plough and a team of oxen, one hand on the stilt and a goad in the other. Mud to the knee, a wool tunic and a straw hat.
Variants.Lore: The best-paid hand on a manor, and the one who talks to the oxen more than to his wife. A straight furrow is a man's whole name in the village.

Variants.Name: peasant
Variants.Description: Works a few strips of the village field and owes days on the lord's land. A patched tunic, bare legs, a sickle or a hoe, and a bent back.
Variants.Lore: Bound to the land he works, and the land to him: a lord may sell the manor, but not move the peasant off it. Midlanders count their villages by ploughs, not by people.

Variants.Name: free farmer
Variants.Description: Owns the land he ploughs and owes no lord a day's work. Better fed and better shod than a peasant, with a good knife at the belt and a timber house of his own.
Variants.Lore: Sits in the assembly, bears arms and answers to the law alone. Northmen hold that a people is only as free as its farmers.

Variants.Name: tenant
Variants.Description: Farms rented land and pays for it in coin or grain at the quarter day. Seen with a loaded cart at the lord's barn, or counting sacks against a tally stick.
Variants.Lore: A lease runs for a term of years or of lives, and the quarrels begin when it ends. A good tenant is one the lord forgets he has.

Variants.Name: share-cropper
Variants.Description: Works another's field with another's seed and keeps a share of the crop. The poorest of those who plough: thin, barefoot, with a borrowed hoe.
Variants.Lore: Half the crop goes to the owner before the family eats. In a bad year the debt is carried over, and the children inherit it.

Variants.Name: paddy farmer
Variants.Description: Stands ankle-deep in a flooded field, bent double, setting green seedlings in rows. A wide conical hat, rolled-up trousers, and a water buffalo near by.
Variants.Lore: Canal folk say the empire is a paddy field: it stands as long as every bank is mended by the one who stands on it.

Variants.Name: rice farmer
Variants.Description: Grows rice on terraces and banked fields, and minds the dykes and sluices that water them. Carries a sickle and sheaves of rice on a shoulder pole.
Variants.Lore: On the lands of the Rainkeepers the water is shared by an old schedule, and the one who opens a sluice out of turn is judged by the whole village.

Variants.Name: millet farmer
Variants.Description: Sows millet and sorghum on dry ground with a short-handled hoe after the first rain. Stands among stalks taller than a person, by round granaries of mud and thatch.
Variants.Lore: Sunlanders pour the first beer of the millet on the ground for those who cleared the field. The granary is the wife's, and nobody opens it without her.

Variants.Name: yam farmer
Variants.Description: Heaps earth into mounds with a broad hoe and stakes the yam vines that climb from them. Carries tubers as long as an arm to the yam barn.
Variants.Lore: A man's standing is the size of his yam barn. The new yam is not eaten until the feast that opens it, however hungry the house is.

Vocations.Description: Works arable land: ploughs, sows, weeds, reaps and threshes, and keeps a few animals and a garden beside it. Most farmers feed their own house first and owe the rest to a lord, a temple or the market.
Vocations.Lore: The common estate, the measure against which every other standing is set. Bound by custom more than by law: the days owed on the lord's land, the common field, the village assembly. Harvest and sowing rule the year and its feasts. The conflicts are with the lord over dues, with the herder over trampled crops, with the miller over his toll. Fantasy twists: a people that will not plough (the Catfolk), a people that works only by day (the Noonfolk), land whose yield a seer blesses.

Vocations.Name: Gardener

Variants.Name: orchard keeper
Variants.Description: Tends rows of fruit trees: prunes in winter, props laden boughs and picks from a ladder. A pruning knife, a basket on the arm and a straw hat.
Variants.Lore: Halflings plant an apple tree at a birth and judge the grown child by the tree. An orchard is wassailed in midwinter with cider and noise.

Variants.Name: vine dresser
Variants.Description: Works a vineyard on a sunny slope: ties the vines to stakes, cuts them back with a hooked knife, and carries grapes in a tall basket on the back.
Variants.Lore: A vineyard is planted for one's grandchildren. The vintage is the one harvest that a whole town turns out for, and is paid in drink.

Variants.Name: olive grower
Variants.Description: Keeps a grove of grey, twisted olive trees on terraces of dry stone. At harvest beats the branches with long poles over cloths spread on the ground.
Variants.Lore: To cut down an enemy's olive trees is a crime in every law of the dry south, because it punishes people not yet born.

Variants.Name: date gardener
Variants.Description: Tends date palms in an oasis garden watered by small channels. Climbs the trunk with a rope sling to dust the flowers and cut the bunches.
Variants.Lore: Saltroad folk say a palm must have its feet in water and its head in fire. A garden is inherited by the tree, and a single palm can have six owners.

Variants.Name: spice grower
Variants.Description: Grows pepper vines, ginger, cardamom or clove trees in shaded hill gardens. Dries the crop on mats in the sun, in a cloud of its scent.
Variants.Lore: The growers have never seen the price their crop fetches at the far end of the road, and the merchants take care that they do not.

Variants.Name: tea grower
Variants.Description: Picks the young leaves from rows of low tea bushes on a misty hillside, into a basket on the back. A wide hat and quick fingers.
Variants.Lore: Canal folk pick the first leaves before the spring rain and send them to the court. What the pickers drink is the dust that is left.

Variants.Name: coffee grower
Variants.Description: Tends coffee shrubs under shade trees on a highland slope, picks the red berries by hand and dries them on raised mats.
Variants.Lore: The drink came down from the highlands with the scholars of the Saltroad folk, who wanted to stay awake over their books.

Variants.Name: tobacco grower
Variants.Description: Grows broad-leaved tobacco in neat plots and hangs the leaves in an airy barn to cure brown. Often seen with a clay pipe of the crop.
Variants.Lore: Halflings grow the best leaf and name each field's crop like a vintage. Their elders settle disputes over a pipe, and nobody may speak until it is lit.

Variants.Name: dye-plant grower
Variants.Description: Grows woad, madder, weld or indigo for the dyers. Hands and forearms are stained blue, red or yellow to the elbow.
Variants.Lore: A woad grower is known by blue hands at any market, and a town that lives by one dye plant guards its seed like coin.

Variants.Name: silk grower
Variants.Description: Keeps mulberry trees and feeds their leaves to trays of pale silkworms indoors. Reels the thread from cocoons floating in a pan of hot water.
Variants.Lore: The Canal folk kept the worm a secret for a thousand years, on pain of death. The rooms are kept quiet: the worms are said to stop eating at a quarrel.

Variants.Name: beekeeper
Variants.Description: Keeps bees in straw skeps or hollow logs at the edge of a garden. Wears a veil of cloth over a wide hat and carries a smoking pot.
Variants.Lore: The bees must be told of a death or a wedding in the house, or they leave. Stillfaces keep bees without smoke and are thought uncanny for it.

Variants.Name: mushroom grower
Variants.Description: Grows mushrooms on beds of dung and straw in cellars, caves and old mine galleries. Works by lamplight with a small knife and a shallow basket.
Variants.Lore: Dwarves and Gnomes grew mushrooms in the dark through the Ashen Years, and have not forgotten who came begging at the gate.

Variants.Name: seedsman
Variants.Description: Raises plants for their seed, sorts it and sells it in small labelled bags. A neat stall of jars, sieves and paper packets.
Variants.Lore: Gnomes keep seed lists that go back to the Old Realms and will sell any seed but the last of a kind.

Variants.Name: grafter
Variants.Description: Joins a twig of a good tree to the stock of a hardy one, binds it with bast and seals it with wax. Carries a small sharp knife and a bundle of cuttings.
Variants.Lore: Gnome grafters set three kinds of apple on one tree for show. Elves call grafting a forced marriage and will not eat the fruit.

Vocations.Description: Tends trees, vines and gardens: crops that stand for years or need daily care, and that are sold more than eaten at home.
Vocations.Lore: Patient work with a long horizon: an olive tree outlives its planter. Orchards and vineyards are wealth that an army can destroy in a day, so gardeners favour peace and strong walls. The luxury crops are regional secrets, guarded by a town or a lineage. Fantasy twists: a grove that only one people can tend, a poison garden, a spice whose source is kept off every map.

Vocations.Name: Herder

Variants.Name: shepherd
Variants.Description: Minds a flock of sheep on open pasture with a crook and a dog. A heavy cloak, a felt hat, a bag of bread and a horn or a pipe.
Variants.Lore: Alone for weeks with the flock, the stars and a pipe. Half the songs of any people were made by shepherds, and half the prophets were shepherds first.

Variants.Name: cowherd
Variants.Description: Drives the village cattle to pasture at dawn and home at dusk, with a long stick and a horn. Boots thick with mud and dung.
Variants.Lore: Sunlanders count wealth, marriage and blood-price in cattle, and a herder knows each beast by name and by song.

Variants.Name: swineherd
Variants.Description: Keeps a herd of bristly pigs in the wood and beats acorns down from the oaks for them in autumn. A long staff, a horn and a ragged tunic.
Variants.Lore: The lowest of the herders in every tale, and the one who turns out to be a lost prince. Pannage in the lord's wood is paid for by the pig.

Variants.Name: goatherd
Variants.Description: Follows a herd of goats over stony hillsides where nothing else can graze. Lean and sunburnt, with a staff, a sling and a waterskin.
Variants.Lore: Dwarves keep goats on the high pastures above the hold and send their young up with them for a summer, to learn the sky.

Variants.Name: reindeer herder
Variants.Description: Moves with a herd of reindeer between forest and tundra. Dressed in furs and embroidered wool, with a lasso, a sled and a tent of hides.
Variants.Lore: The herd decides where the people go, and the herder follows. Asking the size of a herd is as rude as asking the weight of a purse.

Variants.Name: yak herder
Variants.Description: Keeps shaggy yaks on high cold pasture above the tree line. A thick sheepskin coat, a felt hat, a sling, and a black tent of yak hair.
Variants.Lore: Hearthbloods herd where no one else can stand the cold, and burn the dung to feed the fire outside as they feed the one within.

Variants.Name: nomad herder
Variants.Description: Lives in a felt tent and moves with the herds by the season, on horseback. Owns only what a pack animal can carry, and counts wealth in heads.
Variants.Lore: Grass riders say a man who builds a wall has already been conquered. The tent is the wife's, the herd is the family's, and the grass is no one's.

Variants.Name: dairymaid
Variants.Description: Milks the cows morning and evening and churns the cream to butter. A wooden pail, a yoke over the shoulders, a three-legged stool and rolled sleeves.
Variants.Lore: The one servant on a farm with a room that is kept clean. Milk turns in thunder, and when it turns without thunder someone is blamed for a look.

Variants.Name: cheesemaker
Variants.Description: Curdles milk in a great kettle, presses the curd in wooden hoops and turns the wheels of cheese on the shelves of a cool cellar.
Variants.Lore: Halflings age a wheel for each child born and cut it at the wedding. A cheese that old is a boast and a risk.

Variants.Name: horse breeder
Variants.Description: Keeps mares and a stallion on good pasture and raises foals for sale. Judges a horse by its legs and teeth, and wears riding boots every day.
Variants.Lore: Among the Grass riders a bloodline of horses is recited like a bloodline of khans, and is often longer.

Variants.Name: horse breaker
Variants.Description: Tames young horses to the halter, the saddle and the cart, with a long rein in a round pen. Wiry and patient, and often limping.
Variants.Lore: The gentle breakers are the ones people pay for, and the Stillfaces are the best of them: a horse cannot read fear on a face that never moves.

Variants.Name: camel breeder
Variants.Description: Raises camels at the desert edge for milk, wool and the caravans. Robed and veiled against the dust, with a riding stick and a string of animals.
Variants.Lore: Saltroad folk hold that a camel remembers every wrong and waits. A breeder sells the beast and keeps the right to its first calf.

Vocations.Description: Keeps animals on pasture and moves with them: guards, breeds, milks, shears and drives to market.
Vocations.Lore: Lives apart from the village for much of the year, on the summer pasture or the open range, and is thought half wild for it. Wealth is counted in heads. Whole peoples are herders and scorn the plough. The conflicts are over grazing rights, wells, rustling and winter fodder. Fantasy twists: herds of beasts no farmer could keep, mounts bred for one clan only.

Vocations.Name: Fisher

Variants.Name: sea fisher
Variants.Description: Goes out in an open boat with nets and long lines, by sail and oar. Salt-stiff wool, an oiled leather apron, and hands scarred by line and hook.
Variants.Lore: No whistling in the boat, no priest on the quay, no word for the animals of the land while at sea. Northmen name the boat before the child.

Variants.Name: river fisher
Variants.Description: Fishes a river from a flat boat or the bank, with a cast net, wicker traps and a weir of stakes. Barefoot, with a pole and a creel.
Variants.Lore: A river is owned by the stretch, and the right to a weir is older than most titles. Millers and fishers have been at law since the first dam.

Variants.Name: eel trapper
Variants.Description: Sets long wicker traps in reeds and millponds and spears eels in the mud with a many-pronged fork. Carries the catch alive in a wet basket.
Variants.Lore: Rents were paid in eels by the thousand. Nobody knows where the eels come from, and the trappers say they would rather not know.

Variants.Name: shellfish gatherer
Variants.Description: Walks the shore at low tide with a rake, a knife and a basket, for mussels, cockles and oysters. Skirts tucked up and bare feet in the mud.
Variants.Lore: Poor people's work, done by women and children between the tides. The shell heaps behind a shore village are older than the village.

Variants.Name: crab catcher
Variants.Description: Sets baited pots of wicker among the rocks and hauls them by rope from a small boat. The catch goes to market alive, with bound claws.
Variants.Lore: Pots are marked with the owner's knot, and to lift another's pot is the one theft a fishing village does not forgive.

Variants.Name: shrimp catcher
Variants.Description: Pushes a wide net on a frame through the shallows, wading to the waist or behind a horse. Boils the shrimp in a cauldron on the beach.
Variants.Lore: Shoalfolk children take the push net out at the first ebb they can stand in. The catch is boiled on the sand and sold before it cools.

Variants.Name: whaler
Variants.Description: Hunts whales from an open boat with a harpoon on a long line, and cuts the blubber on the shore. Greasy leather, an iron lance and a hard face.
Variants.Lore: Northmen divide a whale by law: so much to the harpooner, so much to the boat, so much to the shore it lands on. The shares are older than their kings.

Variants.Name: sealer
Variants.Description: Hunts seals on ice and skerries with a club, a harpoon and a knife. Dressed in sealskin, dragging the kill on a small sled.
Variants.Lore: The Hoarkin ask the seal's leave at the breathing hole and give its first drink of fresh water back to the dead animal, so that it returns.

Variants.Name: pearl diver
Variants.Description: Dives without air to the oyster beds, with a stone weight on the foot, a nose clip and a net bag. Lean and deep-chested, with reddened eyes.
Variants.Lore: A Shoalfolk diver counts a life in dives, not years. Deaf by thirty, most of them, and proud of it.

Variants.Name: sponge diver
Variants.Description: Dives naked from a small boat with a knife and a flat stone, and cuts sponges from the sea floor. The catch dries in strings on the mast.
Variants.Lore: The divers go down holding a flat stone and come up when the lungs say so. A village counts its widows after every season.

Variants.Name: coral diver
Variants.Description: Brings up branches of red coral from deep rock, by diving or with a weighted wooden cross hung with nets and dragged from a boat.
Variants.Lore: Red coral is hung on children against the evil eye. The divers do not wear it: they say the sea knows its own.

Variants.Name: fish drier
Variants.Description: Splits and guts fish and hangs them by the tail on wooden racks in the wind, or lays them salted on the rocks. Works with a broad knife, among gulls.
Variants.Lore: Dried cod is the bread of the north and keeps for years. The Hoarkin dry fish through the light half of the year, to wake to in the dark half.

Vocations.Description: Takes food and goods from water: with net, line, trap and spear, from a boat or the shore, and by diving.
Vocations.Lore: A hard and uncertain living with its own saints and taboos: words not said at sea, days on which no boat goes out. The catch spoils in a day, so the fisher depends on the salter and the fishmonger. Fishing villages are poor, close and suspicious of the land. Fantasy twists: a people that dives where others drown, things in the net that should not be.

Vocations.Name: Hunter

Variants.Name: hunter
Variants.Description: Hunts game with bow, spear and hounds. Dressed in green and brown wool and leather, with a horn and a long knife at the belt.
Variants.Lore: In the lord's forest the same deed is sport for one man and a hanging for another. A hunter gives the first cut to whoever helped, even if only by keeping quiet.

Variants.Name: trapper
Variants.Description: Sets snares, pits and deadfalls for fur and meat along a line walked every few days. Carries a pack of pelts stretched on hoops.
Variants.Lore: A trap line is property, handed from father to son, and to walk another's line is to ask for a fight. Northmen pay their dues to the south in pelts.

Variants.Name: fowler
Variants.Description: Catches wild birds with nets, limed twigs, decoys and a caller's whistle, in marsh and hedgerow. Carries cages and a pole of dead birds.
Variants.Lore: Paid by the dozen for the lord's table and fined for the same birds on his own. The fowler's whistle is banned in some towns as a thief's signal.

Variants.Name: falconer
Variants.Description: Trains hawks and falcons to hunt and carries one hooded on a thick leather glove. Wears a pouch of meat, a lure on a cord and small bells.
Variants.Lore: A falcon marks its owner's rank more surely than a ring: the law says which bird a king, a lord and a priest may fly. The falconer outranks the cook.

Variants.Name: forager
Variants.Description: Gathers what the wild land gives: nuts, berries, mushrooms, roots and herbs. A basket on the back, a digging stick and a sharp eye.
Variants.Lore: Every village has one who knows where the morels come up and will not say. Elves forage without leaving a sign that they passed.

Variants.Name: honey hunter
Variants.Description: Climbs trees and cliffs to wild bees' nests on ropes of bark, with a smoking torch and a long knife. Comes down with combs in a bark pail.
Variants.Lore: A bird leads the hunter to the nest and is owed its share of the comb. Those who cheat the bird are led to a snake the next time, the Sunlanders say.

Variants.Name: tracker
Variants.Description: Reads the ground for prints, droppings and broken twigs, and follows a beast or a person for days. Travels light and crouches often.
Variants.Lore: Duskreaders track by the warmth a foot leaves on cold sand and can tell how long ago it passed. Courts hire them and do not ask how.

Variants.Name: guide
Variants.Description: Leads strangers through wild land by ways not on any map: the pass, the ford, the safe spring. A staff, a worn cloak and a coil of rope.
Variants.Lore: A guide's word is law on the way, even over a lord. One who loses a traveller does not find work again.

Variants.Name: scout
Variants.Description: Goes ahead of an army or a caravan to see and not be seen. Lightly armed, in dull colours, on foot or on a small quick horse.
Variants.Lore: Widegaze scouts are hired by both sides of the same war and keep to a rule: never report on the one who paid first.

Variants.Name: ratcatcher
Variants.Description: Clears houses, barns and ships of rats with terriers, ferrets, traps and poison. Carries a pole hung with dead rats as a sign.
Variants.Lore: Catfolk hold the trade in every granary town, and are suspected of leaving a breeding pair behind to keep it.

Variants.Name: monster hunter
Variants.Description: Hunts the beasts that hunt people, for a bounty. Scarred, in mismatched armour, with a heavy spear, silvered blades, nets and flasks of oil.
Variants.Lore: The guilds price a contract by the beast and by the widow's share. Few hunters grow old, and the old ones teach.

Vocations.Description: Lives from the wild land: hunts, traps, gathers, and knows the way through it.
Vocations.Lore: Free where the game is free, a poacher where the lord has claimed it. Hunting is the sport of nobles and the bread of the poor, and the two meet in the courts. The hunter is the one who knows the pass, the ford and the safe spring, and is hired for that knowledge by caravans and armies. Fantasy twists: prey that hunts back, a guild that takes contracts on beasts, a people that tracks by scent.

Vocations.Name: Forester

Variants.Name: woodcutter
Variants.Description: Fells and lops small timber and coppice with an axe and a billhook, and carries it out on the back. A poor man in a patched hood.
Variants.Lore: The hero of half the tales and the poorest man in them. He has the right to dead wood, by hook or by crook, and no more.

Variants.Name: lumberjack
Variants.Description: Fells great trees with a long axe and a two-man saw, and hauls the logs with oxen or floats them down a river. Broad-shouldered, in spiked boots.
Variants.Lore: The crews winter in the forest and come down with the logs in spring, with a season's pay and a season's thirst.

Variants.Name: sawyer
Variants.Description: Saws logs into planks over a pit, one man on top of the log and one below in the dust, with a long two-handed saw.
Variants.Lore: Top sawyer and bottom sawyer: one has the skill and the air, the other the sawdust in his eyes. It is a saying for every unequal partnership.

Variants.Name: forest warden
Variants.Description: The lord's officer in the wood: rides its bounds, marks the trees that may fall and fines those who cut or hunt unasked. A green coat, a horn, a bow and a badge.
Variants.Lore: The most hated officer of any lord. Forest law takes a hand for a deer, and half the outlaws in the greenwood were made by a warden.

Variants.Name: grove warden
Variants.Description: Keeps an old or holy wood where no axe may go. Walks it barefoot with a staff, knows every tree, and turns strangers back at its edge.
Variants.Lore: Amberbloods keep the groves where their dead stand as trees. A warden knows each one by its living name.

Variants.Name: resin tapper
Variants.Description: Cuts slanting notches in pine trunks and hangs small pots under them to catch the resin. Sticky hands, a scraping iron and a yoke of pails.
Variants.Lore: Amberbloods will tap a pine and will not let it be bled dry: they know what it is to have resin for blood.

Variants.Name: tree shaper
Variants.Description: Bends, binds and grafts living trees over many years until they grow into arches, bridges and halls. Works with cords, wedges and great patience.
Variants.Lore: An Elf begins a hall that the grandchildren of its first guests will sit in. No other people has the years for the craft.

Variants.Name: firewood seller
Variants.Description: Brings bundled faggots and split logs to town on a donkey or on the back, and cries them in the street.
Variants.Lore: The price of faggots is the first thing a town council fixes in a hard winter, and the firewood seller the first to be accused of hoarding.

Vocations.Description: Fells, hauls and saws timber, cuts firewood, and keeps the wood: plants, coppices and guards it.
Vocations.Lore: Two faces. The woodcutter is a poor man with an axe. The forester is the lord's officer who fines him. Forest law is hated law. Old woods have their own rules about which tree may fall. Fantasy twists: woods with a will, elder trees worth a ship each, peoples who judge every felling.

Vocations.Name: Miner

Variants.Name: ore miner
Variants.Description: Follows a vein underground with a pick, a hammer and iron wedges, by the light of a tallow lamp. A leather cap, a hooded tunic and a leather seat.
Variants.Lore: Free miners answer to their own court and to no lord, in most lands. They leave a share of bread for whatever knocks in the dark, and do not whistle underground.

Variants.Name: prospector
Variants.Description: Walks the hills looking for signs of ore: stained rock, heavy gravel, the plants that grow over metal. Carries a small pick, a pan and a bag of samples.
Variants.Lore: Dwarves register a find at the gate of the hold before telling their own kin. A prospector's map is the one thing a Dwarf will lie about.

Variants.Name: gold washer
Variants.Description: Stands in a cold stream and swirls gravel in a wide wooden pan or over a fleece, for the flecks of gold left behind.
Variants.Lore: Sunlanders wash gold from the rivers in the dry season, and what a woman finds in her pan is hers alone.

Variants.Name: tin streamer
Variants.Description: Digs the gravel of a valley floor and washes it in a channel of running water until the heavy black tin stone is left.
Variants.Lore: The tinners have their own parliament and their own gaol. Their washings silt the harbours downstream, and the lawsuits are as old as the works.

Variants.Name: coal miner
Variants.Description: Cuts coal from a low seam lying on one side, black from head to foot, and drags it out in a basket or a sled.
Variants.Lore: Smiths wanted the coal and towns banned its smoke. The colliers live apart and marry among themselves, like the charcoal burners before them.

Variants.Name: gem miner
Variants.Description: Digs narrow pits and sieves the gravel for rough stones, or chisels them from a rock face. Keeps the finds in a pouch tied inside the shirt.
Variants.Lore: The pit owner searches the miners at the end of the day, and the miners have a hundred ways to swallow a stone.

Variants.Name: crystal miner
Variants.Description: Climbs to clefts high in the mountains and levers clear crystals from their pockets with an iron bar. In a world with magic, also digs the crystals that hold it.
