Variants.Description: Tends the sick in a hospital or a house of healing: washes, feeds, changes dressings and watches through the night.
Variants.Lore: Hospitals are houses of the faith, and the nursing is done by those under a vow. In a plague the nurses stay when the physicians leave.

Variants.Name: herbalist
Variants.Description: Gathers and dries healing plants and makes them into teas, salves and poultices. Bunches of herbs hang from every beam of the house.
Variants.Lore: Elven herbalists have had three human lifetimes to learn the plants. The village herbalist has her grandmother's word, and one accusation between her and the fire.

Vocations.Description: Treats the sick, the wounded and women in childbed: with herbs, the knife, the hand and advice.
Vocations.Lore: Three ranks that despise each other. The learned physician reads and prescribes and never cuts. The barber-surgeon cuts, bleeds and shaves. The village healer and the midwife know herbs and are one accusation away from being called witches. Plague makes and breaks them all. Fantasy twists: healing that works, and its price.

Vocations.Name: Servant

Variants.Name: maid
Variants.Description: A woman servant who sweeps, fetches water, makes the beds and tends the fires. A plain dress, an apron and a linen cap.
Variants.Lore: Hired by the year at the autumn fair, with a mop in her hand to show her work. Most leave to marry, with what they have saved.

Variants.Name: manservant
Variants.Description: A man servant who carries, waits at table, runs errands and guards the door, in the livery colours of the house.
Variants.Lore: Wears his master's colours and takes his master's quarrels with them. In a great house the livery fights the livery of the house across the street.

Variants.Name: cook
Variants.Description: Rules the kitchen of a household: roasts, boils and bakes for the table of the master, and orders the kitchen boys about.
Variants.Lore: The best-paid servant of a great house, and the one a rival tries to hire away. A lord who fears poison is very polite to the cook.

Variants.Name: groom
Variants.Description: Feeds, brushes, saddles and walks the horses of a household, and sleeps in the stable loft.
Variants.Lore: Sleeps over the horses and is the first to know when the master rides, and where. Grass riders make the best grooms and the worst servants.

Variants.Name: nurse
Variants.Description: Looks after the children of a household, from the cradle until they are given to a tutor.
Variants.Lore: The nurse raises the heir and is kept for life. Great men have been ruled from the nursery long after they left it.

Variants.Name: wet nurse
Variants.Description: Suckles another woman's child for pay, in the family's house or her own. Chosen for health and good temper.
Variants.Lore: The child she feeds and her own are milk kin, and in many lands may not marry. A prince's milk brother is the one man he trusts.

Variants.Name: laundress
Variants.Description: Washes linen at the river or in a tub with lye and a beating bat, and spreads it on the grass to bleach. Red, chapped hands.
Variants.Lore: The washing place is the women's parliament. A laundress knows a household's linen and so its sicknesses, its births and its guests.

Variants.Name: valet
Variants.Description: Serves one master in person: dresses and shaves him, keeps his clothes and his chamber, and travels with him.
Variants.Lore: No man is a hero to the one who dresses him. The valet carries the letters that the secretary may not see.

Variants.Name: page
Variants.Description: A boy of good family who serves in a noble house to learn its manners: carries messages, pours wine and holds the cloak.
Variants.Lore: Sent from home at seven to learn another house's manners, and to be a pledge of his father's good conduct.

Variants.Name: taster
Variants.Description: Eats and drinks of every dish before the lord does, as proof against poison. Stands at the lord's shoulder at table.
Variants.Lore: Bitterbloods cannot die of a poisoned dish and can name what was in it, so every court that fears the cup hires one. Halflings taste for the pleasure, and for the cook's honour.

Variants.Name: household steward
Variants.Description: Runs a great household: keeps the keys, the stores and the accounts, and hires and commands the other servants. A staff of office and a sober gown.
Variants.Lore: Rules a hundred servants and stands behind one chair. A lord's house is as honest as its steward, and no more.

Vocations.Description: Works in another's household for board, lodging and a small wage: in the house, the kitchen, the stable and the yard.
Vocations.Lore: Service is a stage of life as much as a class: the young of the poor, and of the not so poor, serve in another house until they marry. A great household is a small court with its own ranks. The servant sees everything and is seen by no one, which makes the vocation the natural spy.

Vocations.Name: Entertainer

Variants.Name: minstrel
Variants.Description: Sings and plays the lute, the fiddle or the pipe at feasts, fairs and inns. Bright travelling clothes and an instrument slung on the back.
Variants.Lore: Classed with vagabonds by the law and seated by the fire by the lord. A minstrel carries news and can pass any gate, which is why half of them are spies.

Variants.Name: bard
Variants.Description: A trained poet-singer who keeps the songs, the laws and the lineages of a people in the head, and is honoured for it at a lord's table.
Variants.Lore: Twelve years of training, and a satire that can raise blisters on a king. A lord who refuses a bard hospitality is finished in three verses.

Variants.Name: harper
Variants.Description: Plays the harp, on the knee or standing, and sings to it. Keeps the instrument in a leather bag and the fingernails long.
Variants.Lore: Among the Elves the harper sits beside the lord and is the people's memory. A harper's hands are protected by a law of their own.

Variants.Name: singer
Variants.Description: Sings for pay, alone or in a choir: in a temple, at a court or in the street.
Variants.Lore: A good voice lifts a peasant's child into a temple choir, and from there to anywhere. It is the one ladder with no toll.

Variants.Name: drummer
Variants.Description: Plays drums for dances, processions and war, and in some lands sends news from village to village by drum.
Variants.Lore: Sunlander drums speak: a message crosses a kingdom in a day. Certain drums belong to the king alone, and are fed like guests.

Variants.Name: praise-singer
Variants.Description: Sings the deeds and the ancestors of a patron, from memory, at every public moment. Can make a name, and unmake it.
Variants.Lore: A hereditary class among the Sunlanders, who keep the genealogies and may say anything. A king without a praise-singer has no past.

Variants.Name: storyteller
Variants.Description: Tells tales to a ring of listeners in a market or a coffee house, with voice and gesture, and stops for coins at the best moment.
Variants.Lore: Stops at the moment of greatest danger and passes the bowl. The tale has been going for forty nights, and the listeners know it by heart.

Variants.Name: poet
Variants.Description: Makes verses to order for weddings, victories and funerals, and recites them. Lives on the gifts of patrons.
Variants.Lore: Northmen pay a poet in gold rings and remember the price in the next poem. A bad verse about a king has cost a poet his head, and a good one has bought it back.

Variants.Name: actor
Variants.Description: Plays parts on a cart or a scaffold stage, in masks and borrowed finery, with a travelling company.
Variants.Lore: Refused burial in holy ground in some lands and kept by kings in others. Swiftborn players learn a part in a night and have played every age of a life by twenty.

Variants.Name: acrobat
Variants.Description: Tumbles, juggles, balances and walks on the hands in the street and at feasts, in tight bright clothes.
Variants.Lore: A family trade, taught from the cradle. The preachers call it the devil's and the crowd pays to see for itself.

Variants.Name: rope dancer
Variants.Description: Walks, leaps and dances on a rope stretched high between two poles or towers, with a long pole for balance.
Variants.Lore: Catfolk walk the rope as others walk a street, and the troupes would rather hire one than train ten.

Variants.Name: dancer
Variants.Description: Dances for an audience, alone or in a troupe, to drum and pipe, in flowing clothes with bells at the ankles.
Variants.Lore: Rainkeeper temple dancers are born to it and are wed to the god. Elsewhere the dance is for a wedding, and everyone joins in by the third cup.

Variants.Name: jester
Variants.Description: A lord's fool: mocks, jokes and tumbles, in a motley coat and a cap with bells, with a bauble on a stick. May say what no one else dares.
Variants.Lore: The fool alone may tell the king the truth, and must make him laugh while he does. An old fool is kept on, like an old hound.

Variants.Name: wrestler
Variants.Description: Fights for prizes at fairs and courts, by grip and throw. Thick-necked, stripped to the waist and oiled or belted.
Variants.Lore: Grass riders hold wrestling as one of the three skills of a man. Hearthbloods wrestle in the snow to keep warm, and villages bet a winter's grain on them.

Vocations.Description: Performs for pay: sings, plays, tells, acts, tumbles, dances or wrestles.
Vocations.Lore: Masterless and on the road, so classed with vagabonds; yet the same person at a court is a poet with a pension. Entertainers carry news and reputations between courts, and a mocking song can do a lord more harm than a raid. Fantasy twists: songs that bind, a people that lives a whole career in seven years.

Vocations.Name: Courtesan

Variants.Name: courtesan
Variants.Description: A companion of the rich, admired for wit, music and beauty, who keeps a fine house and chooses the guests. Dressed above the law's allowance.
Variants.Lore: Educated beyond any wife of the city. Ministers visit her salon to hear what other ministers said, and she is taxed more than a merchant.

Variants.Name: companion
Variants.Description: Hired to keep company at table, on a journey or through an evening: talks, plays, sings and listens.
Variants.Lore: Hired for conversation, and good at it. A Stillface companion gives nothing away by the face, which half the clients find restful and half unnerving.

Variants.Name: kept mistress
Variants.Description: Lives in a house paid for by one lover, outside marriage, with servants and fine clothes, for as long as the favour lasts.
Variants.Lore: Has everything but a contract. A wise one buys the house in her own name within the first year.

Variants.Name: prostitute
Variants.Description: Sells the bed in a licensed house or a back street, and wears the mark the town lays down: a striped hood, a yellow ribbon.
Variants.Lore: Licensed, taxed, marked by law and preached against, often by the same council in the same year. The town's rent from the house repairs its bridge.

Variants.Name: bathhouse attendant
Variants.Description: Serves in a bathhouse: carries water, scrubs backs, brings wine, and for a coin more keeps the guest company.
Variants.Lore: The bathhouse guild insists its members only scrub backs. The town clerk records the insistence each year.

Variants.Name: brothel keeper
Variants.Description: Runs a public house of the trade: holds the licence, the keys and the debts of those who work there.
Variants.Lore: Holds the lease from the town, the bishop or a lord, and pays the watch not to look. Holds the debts of those inside, which is the real lock on the door.

Vocations.Description: Sells company and the bed: from the woman or man of a town's public house to the kept companion of a court, who is paid as much for wit, music and discretion as for anything else.
Vocations.Lore: Tolerated, taxed and despised at once. A town licenses a public house or a street and makes the trade wear a mark; a preacher closes the house and the next council opens it again. At the top the courtesan keeps a salon, reads, plays and is painted, and hears what a minister says when he is off guard, so the vocation is a natural keeper of secrets, beside the servant. Most enter through poverty or are sold into it, and few leave rich. The conflicts are with the church, with the wives of the town and with the keeper who holds the debts. Fantasy twists: a people that changes sex in mid-life, a charm that is more than charm.

Vocations.Name: Noble

Variants.Name: lord
Variants.Description: Holds a castle or a manor and the land around it, judges its people and leads them in war. Fur-lined robes, a signet ring and a sword.
Variants.Lore: Holds his land of someone, and someone holds of him: every lord is another's man. He may hang a thief and may not work with his hands.

Variants.Name: lady
Variants.Description: A noblewoman who rules the household and, when the lord is away, the estate. A long gown, a veil or a headdress, and the keys at her belt.
Variants.Lore: Holds the castle when the lord is away, which is often, and has held it against sieges. Her seal is as good as his, and her memory for kinship is better.

Variants.Name: knight
Variants.Description: A mounted warrior of noble rank, in mail or plate, with lance, sword and a shield painted with his arms. Sworn to a lord and bound by honour.
Variants.Lore: The Midlanders made the knight their ideal: a horse, a harness, a code, and debts to pay for the first two. The songs and the facts have little to say to each other.

Variants.Name: squire
Variants.Description: A young noble who serves a knight, carries his shield, tends his horse and armour, and trains to become one.
Variants.Lore: Seven years of carrying another man's shield. Many stay squires for life, because knighthood costs more than the land brings in.

Variants.Name: landholder
Variants.Description: A lesser noble with one manor: lives on its rents, rides to the hunt, and sits as a justice in the district.
Variants.Lore: The backbone of every county and the despair of every king: too many to ignore, and too poor to buy.

Variants.Name: chief
Variants.Description: The head of a clan or a tribe, by birth and by the consent of the elders. Known by a staff, a cloak or a headdress, and sits in the high seat of the hall.
Variants.Lore: Among the Orcs the chief leads in war and the hearth-mother rules in peace. A chief who loses the elders loses the hall.

Variants.Name: jarl
Variants.Description: A northern lord of ships and halls, in a fur cloak, with gold rings on the arms. Feasts his sworn warriors and leads them over the sea.
Variants.Lore: A Northman jarl is as great as his generosity: a ring-giver. A jarl who hoards is left by his men within the winter.

Variants.Name: khan
Variants.Description: The lord of a herding people of the open plains. Rules from the saddle and from a great felt tent, in silk and fur, with a banner of horse tails.
Variants.Lore: Raised on a felt carpet by the assembly of the Grass riders. Every few generations one khan is raised over all the others, and the settled lands learn his name.

Variants.Name: title-holder
Variants.Description: Holds a title and a seat on a council by rank or purchase. Known by the staff, the cap, the beads or the stool of the title.
Variants.Lore: Among the Sunlanders the title-holders sit as a council that can depose a king. A title is earned, bought or inherited, and each must be fed with gifts.

Variants.Name: head of a great house
Variants.Description: Leads a great family, its lands, its marriages and its feuds, and speaks for it before the ruler. Wears the arms of the house and its oldest jewels.
Variants.Lore: The Twofold give the house to its eldest, who has been both its son and its mother, and count that the only way to know a family.

Vocations.Description: Holds land and people by right of birth or grant: rules, judges, leads in war and lives from rents and dues.
Vocations.Lore: Those who fight, in the old division of society into those who pray, fight and work. Honour, lineage and land are the whole of life, and each is defended with the sword and the lawsuit. A noble who works with his hands loses the rank. Younger sons go to the temple, to war or to the bad. Fantasy twists: houses of another race, bloodlines with a gift or a curse.

Vocations.Name: Official

Variants.Name: steward
Variants.Description: Runs a lord's lands in his name: rides between manors, holds the manor court and audits the accounts. Well dressed, with a staff of office and a clerk.
Variants.Lore: The lord's other self, and often his creditor. A steward who has served three lords of a house knows more of it than any of them did.

Variants.Name: bailiff
Variants.Description: The lord's man on one manor: sees the work done, collects the rents and seizes the goods of those who do not pay.
Variants.Lore: The face of the lord that the village actually sees. The risings begin by burning the bailiff's rolls, and sometimes the bailiff.

Variants.Name: reeve
Variants.Description: A villager chosen for the year to oversee the lord's harvest and answer for it. A peasant with a white rod and a tally stick.
Variants.Lore: A peasant set over peasants for a year, who answers with his own goods for the lord's harvest. No one wants the office and no one may refuse it.

Variants.Name: hayward
Variants.Description: Guards the hedges, the crops and the common meadow against straying beasts, and blows a horn at a trespass.
Variants.Lore: Takes straying beasts to the pound and is cursed for it. His horn at harvest is the signal to begin, and his sheaf is the first.

Variants.Name: magistrate
Variants.Description: Keeps the peace of a town or a district: hears small cases, fines, and sends the rest to the judge.
Variants.Lore: Canal folk magistrates are chosen by written examination and sent far from home, so that they have no cousins to favour.

Variants.Name: judge
Variants.Description: Hears cases and gives sentence in the ruler's name, from a raised seat, in a robe and a cap, with a clerk writing below.
Variants.Lore: Sits with one empty seat beside him for the ruler whose justice it is. Dwarven judges read the written grudge back to both sides before they begin.

Variants.Name: tax collector
Variants.Description: Goes from door to door with a list, a clerk and a guard, and takes the ruler's due in coin or kind.
Variants.Lore: Farms the tax: pays the ruler a sum and keeps what more he can raise. No trade is more hated, and none is bid for so keenly.

Variants.Name: toll keeper
Variants.Description: Sits at a bridge, a gate or a ford with a bar across the road, and takes a coin for every cart and beast.
Variants.Lore: Every bridge and ford has its toll and its story of the traveller who would not pay. Merchants count a road by its tolls, not its miles.

Variants.Name: customs searcher
Variants.Description: Goes through ships and bales at a harbour or a border for goods that owe duty, with a probing rod and a seal.
Variants.Lore: Takes a share of what he seizes, and a present for what he does not. Smugglers budget for the searcher as for the freight.

Variants.Name: weigh-master
Variants.Description: Keeps the public scales of a market, weighs goods for a fee, and stamps the weights that are true.
Variants.Lore: The town's weights are kept in the temple, and false ones are nailed to the door of the weigh house with their owner's name.

Variants.Name: sworn measurer
Variants.Description: Measures grain, cloth, wine and land under oath, with the town's own measures, and settles quarrels over quantity.
Variants.Lore: A heaped bushel or a struck one: riots have begun over the difference. The measurer's oath is taken on the standard measure itself.

Variants.Name: surveyor
Variants.Description: Measures land with a chain and rods, sets boundary stones and draws the plan.
Variants.Lore: The boundaries are walked each year with the village boys, who are bumped on each stone so that they will remember it.

Variants.Name: mayor
Variants.Description: The head of a town council, chosen by its leading citizens. A chain of office, a furred gown and the town seal.
Variants.Lore: Chosen for a year by the guilds, and usually from the same six families. A mayor answers to the lord for the town and to the town for the lord.

Variants.Name: herald
Variants.Description: Knows every coat of arms, carries a lord's messages in war and peace, and proclaims at tournaments. Wears a short coat with the lord's arms.
Variants.Lore: A herald is safe on any battlefield, and counts the noble dead afterwards by their arms. He decides who may bear what, and is paid for deciding.

Variants.Name: town crier
Variants.Description: Calls out news and orders in the streets, with a bell or a drum and a loud voice.
Variants.Lore: What the crier has called three times is law, and no one may plead that they did not hear. To strike a crier is to strike the town.

Variants.Name: envoy
Variants.Description: Carries a ruler's words to another court and brings back the answer, with letters, gifts and a small retinue.
Variants.Lore: An envoy's person is sacred, and killing one is the oldest cause of war. Lanternkin envoys carry their sovereign's word and their own glowing pledge of it.

Variants.Name: treasurer
Variants.Description: Keeps the chest and the accounts of a ruler, a town or a temple, and counts coin on a chequered cloth.
Variants.Lore: Accounts are reckoned on a chequered cloth with counters, before witnesses. The treasurer is the minister most often hanged at a change of reign.

Variants.Name: gaoler
Variants.Description: Keeps the prison: locks, feeds and guards those held, and takes fees from them for every comfort. A ring of great keys.
Variants.Lore: Unpaid by the town: he lives on what the prisoners pay for a bed, a fire and lighter irons. A rich man's prison is an inn with a lock.

Vocations.Description: Carries out the orders of a ruler, a lord, a town or a temple: collects, counts, judges, inspects and announces.
Vocations.Lore: The reeve was "the pivot man of the manorial system": a peasant, chosen each year, who answered with his own goods for the lord's harvest. Above him the bailiff and the steward ride between manors and audit the rolls. Officials are hated for the tax and needed for the peace, and every one of them is assumed to take a cut. Fantasy twists: an office that passes by examination, a judge who can tell a lie when he hears one.

Vocations.Name: Soldier

Variants.Name: man-at-arms
Variants.Description: A trained fighter in mail and plate, on foot or mounted, with sword, shield and poleaxe. Serves a lord for pay or land.
Variants.Lore: The Midlanders' wars are fought by a few hundred of these and their followers. A harness costs a farm, and is stripped from the dead before they are cold.

Variants.Name: archer
Variants.Description: Shoots a long bow as tall as a person. A padded jacket, an open helmet, a bracer on the arm and a sheaf of arrows at the belt.
Variants.Lore: The Elves put every one of their people behind a bow, and so a few hold a forest against many. Among the Midlanders the yeoman must practise every feast day by law.

Variants.Name: crossbowman
Variants.Description: Shoots a crossbow, spanned with a hook or a crank, from behind a tall standing shield. Carries a quiver of short bolts.
Variants.Lore: A weapon that lets a townsman kill a knight, and so it was banned by the temple, and hired by every prince. The best companies come from the port cities.

Variants.Name: spearman
Variants.Description: Fights in a close rank with a long spear and a shield, in a padded coat and an iron cap.
Variants.Lore: The levy of every people: a spear, a shield and a neighbour on each side. Orc spears held the lines of the fallen Realms, and are still for hire.

Variants.Name: mounted archer
Variants.Description: Shoots a short recurved bow from the saddle at the gallop, in any direction. A light coat, a quiver at the hip and a string of spare horses.
Variants.Lore: A Grass rider shoots at the moment all four hooves are off the ground. The settled peoples have never found an answer except a wall.

Variants.Name: cavalryman
Variants.Description: Fights on horseback with lance and sword, in armour of mail, scale or quilted cloth, the horse often armoured too.
Variants.Lore: The Sunlander kingdoms of the long grass ride in quilted armour, horse and man. The cavalry is the king's, and the horses die of the forest fly further south.

Variants.Name: sergeant
Variants.Description: A veteran who keeps a small troop in order, in the line and in camp. Carries a halberd or a staff and a loud voice.
Variants.Lore: A captain commands the company and the sergeant runs it. He is the one the recruits fear and the one the old soldiers follow.

Variants.Name: captain
Variants.Description: Commands a company, hires it out and divides the pay. Better armour, a sash or a plume, and a clerk for the muster roll.
Variants.Lore: Signs the contract, draws the pay and answers for the company's deeds, to the paymaster, if not to the law. Some captains end as lords of what they were hired to defend.

Variants.Name: mercenary
Variants.Description: Fights for whoever pays, in a company under its own banner and law. Gaudy, slashed clothes, mismatched armour and old scars.
Variants.Lore: A free company fights for the contract and not a day longer. Orcs and Dwarves both hire out, and neither has ever been bought twice in the same war.

Variants.Name: drill master
Variants.Description: Trains recruits to stand, march and strike as one, on the drill yard, with a staff and endless repetition.
Variants.Lore: The Flinchless are bred from a legion and drill as others pray. A man who cannot feel a blow must be taught to notice one.

Variants.Name: marine
Variants.Description: A soldier who fights from ships: boards over the rail and shoots from the fighting tops. Light armour, a short sword and a boarding axe.
Variants.Lore: Paid a share of the prize, and so keen to take a ship whole. Northmen do not have the word: every one of their sailors is one.

Variants.Name: champion
Variants.Description: Fights single combats for a lord, an army or a party in a trial by battle. The best armed and most feared of a host.
Variants.Lore: Trial by battle lets the old, the sick and the temple hire one to fight in their place. A champion who loses is fined as a perjurer.

Vocations.Description: Fights for pay, for a lord or for an oath: in the field, on the wall and at sea.
Vocations.Lore: A trade like another, hired by the season and paid late. In peace the soldier is a guard, a bully or a bandit; in war a looter. Companies have their own law, share out plunder by rank and sell themselves to the higher bidder. Veterans come home with scars, a little money and no craft. Fantasy twists: a people that feels no pain, companies of another race for hire.

Vocations.Name: Guard

Variants.Name: watchman
Variants.Description: Keeps watch over a place by day or night, with a staff, a lantern and a rattle or a horn to raise the alarm.
Variants.Lore: Every householder owes his turn at the watch, and the rich pay a poor man to take theirs. So the watch is old, cold and easily bought.

Variants.Name: town guard
Variants.Description: Keeps order in the streets in the town's colours, with a halberd or a club, a helmet and a padded coat.
Variants.Lore: Paid by the council and loyal to whoever is in it. The guard knows every thief in the ward by name and arrests the ones who are behind with their dues.

Variants.Name: gate guard
Variants.Description: Stands at a town gate, looks over those who enter, and closes the gate at dusk. A spear, a helmet and a brazier in winter.
Variants.Lore: The gate closes at dusk and a late traveller sleeps outside, whoever he is. The gate guard's small door opens for a coin, as everyone knows.

Variants.Name: night watch
Variants.Description: Walks the dark streets in a small band after curfew, with lanterns and staves, and calls the hours.
Variants.Lore: Duskreaders see a warm body in the dark, and Catfolk hear one. A town with either on its night watch is a bad town for a burglar.

Variants.Name: bodyguard
Variants.Description: Stays within arm's reach of one person and stands between that person and harm. Well armed, watchful and silent.
Variants.Lore: Rulers choose their guard from far away: a stranger has no cousin with a claim. Northmen serve southern courts as sworn guards, and the Flinchless stand where the blade will come.

Variants.Name: caravan guard
Variants.Description: Rides with a caravan for a season's pay, armed with bow and spear, and sleeps by the bales.
Variants.Lore: Hired at one end of the road and paid at the other, so that he arrives. In the worst country the guards are hired from the bandits' own people.

Variants.Name: road warden
Variants.Description: Patrols a stretch of road on horseback against robbers, and helps travellers in trouble.
Variants.Lore: The Widegaze patrol the plains roads and see a robber band a day off. Where there is no warden, the merchants pay the robbers directly.

Variants.Name: pass warden
Variants.Description: Holds a mountain pass from a small tower: takes the toll, guides travellers over and brings them down from the snow.
Variants.Lore: Hearthbloods hold the high passes, where no one else can winter. Midlanders and Northmen pay them as wardens and fear them in a hungry year.

Variants.Name: lookout
Variants.Description: Watches from a tower or a hilltop for sails, smoke and riders, and signals with a horn, a flag or a mirror.
Variants.Lore: A Widegaze on a tower is worth a troop on the wall, and they sell the service to every side.

Variants.Name: beacon keeper
Variants.Description: Tends a pile of wood and pitch on a height, ready to light it as a warning fire or to guide ships.
Variants.Lore: A chain of fires carries a warning across a kingdom in a night. The keeper who lights it without cause hangs, and so does the one who sleeps.

Variants.Name: granary warden
Variants.Description: Guards a town's grain store against thieves, fire, damp and vermin, and sleeps beside it.
Variants.Lore: Catfolk cannot eat grain, so every city trusts them to guard it. They take their pay in meat and in the rats.

Variants.Name: vault keeper
Variants.Description: Guards a treasury behind iron doors and many locks, and knows who may enter and what lies on each shelf.
Variants.Lore: Among the Dwarves the office passes within one family, and the keeper may refuse the lord himself entry without the second key.

Variants.Name: firefighter
Variants.Description: Watches for fire from a tower and fights it with leather buckets, ladders, axes and long hooks to pull down burning thatch.
Variants.Lore: The Flinchless go into a burning house without a thought, and are counted and examined when they come out, since they do not know when they are burnt.

Vocations.Description: Keeps watch and order in one place: a gate, a wall, a road, a store, a person.
Vocations.Lore: The watch is a duty of every householder that the rich pay others to do, so the guard is a poor man with a lantern and a staff. He knows every face in his ward and can be bought for a drink. A bodyguard or a vault keeper is another matter: chosen for loyalty and paid for it.

Vocations.Name: Priest

Variants.Name: village priest
Variants.Description: Serves one village and its small temple: leads the rites, blesses fields and marriages, buries the dead, and farms a field of his own. A plain robe and worn shoes.
Variants.Lore: A farmer's son with a little learning, who ploughs his own strip and knows every sin in the parish. The village pays him in eggs.

Variants.Name: temple priest
Variants.Description: Serves in a great temple, one of many under a high priest: tends the altar, the lamps and the offerings, in rich vestments on feast days.
Variants.Lore: A great temple is a great estate, and its priests are landlords, bankers and judges. The high priest is a lord's younger son, more often than not.

Variants.Name: chaplain
Variants.Description: The priest of a lord's household, a ship, a guild or a company of soldiers. Says the rites and often writes the letters.
Variants.Lore: Reads and writes for a lord who can do neither. He hears the lord's confession, and so is never dismissed.

Variants.Name: shaman
Variants.Description: Speaks with spirits for a people, in a trance, with a drum and a rattle. A coat hung with bones, feathers and iron charms.
Variants.Lore: Among the Grass riders the shaman rides to the sky on the drum and may rebuke the khan. The calling comes as a sickness, and nobody asks for it.

Variants.Name: monk
Variants.Description: A man who lives under a rule in a monastery: prays at the set hours, works and copies books. A coarse habit with a hood and a rope belt.
Variants.Lore: The monasteries kept the books through the Ashen Years, and the seed corn. They have been rich ever since, and reformed every century.

Variants.Name: nun
Variants.Description: A woman who lives under a rule in a convent: prays at the set hours, sews, teaches and nurses. A plain habit and a veil.
Variants.Lore: The one life where a woman may read, rule an estate and answer to no husband. Great ladies retire to a convent, and some govern from it.

Variants.Name: friar
Variants.Description: A brother of a begging order who walks the roads and preaches in the market place. A patched habit, sandals, a staff and a bowl.
Variants.Lore: Sworn to own nothing, and welcome in the towns for it. The parish priests hate them for hearing confessions more cheaply.

Variants.Name: hermit
Variants.Description: Lives alone in a hut or a cave to pray, on what visitors bring. A long beard, a rough robe, and often a tame animal.
Variants.Lore: The village feeds its hermit and asks advice in return. A lord builds a hermitage in his park and hires a man to fill it.

Variants.Name: ascetic
Variants.Description: Has given up every comfort for holiness: nearly naked, smeared with ash, thin from fasting, with matted hair.
Variants.Lore: Rainkeepers hold that the last stage of a good life is to walk away from it. Kings come out to bow to men who own nothing.

Variants.Name: sexton
Variants.Description: Keeps a temple and its graveyard: rings the bell, lights the lamps, sweeps the floor and digs the graves.
Variants.Lore: Knows who lies where, and who was put there in a hurry. The sexton's spade and the sexton's tales are both older than he is.

Vocations.Description: Serves a god or the spirits for a community: leads the rites, marks birth, marriage and death, teaches, and keeps the holy place. Includes those who live under a rule apart from the world.
Vocations.Lore: Those who pray. The village priest is a farmer's son with a little learning and a field of his own; the high priest is a lord. A monastery is a great estate with a rule: the cellarer feeds it, the sacrist keeps the church, the infirmarian nurses, the precentor leads the singing, the guest-master receives travellers. The clergy are judged by their own courts and pay no lay tax. Fantasy twists: gods that answer, rites that hold something back.

Vocations.Name: Scribe

Variants.Name: clerk
Variants.Description: Writes and keeps records for a lord, a court or a merchant. A pen case and an ink horn at the belt and ink on the fingers.
Variants.Lore: Half a priest: tonsured, and tried only by the temple's court. A man who can read a verse aloud may claim to be one and save his neck.

Variants.Name: copyist
Variants.Description: Copies books by hand at a sloped desk, line by line, with a quill in one hand and a knife in the other.
Variants.Lore: Paid by the line. At the end of a book the copyist writes his own words: the work is done, give the writer a drink.

Variants.Name: notary
Variants.Description: Draws up contracts, wills and deeds in the right form and marks them with a personal sign that makes them valid.
Variants.Lore: Lanternkin notaries mix a drop of their blood into the ink: the signature glows while the notary lives, and the world's contracts rest on it.

Variants.Name: bookkeeper
Variants.Description: Keeps a merchant's accounts in ledgers, with a counting board or an abacus, and balances them at the year's end.
Variants.Lore: The Saltroad folk kept the books when everyone else burned theirs, and their way of writing every sum twice is the one all merchants use.

Variants.Name: secretary
Variants.Description: Writes the letters of one master, keeps his seal and his secrets, and travels with him.
Variants.Lore: The keeper of secrets, as the word says. A ruler's secretary writes in the ruler's own hand, and has done so in the ruler's absence.

Variants.Name: advocate
Variants.Description: Pleads cases before a court for a fee, in a long robe, with a bundle of papers and a ready tongue.
Variants.Lore: Paid by both the winner and the loser, and so never out of pocket. The saint of the lawyers is admired for having been an honest one.

Variants.Name: records clerk
Variants.Description: Keeps an archive: rolls, charters and registers on shelves and in chests, and finds the one that proves a right.
Variants.Lore: Dwarves keep every contract and every grudge in writing, and the clerk who can find a deed six hundred years old is a power in the hold.

Variants.Name: printer
Variants.Description: Sets small metal letters in a frame, inks them and pulls sheets on a wooden screw press. Fingers black with ink.
Variants.Lore: The Canal folk print from carved blocks and from clay letters. Elsewhere the copyists' guild has had presses broken, and then bought one.

Variants.Name: bookbinder
Variants.Description: Folds and sews the written or printed sheets of a book onto cords and laces them into boards, ready for the cover.
Variants.Lore: A book is sold as loose sheets, and bound to the buyer's purse. The binder is the first to read it whole, and the only one who never has time.

Variants.Name: bookseller
Variants.Description: Sells and lends books from a small shop near a temple or a school, and orders copies made.
Variants.Lore: Sworn to the college, which fixes the price and inspects the copies. The forbidden books are in the back, and cost double.

Variants.Name: witness for hire
Variants.Description: Attends deals, oaths and handings-over for a fee, remembers exactly what was seen and said, and swears to it before a court.
Variants.Lore: A Widegaze sees the whole room at once and forgets nothing of it. Courts in the plains will take the word of one against three others.

Vocations.Description: Writes for others: letters, deeds, accounts, court rolls and copies of books; and knows the forms that make a writing valid.
Vocations.Lore: Literacy is a trade. The clerk is often in minor orders and half a priest; the notary's sign makes a contract stand in any court; the advocate is rich and unloved. Scribes serve whoever pays, know every secret that was ever put in writing, and can forge it. Fantasy twists: a people whose word is physically binding, script that only some eyes can read.

Vocations.Name: Scholar

Variants.Name: teacher
Variants.Description: Teaches a craft of the mind to those who come: reading, reckoning, law or the holy books, wherever there is a room and pupils.
Variants.Lore: Paid by the pupil and by the week, and so always hungry in summer. The Twofold say no one should teach before living both halves of a life.

Variants.Name: schoolmaster
Variants.Description: Keeps a school for boys, teaches them their letters and the old tongue, and keeps order with a birch rod.
Variants.Lore: Teaches the old tongue of the Realms with a rod. Every great man remembers his schoolmaster, and few fondly.

Variants.Name: tutor
Variants.Description: Lives in a rich house and teaches its children alone, in manners as much as in letters.
Variants.Lore: Elves serve as tutors at human courts, and have taught the grandfather, the father and the son the same lesson with the same result.

Variants.Name: professor
Variants.Description: A master of a college, who lectures from a raised chair to benches of students, in a gown and a cap.
Variants.Lore: A college of masters answers to no town court and may go on strike. When it does, it walks out and founds another city's college.

Variants.Name: sage
Variants.Description: Old and learned in many things, sought out for counsel by rulers and common folk. Lives simply among books and scrolls.
Variants.Lore: The Orcs call theirs the greybacks, and a war band does not ride without asking one. Elsewhere a sage is someone a king consults too late.

Variants.Name: astronomer
Variants.Description: Watches the sky at night from a roof or a tower with an astrolabe and a quadrant, and keeps tables of the stars and the calendar.
Variants.Lore: The Saltroad folk named most of the stars. The Noonfolk, who sleep at sunset, have never seen one, and take astronomy on trust.

Variants.Name: mathematician
Variants.Description: Works with number and figure, on a slate, a sand tray or paper: reckons calendars, taxes, vaults and the paths of the stars.
Variants.Lore: The Rainkeepers have a sign for nothing, and reckon with it faster than anyone. Tax, temple and reservoir are all sums.

Variants.Name: lore keeper
Variants.Description: Keeps the old knowledge of a people, in memory or in ancient books, and teaches it to a chosen few.
Variants.Lore: Elven lore keepers remember the Dawn at second hand, from someone who was there. They correct the histories of others, tiresomely, and are right.

Variants.Name: chronicler
Variants.Description: Writes down year by year what happens in a realm, a town or a monastery, from what is seen and what is told.
Variants.Lore: Swiftborn chroniclers write a generation every ten years and keep the fullest annals in the world. Everyone else's chronicle begins with the Ashen Years.

Variants.Name: librarian
Variants.Description: Keeps a library: chains the books to the desks, lists them, mends them and decides who may read.
Variants.Lore: Books are chained, and a curse is written in each against the thief. The librarian adds to the curse from experience.

Variants.Name: keeper of genealogies
Variants.Description: Keeps the family trees of a people, in long rolls or by heart, and settles who is kin to whom and who inherits.
Variants.Lore: Halflings know their cousins to the ninth degree and will recite them at dinner. An inheritance is settled by the keeper before it reaches a court.

Vocations.Description: Studies and teaches: letters, law, the stars, numbers, the past.
Vocations.Lore: Learning is slow, costly and mostly in the hands of the temple. A school teaches boys their letters; a college of masters and students is a rare and privileged body that answers to no town court. Scholars are poor until a patron finds them. Fantasy twists: lore older than the kingdoms, an examination that makes or breaks a house.

Vocations.Name: Mage

Variants.Name: wizard
Variants.Description: A learned mage, trained for years from books: a long robe, a staff, a pouch of components and a tower room full of scrolls and instruments.
Variants.Lore: Ten years in a college, an oath to it for life, and a ruler and a temple watching. The sorcerer-kings were wizards once, and no one has forgotten.

Variants.Name: sorcerer
Variants.Description: A mage by birth and not by study: the power comes unasked and shows in the eyes or the hands. Often young, untaught and feared.
Variants.Lore: A village fears the child and a college claims it. Those the college does not find in time are found by a cabal, or by a mob.

Variants.Name: enchanter
Variants.Description: Works on minds and on things: charms, illusions and lasting spells laid on places and objects. Soft-spoken and richly dressed.
Variants.Lore: The law of most lands voids a contract made under a charm, and so every notary keeps a test for one. A proven charm on a ruler is treason.

Variants.Name: court mage
Variants.Description: A ruler's own mage: advises, wards the palace, reads the signs and stands near the throne. Fine robes and the ruler's badge.
Variants.Lore: The first to be blamed when the harvest fails and the last to be dismissed. A court mage serves the throne, and reports to the college.

Variants.Name: battle mage
Variants.Description: A mage trained for war: throws fire and lightning, breaks gates and shields the line. Wears a robe over armour, with a staff shod with iron.
Variants.Lore: A captain pays a mage ten soldiers' wages and guards him with twenty. The colleges forbid their members to face each other in the field, and the oath mostly holds.

Variants.Name: hedge wizard
Variants.Description: A self-taught country mage with a few true spells, who mends, finds and wards for farmers in return for food.
Variants.Lore: Unlicensed, half taught and useful. The college calls them a danger, and the village calls them when the well goes sour.

Variants.Name: rune carver
Variants.Description: Cuts signs of power into stone, wood, bone and iron, and reddens them, so that the thing is bound to a purpose. Carries chisels and a knife.
Variants.Lore: Northmen say the runes were won by hanging nine nights on a tree. A carver who cuts a rune he does not understand does harm, and the stones say so.

Vocations.Description: Works magic by learning or by gift: casts, wards, enchants and advises.
Vocations.Lore: The learned mage is a scholar with a dangerous subject: trained for years in a college or by a single master, bound by the college's oath, and watched by temple and crown. The born mage is a child that a village fears and a college claims. Mages serve courts as advisers and weapons, and are the first blamed when a harvest fails. Typical conflicts: college against cabal, mage against witch hunter.

Vocations.Name: Alchemist

Variants.Name: apothecary
Variants.Description: Keeps a shop of drugs, spices and sweets in rows of labelled jars, and mixes what the physician prescribes with a mortar and small scales.
Variants.Lore: Sells sugar, spice, drugs and poison over one counter, and is inspected by the physicians, who hate the trade and need it.

Variants.Name: alchemist
Variants.Description: Seeks to turn one substance into another, and lead into gold, with furnace, still and retort, in a cluttered and smoky workroom.
Variants.Lore: Princes keep them like hawks and hang them, in a gilded robe, when the gold does not come. What they find by the way has been worth more.

Variants.Name: potion maker
Variants.Description: Brews draughts that work, where there is magic: for healing, strength, sleep or love, sealed in small stoppered flasks.
Variants.Lore: A college seals each flask and answers for it. An unsealed potion is cheaper, and has made some widows and a few fortunes.

Variants.Name: antidote maker
Variants.Description: Prepares cures for venoms and poisons, and sells them to courts that fear the cup.
Variants.Lore: The Bitterbloods were bred as tasters, became poison themselves, and now sell the cure. They price it by what the buyer fears.

Variants.Name: poisoner
Variants.Description: Prepares poisons from plants, minerals and venoms, and knows the dose, the taste and the delay of each. Sells with no questions asked.
Variants.Lore: Called a seller of inheritance powder. The Bitterbloods keep a hidden school of the art, which most of their own people would like to see closed.

Variants.Name: perfumer
Variants.Description: Distils the scents of flowers, resins and musk into oils and waters, and blends them in tiny bottles.
Variants.Lore: Stillfaces speak by scent and compose perfumes as others write letters. What a court wears as fashion, a Stillface reads as a sentence.

Variants.Name: embalmer
Variants.Description: Prepares the dead to last: washes, opens and fills the body with salts, resins and spices, and wraps it in linen.
Variants.Lore: Brinefolk learned to keep their dead in the salt of their dried sea. Other peoples hire them for kings, and stand well back.

Variants.Name: maker of insect smoke
Variants.Description: Makes coils, cakes and powders that burn with a smoke that drives off flies and fever-bearing midges, in swamp and jungle country.
Variants.Lore: A Bitterblood craft of the fever swamps. A town that burns the smoke each dusk loses fewer children, and does not ask what is in it.

Vocations.Description: Prepares substances: medicines, poisons, perfumes, acids, pigments and, by repute, gold.
Vocations.Lore: The respectable end is the apothecary, a guild shopkeeper who sells spices, drugs and sweets alike. The other end works at night with a furnace and a patron's money, promising gold. Both are licensed, taxed and suspected. An alchemist's shop is where a healer buys, a mage orders and a murderer asks no questions. Fantasy twists: potions that work, a people immune to their own poisons.

Vocations.Name: Seer

Variants.Name: diviner
Variants.Description: Reads the answer to a question in thrown bones, shells, sticks or the entrails of a beast, on a mat or a marked tray.
Variants.Lore: Sunlander diviners serve a king's court and a farmer's doubt with the same sixteen figures. The client does not say the question aloud.

Variants.Name: astrologer
Variants.Description: Casts the chart of the heavens for a birth or a decision, from tables and an astrolabe, and names the lucky and unlucky days.
Variants.Lore: No Rainkeeper marries, sows or builds without the chart. The court astrologer's forecast of a king's death is treason, even when asked for.

Variants.Name: geomancer
Variants.Description: Reads the land and its hidden currents, and says where a house, a grave or a town should stand and which way it should face.
Variants.Lore: The Canal folk will not dig a grave or a canal without one. A family's luck is in its ancestors' graves, and lawsuits are fought over a hill.

Variants.Name: soothsayer
Variants.Description: Foretells for a coin at a market or a gate, from the palm, the face or a flight of birds.
Variants.Lore: Tells a traveller what a traveller wants to hear. Now and then one tells the truth by mistake, and is run out of town for it.

Variants.Name: oracle
Variants.Description: Speaks for a god or a spirit at a holy place, in a trance, in riddling words that priests write down.
Variants.Lore: Kings send to the oracle before a war and hear what both sides can read as victory. The priests who write the answer down are the ones to bribe.

Variants.Name: medium
Variants.Description: Lets the dead and the spirits speak through the mouth, in a darkened room, for those who mourn or need an answer.
Variants.Lore: The temple forbids it and the bereaved come anyway. What speaks is not always the one who was called.

Variants.Name: dowser
Variants.Description: Walks the ground with a forked hazel twig that dips over hidden water, ore or lost things.
Variants.Lore: The miners swear by the rod and the scholars cannot make it work. The dowser is paid only on a strike, and is paid often enough.

Variants.Name: well-finder
Variants.Description: Finds water in dry land, by signs in the sand, the plants and the stars, or by a sense others lack, and marks where to dig.
Variants.Lore: Duskreaders see where the cool of water lies under hot sand. They have sworn to keep quiet about how, and the Saltroad folk pay them not to explain.

Variants.Name: weather watcher
Variants.Description: Reads the sky, the wind and the beasts and says what weather comes, for sowers, herders and sailors.
Variants.Lore: The Widegaze see a storm a day before it breaks and move the herds. A harbour pays its watcher a share of every ship that did not sail.

Variants.Name: wise woman
Variants.Description: An old woman of the village who knows herbs, births, charms and omens, and is asked before the priest is.
Variants.Lore: Called to every birth and every deathbed. The priest tolerates her until the bishop visits.

Variants.Name: hedge witch
Variants.Description: Lives at the edge of the village, with a cat, a cauldron and a garden of strange plants, and makes charms, cures and curses.
Variants.Lore: Feared in daylight and visited after dark. When the cattle die she is the first to be named, by the same people who bought the charm.

Variants.Name: cunning man
Variants.Description: A village man who finds thieves and lost goods, lifts curses and names witches, with a book, a sieve and a pair of shears.
Variants.Lore: Makes his living from undoing witches' work, and so needs witches. He names one when business is slow.

Vocations.Description: Knows what others do not: reads signs, finds water and lost things, speaks with spirits, lifts and lays curses.
Vocations.Lore: The village's own magic, cheap, unlicensed and older than the temple. The seer is consulted for a lost cow, a sick child, a good day to sow, and is the first accused when things go wrong. At a court the same art is the astrologer's, well paid and politically deadly. The line between seer, healer and priest is thin, and the temple polices it. Typical conflicts: seer against priest, and the inquisition against anyone unlicensed.

Vocations.Name: Labourer

Variants.Name: day labourer
Variants.Description: Waits at the hiring place each dawn and takes whatever work is offered for the day. A worn tunic and bare hands.
Variants.Lore: Stands at the cross each dawn with the tool of his trade in his hand. After the plague the law fixed the wage, and no one has ever been paid it.

Variants.Name: field hand
Variants.Description: Works another's fields through the year for a wage and a meal: hoes, weeds, spreads dung and threshes.
Variants.Lore: Noonfolk work from first light to last and need no dinner: they live on the sun. They lie down where they stand at sunset, and farmers plan the day around it.

Variants.Name: harvest hand
Variants.Description: Hired for the weeks of harvest: reaps with a sickle or mows with a scythe, binds the sheaves, and moves on.
Variants.Lore: Swiftborn gangs follow the harvest north through the summer. They have thirty years in all, and do not spend one idle.

Variants.Name: builder's labourer
Variants.Description: Mixes mortar and carries stone and brick up the ladders in a hod, for the masons on the scaffold.
Variants.Lore: Carries a ton up the ladders in a day, for a third of the mason's wage. The one who falls is not named in the accounts.

Variants.Name: digger
Variants.Description: Digs with spade and pick wherever earth must be moved: foundations, moats, cellars and banks.
Variants.Lore: Every castle moat and city ditch was dug with a wooden spade by men like these. Orcs dig for hire, and are fed from the same pot as the soldiers.

Variants.Name: ditcher
Variants.Description: Cuts and clears the ditches and drains of fields and roads, standing in water in long boots.
Variants.Lore: Hedging and ditching are winter work, when nothing else pays. Fen country lives or drowns by its ditchers.

Variants.Name: dock hand
Variants.Description: Loads and unloads ships at the quay: rolls barrels, carries sacks and works the treadwheel crane.
Variants.Lore: Hired by the tide at the quay gate, and loyal to the gang. A port's strikes begin here, and a port's smuggling.

Variants.Name: quarry hand
Variants.Description: Clears rubble, hauls sledges and turns the windlass in a quarry, under the orders of the quarriers.
Variants.Lore: Works beside the convicts and is told from them only by going home at night.

Variants.Name: peat cutter
Variants.Description: Cuts bricks of peat from a bog with a long narrow spade and stacks them in small heaps to dry.
Variants.Lore: Each household has its bank on the bog by right. Now and then the spade turns up a body from the Dawn, tanned like leather, and it is put back with a prayer.

Variants.Name: ice cutter
Variants.Description: Saws blocks of ice from a frozen lake in winter and hauls them to an ice house packed with straw.
Variants.Lore: Hearthbloods cut ice for the pleasure of the cold, and sell it in the south for the price of wine.

Variants.Name: gravedigger
Variants.Description: Digs the graves and fills them in, with a spade and a pick, and buries the poor and the plague dead that no one else will touch.
Variants.Lore: Digs the grave before he knows who it is for, the saying goes. In a plague he is the one man in town who is never short of work or company.

Vocations.Description: Sells the strength of the body by the day: digs, carries, loads, mows, threshes and cleans, wherever hands are wanted.
Vocations.Lore: The landless and the toolless. In the country the labourer has a cottage and a garden and works other men's fields; in the town he waits at the hiring place each dawn. Wages are set by law after a plague and paid above it. The labourer is the reserve of every other vocation and the first to go hungry.

Vocations.Name: Beggar

Variants.Name: beggar
Variants.Description: Sits at a temple door or a bridge in rags, with a bowl and a staff, and asks for alms.
Variants.Lore: Alms are a duty in every faith, and so the beggar does the giver a service. Good pitches are owned, inherited and rented out.

Variants.Name: pauper
Variants.Description: Too poor to live without help, and on the parish's or the temple's list for bread and a little coin.
Variants.Lore: The honest poor, known to their neighbours and entered on a list. The list is read out, which is the price of the bread.

Variants.Name: vagrant
Variants.Description: Wanders from place to place with no home, no master and no trade, and is whipped on by every town.
Variants.Lore: A masterless man is an offence in himself. The law brands him at the first town, whips him at the second and hangs him at the third.

Variants.Name: almsman
Variants.Description: An old or worn-out person housed and fed by a charity, in return for prayers for the founder. A plain gown with a badge.
Variants.Lore: Wears the founder's badge and prays for the founder's soul at fixed hours. A place in the almshouse is in a lord's gift, and is asked for years ahead.

Variants.Name: cripple
Variants.Description: Cannot work for a lost or twisted limb, blindness or sickness, and begs on a crutch, a low wheeled board or behind a guide.
Variants.Lore: Old soldiers, mostly. Some sores are painted on, and the beggars' brotherhood teaches how, and takes a share.

Variants.Name: pilgrim
Variants.Description: Walks to a holy place on a vow and lives on alms along the way. A broad hat, a staff, a scrip and the badge of the shrine.
Variants.Lore: A pilgrim is safe on the road by custom and fed by law. Some are sent on pilgrimage as a sentence, and some are paid to go for another.

Variants.Name: refugee
Variants.Description: Driven from home by war, famine or plague, on the road with a bundle, children and nothing else.
Variants.Lore: In the Ashen Years whole peoples took the road. Every race tells of the gate that opened to it, and of the one that did not.

Variants.Name: street orphan
Variants.Description: A child without family who lives in the street, runs errands, begs and steals, and sleeps in doorways.
Variants.Lore: The guilds take a few as apprentices and the gangs take more. Swiftborn orphans are grown at seven and gone before a charity has met to discuss them.

Vocations.Description: Lives on alms: too old, sick, maimed or unlucky to work, or unwilling.
Vocations.Lore: The deserving poor have a place: at the temple door, on the almoner's list, in the hospital. The sturdy beggar is whipped out of town. Beggars see and hear everything in a street and sell it. Fantasy twists: a beggars' king, a curse that passes with the coin.

Vocations.Name: Thief

Variants.Name: cutpurse
Variants.Description: Cuts the strings of a purse in a crowd with a small sharp blade, and is gone before it is missed.
Variants.Lore: Works the crowd at a hanging, where another cutpurse is being hanged. Trained on a purse hung with bells.

Variants.Name: pickpocket
Variants.Description: Lifts coins and trinkets from belts and sleeves with light fingers, often as one of a pair: one jostles, one takes.
Variants.Lore: Children, mostly, with a master who takes the lot and feeds them. A lost ear tells the watch it is not the first offence.

Variants.Name: burglar
Variants.Description: Breaks into houses by night, over the roof or through the shutter, with a hooked bar, a dark lantern and soft shoes.
Variants.Lore: Breaking a house at night is hanged where the same theft by day is fined. Catfolk make the best burglars and the best night watch, and each knows it.

Variants.Name: fence
Variants.Description: Buys stolen goods cheap and sells them on, behind the front of an honest shop.
Variants.Lore: The law hangs the thief and fines the receiver. The fence keeps a pawnshop, an alibi and the watch captain's wife in ribbons.

Variants.Name: smuggler
Variants.Description: Carries goods past the customs by night, in hidden coves, false bottoms and mountain paths.
Variants.Lore: Whole coasts live by it, priest and squire included. Shoalfolk hold that the customs line is drawn on land and does not apply to them.

Variants.Name: forger
Variants.Description: Makes false seals, deeds, letters and coin, with a steady hand, stolen models and a small press.
Variants.Lore: A false charter has made many an abbey rich. To forge the ruler's coin is treason, and the forger is boiled.

Variants.Name: swindler
Variants.Description: Lives by tricks: loaded dice, false relics, a sad story or a sure investment. Dressed to be trusted.
Variants.Lore: Sells the same pig's bones as a saint in every town. An honest man cannot be cheated, the swindlers say, and they have met very few.

Variants.Name: blackmailer
Variants.Description: Learns secrets and is paid to keep them: a letter kept, a servant bribed, a quiet word.
Variants.Lore: The servant's trade, turned to account. It ends when the victim has nothing left, or a friend with a knife.

Variants.Name: enforcer
Variants.Description: The hard hand of a gang: collects its dues, breaks fingers and guards its master, with a cudgel and a knife.
Variants.Lore: Orcs and old soldiers. A gang's peace is kept by one and the watch is glad of it, most nights.

Variants.Name: poisoner
Variants.Description: Kills for pay with a dose in the cup or the dish, and gets close as a servant, a cook or a guest.
Variants.Lore: The weapon of the weak and of the court. The Stillfaces smell it in the cup, and the great houses hire them for exactly that.

Variants.Name: hired killer
Variants.Description: Kills for pay with a blade, a cord or a bolt from the dark, and leaves no name. Plain clothes and a face no one remembers.
Variants.Lore: The brotherhoods take a contract and keep it even after the client is dead. A ruler who uses them once is never sure of being the last to.

Vocations.Description: Takes by stealth or deceit, in a town: cuts purses, breaks houses, receives, smuggles, forges, and kills for pay.
Vocations.Lore: Crime in a town is organised like a craft: with masters, territories, dues and a peace of its own. The fence is a shopkeeper by day; the smuggler is a sailor or a carter who carries one more bale. The law hangs the poor thief and fines the rich one.

Vocations.Name: Bandit

Variants.Name: highwayman
Variants.Description: Stops travellers on the road, mounted and masked, with a sword or a bow, and takes purse and horse.
Variants.Lore: A ruined gentleman in the ballad, a deserter in fact. He is hanged at the crossroads he worked, and the ballad is sold at the hanging.

Variants.Name: robber
Variants.Description: One of a band that lies in wait in a wood or a pass and falls on those who come by. Ragged and armed with what was taken.
Variants.Lore: Unpaid soldiers and landless sons. The band has a captain, shares and a law of its own, harsher than the king's.

Variants.Name: raider
Variants.Description: Rides or sails with a war band to strike a village, take cattle, goods and captives, and be gone before help comes.
Variants.Lore: For the Northmen and the Grass riders a raid is a season's honest work, sung about afterwards. The people raided keep a different account.

Variants.Name: rustler
Variants.Description: Steals cattle, horses or sheep by night, drives them far and changes their marks.
Variants.Lore: Among the cattle peoples a young man is not grown until he has lifted a cow from a neighbour. The neighbour's young men feel the same.

Variants.Name: poacher
Variants.Description: Takes the lord's game by night with snares, a bow and a quiet dog, and sells the meat or eats it.
Variants.Lore: The village does not count it a theft, and the lord counts it worse than one. A poacher's wife sells rabbits to the warden's cook.

Variants.Name: outlaw
Variants.Description: Put outside the law for a crime or a debt, and living in the wild where anyone may kill him. A hood, a bow and a hunted look.
Variants.Lore: A wolf's head: anyone may kill him and no one may feed him. The greenwood songs are about the one who was wronged, and the forest holds the others.

Variants.Name: pirate
Variants.Description: Takes ships at sea and raids the coasts, from a fast vessel. Armed with cutlass, axe and boarding hooks.
Variants.Lore: The crew votes on the captain and shares by written articles. With a ruler's letter the same man is a privateer and dines with the governor.

Variants.Name: wrecker
Variants.Description: Lives on a dangerous coast and plunders ships that strike, and on a dark night shows a false light to bring one in.
Variants.Lore: The shore claims what the sea gives, and no law has ever got the better of that. The prayer on such a coast is not for no wrecks, but for wrecks here.

Variants.Name: rebel
Variants.Description: Has taken up arms against the ruler, with a band in the hills, for a lost cause, a creed or a rival claimant. Armed with farm tools and captured weapons.
Variants.Lore: A rebel who wins is a founder, and the chronicles are rewritten. The Ashen Years made more of them than any king did.

Vocations.Description: Takes by force, outside the towns: robs on the road, raids, rustles, poaches, and at sea takes ships.
Vocations.Lore: Most bandits were something else first: a soldier without pay, a peasant without land, a herder in a hungry year. The outlaw is outside the law's protection and may be killed by anyone. Some bands are a lord's deniable arm, some a people's resistance, some only hungry. Raiding is a season's work for whole peoples, with no shame in it.

Tools.Name: Heavy plough
Tools.Description: A heavy plough carries an iron coulter, a vertical blade mounted like a knife that slices the soil ahead of the share. It cuts long narrow strips and deep furrows (ridge and furrow), which lets heavy, poorly drained soil be farmed, and it was pulled by teams of up to eight oxen. An iron coulter excavated at Lyminge in Kent is dated to the first half of the 7th century.
Tools.Lore: Midlanders say the heavy plough is the one thing the Old Realms left that still does what it was made for. Eight oxen are more than one farm owns, so a plough team is shared, and half the quarrels of a river plain start over whose strip it turns first. The Catfolk will guard the grain but never walk behind it.

Tools.Name: Sickle
Tools.Description: A curved, hand-held iron tool whose cutting edge is the inside of the curve and is serrated. It harvests cereal crops or cuts grass for hay: the blade is drawn against the base of the stems and cuts them with a sawing action. The Pitt Rivers Museum holds English examples, among them an ancient socketed iron sickle.
Tools.Lore: On the reservoir lands of the Rainkeepers the sickle is handed down with the field, and a child is counted as grown the first harvest it keeps pace with the row. Swiftborn harvest hands hire out by the sickle and bring their own: they have too few seasons to waste one on a borrowed blade.

Tools.Name: Flail
Tools.Description: A wooden staff with a shorter stick, the swingle or swipple, hung from it by a leather hinge or thong so that it swings freely. It is used to thresh corn by hand and separate the grain from the husks. The Pitt Rivers examples are English, the one dated example from Sussex in 1894.
Tools.Lore: Threshing is winter work, done on the barn floor when the fields are shut. The Flinchless thresh in pairs and stop at a fixed count, because a man who cannot feel the swingle catch his own head must be watched by another.

Tools.Name: Scythe
Tools.Description: A long steel blade fastened by a tang at its heel to a shaft (the snath or sned), usually of willow or ash, with two hand grips. The mower keeps the heel of the blade close to the ground and the toe a little above it, and a good mower cuts about an acre a day. Good mowing depends on whetting the blade often with a stone.
Tools.Lore: Hay harvest is when a farm hires, and a day labourer with a scythe and a whetstone of his own is paid half again what a field hand gets. The Noonfolk mow from first light and lay the scythe down where they stand at sunset, so that nobody trips on it in the dark they never see.

Tools.Name: Spade iron
Tools.Description: Medieval spades generally had wooden blades, sometimes fitted with a separate iron cutting edge. A U-shaped spade iron from Wick in the Vale of Glamorgan is 274 mm long and was held to the wooden blade by a groove along its inner edge and two lugs. In 1356 the stock of a London ironmonger included a "spadierne", a spade iron.
Tools.Lore: Iron is too dear to make a whole spade of, so only the edge is shod and the smith re-lays it when it wears thin. A Halfling garden plot is dug with a spade cut to its owner's height, and lending it is a mark of friendship that is noticed.

Tools.Name: Bee skep
Tools.Description: A domed basket hive of woven straw, about 14 inches across, with willow strips inside to strengthen the dome. The bees fix their combs directly to the walls. Wicker hives of privet or hazel daubed with manure and clay were also used. Domed straw skeps were typical in the 16th century.
Tools.Lore: Honey is the sugar of every land too cold for cane, and a row of skeps under the orchard wall is a Halfling household's savings. The Stillfaces keep bees without smoke: they say a hive tells by its scent when it may be opened.

Tools.Name: Billhook
Tools.Description: An iron blade with a hooked end set on a wooden handle, used for cutting branches. Museum Wales holds an excavated iron billhook from Radyr near Cardiff with an iron collar for its handle, catalogued as medieval or post-medieval. The record notes that the form has changed little since Roman times.
Tools.Lore: The vine dresser, the hedger and the firewood cutter carry the same hook, ground to three different edges. An Amberblood grove warden will let a stranger carry a billhook into the trees, but not an axe.

Tools.Name: Shepherd's crook
Tools.Description: A wooden shaft with a metal hook. The Food Museum example is 129 cm long and was used by a shepherd on a Suffolk farm from 1855.
Tools.Lore: A Midlander shepherd is hired at the autumn fair by standing with his crook in his hand. The Widegaze range herders carry one too, though they rarely need to walk to the sheep to know which one is missing.

Tools.Name: Iron shears
Tools.Description: Iron shears with two long blades and a round knob at the end of the handle, 137 mm long, from London, early 15th century. A manuscript of about 1475-1525 (British Library, Harley 1892) shows a woman shearing a sheep with shears, and another (Harley 6563) a tailor cutting out a coat with them.
Tools.Lore: Wool is the fibre of the cold and temperate lands, and the shearing of early summer brings the whole household to the fold. A tailor's shears are smaller and kept sharper, and in a town of the Canal folk they are weighed with the cloth so that no customer pays for what was trimmed away.

Tools.Name: Plunge churn
Tools.Description: A tall coopered oak barrel bound with iron bands, tapering from the base to a loose collar. A plunger on a long wooden handle is worked up and down and turned to churn the cream to butter. Museum Wales says the type was common from the 1600s to the late 1800s.
Tools.Lore: Butter and cheese are how milk keeps through winter, and the dairymaid's churn song sets the pace of the plunger. The Hearthbloods trade for butter by the tub: a people who must feed the fire inside them twice a day do not haggle long over fat.

Tools.Name: Seine net
Tools.Description: A seine is a fishing net weighted at the bottom and floated at the top, cast into the water and hauled in from the bank or a boat. 1,109 lead-alloy sinkers from such a net were found in a 15th-century wreck in the Thames at Blackfriars. The net is calculated at about 56.5 m long and needed several people to handle.
Tools.Lore: A seine is too long for one family, so the net belongs to the boat's company and the catch is split by shares. The herring nets of the Northmen are barked brown with tree tannin each spring, and the Shoalfolk knot theirs of bast that does not rot in brackish water.

Tools.Name: Eel trap
Tools.Description: A trap woven from green willow, with a mouth cone and a second, narrower inner cone that the eel must pass to reach the bait. The far end is closed with a stopper. Small traps (grigs) were laid at dusk, weighted with stones and baited with small fish or fish gut. Large ones (bucks) were mounted on stages across a river to take migrating eels. The Luttrell Psalter of about 1330 shows a wicker eel trap.
Tools.Lore: Eels are rent in many river lands: a mill or a weir owes its lord so many sticks of them a year. The osier for the trap is cut from the same willows that hold the bank.

Tools.Name: Eel spear
Tools.Description: A hand-forged iron spear head with several barbed prongs, thrust into river mud to catch eels. The London Museum example is 430 mm long, came from the Thames foreshore and is dated to the 17th or 18th century. The record notes that eel spears were officially illegal.
Tools.Lore: Where the fishing of a river is let to one holder, the spear is the poor man's tool and the water bailiff's grievance. The Hoarkin use a longer one through a hole in the sea ice, and have no bailiff to ask.

Tools.Name: Boar spear
Tools.Description: A heavy hunting spear with a steel head on a wooden shaft. A German example of about 1550 in the Metropolitan Museum is 220 cm long overall, with a head of 33 cm, and weighs about 1.7 kg.
Tools.Lore: The wild boar of the broadleaf forest is game for a lord and a danger to a farm, so the spear hangs in halls and in barns alike. Where the Supernatural runs high the same spear is carried against worse, by the monster hunters who are paid by the head.

Tools.Name: Falcon's hood
Tools.Description: A snug leather hood placed over a falcon's head to train the bird and to keep a trained falcon quiet and still on the falconer's glove. Most have a plume on top that also serves as a handle for taking it off. The V&A example, early 17th century and probably English, is tooled and gilded leather with embroidered velvet.
Tools.Lore: The Grass riders fly eagles from the saddle and hood them in felt and horsehide. At a Midlander court the falconer ranks above the huntsman, and the hood of the lord's best bird is worth more than the falconer's coat.

Tools.Name: Hunting horn
Tools.Description: A horn carved from an elephant tusk, called an oliphant. The V&A example is 54.5 cm long, from southern or central Italy, of the first half of the 11th century. Its carved bands show a stag, a deer, dogs or wolves, mounted hunters with hawks and a mounted man blowing a horn. The museum takes this piece to be probably ceremonial.
Tools.Lore: A plain hunter's horn is a cow's. A lord's is ivory traded up from the Sunlander savanna or walrus tooth bought from the Hoarkin, and each call on it has one meaning that every beater knows.

Tools.Name: Longbow
Tools.Description: A bow made from a single piece of yew, 1.84 to 2.11 m long, mostly D-shaped in section. The draw weights are estimated at 65 to 175 lb. 172 were recovered from the Mary Rose, with over 2,000 complete arrows, mostly of poplar. They are the only English longbows that can be dated precisely.
Tools.Lore: Yew is a timber of the map, and a kingdom that depends on archers buys staves from wherever it grows. Elven and Amberblood bowyers are counted the best, and the same bow that wins a lord's battle takes his deer on the way home.

Tools.Name: Felling axe
Tools.Description: The Science Museum Group holds two medieval iron axe heads dated to the 14th or 15th century, catalogued among its hand tools.
Tools.Lore: Timber is the first resource a new settlement spends, and the woodcutter's axe is what it spends it with. Elves count the trees that fall to it, and the Amberblood wardenships hold that one who cuts without leave owes the grove a life: usually not his own, but a sapling tended for twenty years.

Tools.Name: Two-man saw
Tools.Description: A long saw worked by two men to cut timber lengthwise. The top sawyer stood on the log and guided the saw, and the bottom sawyer pulled it from underneath. In the Middle Ages the log was raised on trestles, as medieval drawings show. Sawpits were in use by the early 16th century and in time replaced trestles on well-drained ground.
Tools.Lore: The top sawyer is the master and the one below takes the sawdust in his eyes, which is why "under-sawyer" is an insult in most timber towns. Shipyards and great halls keep a pair of sawyers the year round.

Tools.Name: Miner's iron and hammer
Tools.Description: Agricola describes iron tools of one shape, broad and square at the top to take the hammer and pointed at the bottom, most with an eye for a wooden handle. The one in daily use is three quarters of a foot long. The miner holds the handle in one hand, sets the point against the rock and strikes the head with a hammer. Small hammers are held in one hand, larger ones swung with both.
Tools.Lore: Crossed, the iron and the hammer are the badge on every Dwarven mine gate and on the seal of every mining contract kept behind it. A Dwarf is buried with the iron he was given as an apprentice, worn to half its length.

Tools.Name: Wedge, crowbar and pick
Tools.Description: Agricola's wedge is driven into cracks in the rock with the largest hammer. His crowbars are of two kinds, both pointed at one end: a round one to pierce through to a flooded shaft and a flat one to knock out rock that fire has softened. The miner's pick is pointed, unlike the peasant's wide one, and digs the softer ore.
Tools.Lore: Hard rock is first cracked with a wood fire and then prised out with wedge and bar, so a mine eats timber and fuel before it yields any ore. The Hearthbloods work the high winter mines that no one else can stand, and are paid in food.

Tools.Name: Windlass
Tools.Description: A wooden barrel resting in iron sockets on posts set over the shaft, turned by cranks at its ends. A rope wound round the barrel has an iron hook at each end for the bail of a bucket. Two strong men turn it to raise buckets of ore, earth or water. A second form adds a wheel, which can carry lead weights to keep it turning.
Tools.Lore: Windlass work is where a mine puts its hired hands and its greenest apprentices: Orc quarry hands and porters are sought for it. A well digger in the dry lands of the Saltroad folk uses the same machine and calls it by the same word as the well.

Tools.Name: Divining rod
Tools.Description: A forked twig, usually cut from hazel. Agricola (1556) reports that dowsers used hazel for silver, ash for copper, pitch pine for lead and tin, and rods of iron or steel for gold. The dowser grips the two branches in clenched fists and walks over the hills, and the twig is said to turn when his feet are over a vein.
