Flora.Lore: A Sunlander cattle fold is fenced with cut thorn. The gum tappers work the same trees their grandmothers scarred.

Flora.Name: Frankincense tree
Flora.Description: Evergreen tree to 8 m of dry mountains and desert woodland. The resin is burnt as incense and used in perfume and medicine. Pliny has it cut in summer and again in spring, the gatherers kept from women and funerals, and the gum taxed before it may leave.
Flora.Lore: Saltroad incense gatherers inherit their trees by name and may not sell them outside the clan.

Flora.Name: Myrrh tree
Flora.Description: Spiny deciduous shrub or small tree of about 5 m, of desert scrub on shallow limestone soil. The resin that weeps from cuts in the bark is used in medicine, perfume, incense and embalming. Pliny has the trees cut twice a year.
Flora.Lore: The Brinefolk embalmers are its best customers.

Flora.Name: Dragon's blood tree
Flora.Description: Evergreen tree of about 9 m with a dense umbrella crown, on rock and limestone. Its red resin is used in medicine, varnish, pottery colour and cosmetics.
Flora.Lore: Pliny's tale that the red is the blood of a dragon crushed by an elephant is told of this resin too. Apothecaries sell it by the tear.

Flora.Name: Baobab
Flora.Description: Deciduous tree to about 20 m with a swollen trunk up to 10 m across, of the thorn woodlands of the savanna. The fruit pulp, leaves and seeds are eaten. The bark gives cordage and cloth.
Flora.Lore: A village meets under its baobab. The Sunlander council that can depose a king sits in the shade of the oldest.

Flora.Name: Mesquite
Flora.Description: Thorny flat-topped tree of 5 to 10 m on light sandy soils of arid land. The pods make flour and drink. Posts, firewood and charcoal, and a tannin.
Flora.Lore: The pod flour keeps a year. Duskreader night markets price everything else against it.

Flora.Name: Teak
Flora.Description: Large, mostly deciduous tree over 30 m of the tropical deciduous forests. A first-rate timber. Bark and leaves give a dye.
Flora.Lore: Rainkeeper kings own every teak in the realm, standing or fallen, and mark each with a seal.

Flora.Name: Sal
Flora.Description: Tree of 20 to 25 m, the main forest tree of its range. Timber. The resin is burnt as incense and caulks boats. The seed gives a butter and a lamp oil, and the leaves serve as plates.
Flora.Lore: A Rainkeeper feast is eaten off sal leaves, and the count of leaves swept up is the count of guests.

Flora.Name: Sandalwood
Flora.Description: Small slow evergreen tree of 4 to 20 m of dry deciduous and scrub forest. The scented heartwood is carved, burnt as incense and pressed for a perfume oil.
Flora.Lore: The tree is weighed, not measured, and the roots are dug: nothing of it is left in the ground.

Flora.Name: Banyan and sacred fig
Flora.Description: Wide-crowned evergreen figs of 15 to 30 m that often start as a seedling on another tree. The banyan drops roots from its branches. Fruit, medicine, a bark fibre, and a latex used as varnish and sealing wax. Pliny wonders at the tree whose branches root and make arbours for shepherds.
Flora.Lore: A Rainkeeper village council of five sits under one, and nothing said outside its shade is binding.

Flora.Name: Neem
Flora.Description: Fast, long-lived evergreen of about 15 m with a dense crown. Bark, leaves and seed are a mainstay of medicine. Timber, firewood, and a resin used in soap.
Flora.Lore: Twigs for the teeth, leaves in the grain bin, a branch at the door in fever time.

Flora.Name: Kapok
Flora.Description: Deciduous tree of 10 to 30 m, at times 70 m, often spiny and buttressed. The floss around the seeds is a fibre for stuffing. The soft wood is of low grade.
Flora.Lore: The tallest tree of the forest and the ladder of the dead. Boughwalkers build no platform in one.

Flora.Name: Mahogany
Flora.Description: Slow evergreen of 30 to 40 m of mixed forest and riverbanks. A high-class furniture timber. The bark gives a dye and a tannin.
Flora.Lore: One log floated to the coast buys a village's salt for a year.

Flora.Name: Ebony and rosewood
Flora.Description: Ebony is a slow evergreen to 20 m with a black heartwood for furniture, instruments and carving. Rosewood is a tree of 30 to 40 m of monsoon forest with a high-value timber. Pliny notes ebony carried in a triumph.
Flora.Lore: The black keys of every court harp were once one tree, and its stump is still shown.

Flora.Name: Rubber tree
Flora.Description: Fast deciduous tree, over 40 m in the wild, of riverbanks and flooded rain forest. Its latex is the main source of natural rubber.
Flora.Lore: Boughwalkers seal their rope bridges with it. Lowlanders buy it for balls and for the soles of thieves.

Flora.Name: Cinnamon
Flora.Description: Slow evergreen of 7 to 18 m of moist forest, kept as a bush when cultivated. Bark and leaves flavour food, and the oils go to incense and medicine.
Flora.Lore: See the cinnamon bird. Rainkeeper spice growers peel it by the quill.

Flora.Name: Clove and nutmeg
Flora.Description: Evergreen trees of maritime forest and humid volcanic lowlands. The clove is a dried flower bud, taken as a spice and for toothache. The nutmeg seed and its mace are spices, and about 8 g of ground nutmeg can kill.
Flora.Lore: Each grows on a handful of coasts. Wars of the Scattered Age have been fought over a single grove.

Flora.Name: Agarwood
Flora.Description: Evergreen tree of about 20 m of primary and secondary forest. A dark resin forms in the wood and is burnt as incense, used in perfume and medicine. The inner bark gives a fibre for cloth and rope.
Flora.Lore: Only a wounded tree makes the resin, and one in many. The gatherers say the tree must first be given a grief.

Flora.Name: Fever-bark tree
Flora.Description: Evergreen shrub or small tree of 6 to 20 m of cool humid mountains between 1,200 and 3,000 m. The bark is the remedy for fevers and malaria. Too much brings headache, deafness and blindness. In the generator it stands where the rain forest climbs.
Flora.Lore: Bitterblood apothecaries sell it and are the only ones trusted to dose it.

Flora.Name: Logwood
Flora.Description: Thorny, gnarled tree to about 15 m of flat marshy lowland that rivers flood. The heartwood gives red and darker dyes, which is its main use. The flowers give honey.
Flora.Lore: Cut by gangs who live half the year in the swamp and are paid in the other half, if they come out.

Flora.Name: Flame of the forest
Flora.Description: Slow, crooked deciduous tree of 5 to 15 m of drier plains and grassland. The flowers give a yellow to orange dye. A red gum, a bark fibre, and a soft wood that lasts under water.
Flora.Lore: It flowers leafless at the end of the dry season. Twofold set the Going out by its bloom.

Flora.Name: Quebracho
Flora.Description: Tree of 20 to 25 m of dry plains. The wood is very durable, for posts, and a good fuel. Tannin is extracted from bark and heartwood on a commercial scale.
Flora.Lore: An axe that fells one is retired and hung up.

Flora.Name: Mangrove
Flora.Description: Trees and shrubs of muddy, salt or brackish shores. The red mangrove stands 5 to 20 m on arching stilt roots. Timber for posts and marine piling, firewood and charcoal, and a bark that tans. The grey mangrove gives boat timber and red and brown dyes.
Flora.Lore: Shoalfolk do not cut the seaward row. The one town that did is a sandbar now.

Flora.Name: Nipa palm
Flora.Description: Clumping palm with leaves to 6 m from a stem that lies in the mud of tidal flats. The sap gives syrup, sugar, vinegar and drink. The leaves thatch and are woven into baskets and mats.
Flora.Lore: Every roof in a Shoalfolk town is nipa, renewed after the storm season by the whole street.

Flora.Name: Dwarf willow
Flora.Description: The "low willows" that Britannica lists with the sedges, cotton grass and rushes of the tundra, where plants keep close to the ground against the wind. No species page was opened.
Flora.Lore: The Hearthbloods' only firewood above the tree line, cut with a knife and carried in a hat.

Flora.Name: Labrador tea
Flora.Description: Evergreen shrub of about 1 m of acid bogs. The aromatic leaves make a tea for coughs and colds and stood in for hops in beer. They repel insects. Brewed long in a closed pot, they are narcotic.
Flora.Lore: A Northmen ale brewed with it is called "the quarrel": it goes to the head and then to the fists.

Flora.Name: Bog myrtle
Flora.Description: Deciduous shrub of about 2 m of bogs, fens and wet heath. Leaves and fruit flavour ale. A wax for candles, a yellow dye, and a repellent of insects and moths. Not for the pregnant.
Flora.Lore: The ale herb of every people north of the hop line.

Flora.Name: Hawthorn
Flora.Description: Thorny deciduous shrub to 6 m of woods, hedges and thickets. The fruit is eaten. A remedy for the heart. It is planted as a hedge and a windbreak and gives tool handles and fuel.
Flora.Lore: Halfling fields are hawthorn-hedged, and a gap in the hedge is a gap in the law.

Flora.Name: Elder
Flora.Description: Fast deciduous shrub of about 6 m of hedgerows and rich disturbed ground. Flowers and cooked fruit go into wine and preserves. Dyes from bark and fruit. The leaves keep insects off and are poisonous.
Flora.Lore: Nobody burns elder or cuts it without asking. What is asked is not agreed between any two villages.

Flora.Name: Heather
Flora.Description: Evergreen shrub of about 0.6 m of acid moors and heaths. It flavours beer, gives a yellow dye and a tannin, and serves as fuel, thatch, brooms, bedding and rope.
Flora.Lore: A moorland house is heather from the roof to the bed to the fire.

Flora.Name: Sagebrush
Flora.Description: Evergreen shrub of about 2.5 m of dry plains and hills. A bitter leaf tea for colds and aches. Fuel, tinder, a bark fibre and a yellow dye. The seeds are ground for meal.
Flora.Lore: The smell of the cold desert after rain. Brinefolk say they can smell it through a wall of salt.

Flora.Name: Ephedra
Flora.Description: Evergreen shrub of about 0.4 m of desert, sandy ground and mountain slopes. An old remedy for asthma and hay fever. Dangerous to a weak heart.
Flora.Lore: Grass rider post riders chew it to stay in the saddle for two days. The third day is paid for.

Flora.Name: Saltbush
Flora.Description: Evergreen shrub of about 1.8 m of sandy and gravelly desert. Leaves are eaten cooked and the seed ground. Fodder, a windbreak, and a lather for washing.
Flora.Lore: Where it grows the well is brackish and the mutton needs no salt.

Flora.Name: Camel thorn
Flora.Description: Deciduous spiny shrub to 2 m of saline, dry and barren ground. A sweet "manna" forms on the twigs and pods. The root is a famine food.
Flora.Lore: The manna is shaken onto a cloth at dawn. Caravan law gives it to whoever spread the cloth, on anyone's land.

Flora.Name: Creosote bush
Flora.Description: Slow evergreen shrub of about 4 m of hot desert. A leaf tea for wounds and chests that harms the liver if taken long. Its resin keeps fat from going rancid.
Flora.Lore: A ring of bushes is one plant older than any kingdom, the Duskreaders say, and they hold their markets inside the rings.

Flora.Name: Saguaro
Flora.Description: Columnar ribbed cactus that branches at about 5 m and reaches 15 m. It first flowers at 50 to 75 years and lives 150 to 200. The fruit is eaten, and the woody skeleton is used.
Flora.Lore: A giant with its arms raised marks a grave or a well. The traveller is expected to know which.

Flora.Name: Sisal and agave
Flora.Description: Evergreen succulent rosette of 1.5 to 2 m of the drier tropics that sends up one flower stem of 5 to 6 m and dies. Leaf fibre for rope, nets and paper. A fermented drink from the heart. Living fences.
Flora.Lore: Noonfolk estates are fenced with it, and the fence is the rope walk's raw stock.

Flora.Name: Mastic
Flora.Description: Slow evergreen shrub of about 5 m of dry hillsides near the sea. The resin is chewed and flavours food. Varnish, a fixative for perfume, and a tannin.
Flora.Lore: Chewed by sailors to sweeten the breath before they lie to the harbour master.

Flora.Name: Oleander
Flora.Description: Fast evergreen shrub of about 4 m of river banks and gravels. The whole plant is very poisonous: one leaf has killed a child. A hedge and an insecticide.
Flora.Lore: An army once roasted its meat on oleander spits, the story goes. The other army won without a fight.

Flora.Name: Henna
Flora.Description: Evergreen shrub or small tree to 7 m of dry scrub and riverbeds. The leaves dye hair, skin and nails. The flowers give a perfume oil.
Flora.Lore: A Saltroad bride's hands are painted with the route of her family's caravan.

Flora.Name: Tea
Flora.Description: Slow evergreen shrub of about 4 m of shaded mountain forest. The leaf is drunk as a stimulant and an astringent. The seed gives an oil.
Flora.Lore: Canal folk grow it on the hills above the paddies. An official's rank shows in the leaf he is served.

Flora.Name: Coffee
Flora.Description: Evergreen shrub of 1.5 to 3 m of the understorey of humid highland forest. The roasted seed is a stimulant drink. In the generator it stands on tropical highlands.
Flora.Lore: Saltroad coffee growers sell the bean and keep the husk for themselves.

Flora.Name: Indigo
Flora.Description: Erect shrub of 1 to 2 m of the tropics. The leaves give a deep blue dye.
Flora.Lore: The dyers' quarter is downstream and downwind, and its people are known by their forearms.

Flora.Name: Cotton
Flora.Description: Plant of about 1.5 m known only from cultivation. The seed floss is spun for cloth and used as stuffing. Twine, rope and paper. The seed gives an oil. Pliny knew of trees that bear wool.
Flora.Lore: Rainkeeper cotton weavers clothe three peoples and pay the temple a tenth of every bolt.

Flora.Name: Mistletoe
Flora.Description: Evergreen shrub about 1 m across that grows on the branches of poplar, apple and other trees. It slows the heart and calms. All parts are slightly poisonous.
Flora.Lore: Pliny's druids cut it from an oak on the fifth day of the moon, a priest in white with a golden sickle, and catch it in a white cloak. Taken in drink it makes barren beasts fertile and is an antidote to all poisons. Frazer takes it for the golden bough.

Flora.Name: Arctic poppy
Flora.Description: Short-lived perennial of about 0.3 m on stony slopes and river gravels of the far north. Flowers and capsules ease pain and scurvy. The flowers give red and beige dyes. Mildly toxic.
Flora.Lore: It turns its face with the sun through the nightless summer. Hoarkin children are told it is counting the days for them.

Flora.Name: Fireweed
Flora.Description: Fast perennial of about 1.7 m on rocky and waste ground and woodland edges. Shoots, leaves and pith are eaten. The stems give cordage and the seed hairs tinder. An astringent for the gut and for burns.
Flora.Lore: The first colour on burnt ground. Charcoal burners' camps are found by it the year after.

Flora.Name: Tulip
Flora.Description: Bulb with a few blue-green leaves and one bell-shaped flower, native to the inner steppe lands. Grown in gardens for a thousand years, and once the object of a trade mania.
Flora.Lore: Grass riders pick the wild ones for a girl's hair. In Canal folk cities a striped bulb has been sold for a house.

Flora.Name: Sunflower
Flora.Description: Fast annual of 0.5 to 3 m of open dry plains. Seeds and their oil are eaten. A yellow dye from the flowers, a purple-black one from the seeds, and fibre from the stem.
Flora.Lore: Noonfolk, who live by the sun, plant it at the field corners and take its turning as a salute.

Flora.Name: Coneflower
Flora.Description: Perennial of about 1.2 m of dry limestone prairie. The root is a remedy for sores, wounds and burns and against infection.
Flora.Lore: The Flinchless, who do not feel their wounds, are taught to chew it whenever they see their own blood.

Flora.Name: Peony
Flora.Description: Perennial of about 0.6 m of rocky woods and meadows on limestone. The root calms spasms and was given for the falling sickness. The whole plant is poisonous in quantity.
Flora.Lore: Canal folk courts grow a hundred kinds, and an official is judged by his peony bed.

Flora.Name: Asphodel
Flora.Description: Perennial of about 1 m of dry hills, rough ground and mountain meadows. The tubers are a cough remedy, were once eaten, and are fermented for spirit. The root is poisonous raw.
Flora.Lore: It covers the fields no one ploughs any more. The dead are said to walk in a meadow of it.

Flora.Name: Saffron crocus
Flora.Description: Small corm about 0.1 m high, not known wild. The dried styles flavour and colour food and give a yellow dye. A sedative. Five to ten grams can kill.
Flora.Lore: Picked before sunrise by the Swiftborn. A pound is a hundred thousand flowers and a month of fingers.

Flora.Name: Dog rose
Flora.Description: Fast deciduous shrub of about 3 m of hedges, scrub and roadsides. The hips are taken against colds and scurvy and made into syrup, jam and tea. The petals are eaten.
Flora.Lore: A rose over a door means the house keeps a secret. Over an inn, that it keeps everyone's.

Flora.Name: Lavender
Flora.Description: Slow evergreen shrub of about 1.2 m of dry, grassy, rocky slopes, often on chalk. The oil scents soap and perfume, calms and cleans wounds, and the flowers keep insects away.
Flora.Lore: Midlander washerwomen take their trade name from it, and their guild is older than the weavers'.

Flora.Name: Rose of Jericho
Flora.Description: Small grey desert plant that curls its branches into a ball when dry and opens to 30 cm across when wetted.
Flora.Lore: Saltroad midwives set a dry one in water when labour begins. The child is due when it has opened.

Flora.Name: Rafflesia
Flora.Description: A parasite with no leaves, roots or stem, living as threads inside a forest vine. Only the flower shows: about 1 m across, up to 11 kg, smelling of carrion.
Flora.Lore: Bitterbloods call it the honest flower: it smells like what it is.

Flora.Name: Roseroot
Flora.Description: Evergreen clumping perennial of about 0.3 m in the crevices of mountain rocks and sea cliffs of the cold north. A tonic against fatigue. Leaves, shoots and roots are eaten.
Flora.Lore: Northmen crews chew it on the oar bench. A bride is given a root so that the house will have strong sons.

Flora.Name: Yarrow
Flora.Description: Upright perennial of about 0.6 m of meadows and pastures. Used for wounds and bleeding, colds and fevers. A hop substitute in beer, and a yellow and green dye.
Flora.Lore: Soldier's woundwort. A Flinchless drill master will not march without a sack of it.

Flora.Name: Wormwood
Flora.Description: Perennial of about 1 m of waste land, rocks and screes. A bitter tonic for the liver and digestion and a worm remedy. It drives off insects and mice. Poisonous in quantity.
Flora.Lore: Strewn in a granary against mice, and steeped in the spirit that Orc hearths drink before a raid.

Flora.Name: Liquorice
Flora.Description: Perennial to about 1.2 m of dry open places, spreading by rhizomes. The root sweetens and flavours and soothes coughs. Too much raises the blood pressure.
Flora.Lore: Caravan children are paid in liquorice root, and so are informers.

Flora.Name: Chamomile
Flora.Description: Annual to 0.5 m of sandy arable land and saline steppe. The flower tea calms the stomach and the nerves. A yellow dye and a hair rinse.
Flora.Lore: The Halfling answer to every illness, and to most bad news.

Flora.Name: Sage
Flora.Description: Upright evergreen shrub of about 0.6 m of dry banks and stony ground. Antiseptic and astringent, a gargle. It flavours food. Toxic in excess.
Flora.Lore: "Why should he die who has sage in his garden" is a Midlander proverb and a Saltroad joke.

Flora.Name: Thyme and rosemary
Flora.Description: Evergreen shrubs of dry slopes, rocks and scrub near the sea, thyme a mat of 0.2 m and rosemary a bush of 1.5 m. They flavour food. Thyme is a remedy for coughs, rosemary a tonic for low spirits. Their oils go into soap and perfume.
Flora.Lore: Rosemary is carried at weddings and funerals. The same sprig will do for both, say the Swiftborn, who have little time between.

Flora.Name: Opium poppy
Flora.Description: Annual of about 0.6 m, not known wild. The dried latex kills pain and brings sleep and is highly addictive. The seeds and their oil are eaten, and the oil serves for lamps and paint.
Flora.Lore: The surgeon's friend and the debtor's ruin. In many towns only the temple may sell it.

Flora.Name: Valerian
Flora.Description: Perennial of about 1.5 m of grassland, scrub and woods. The root is a tranquilliser, for sleep and cramps. Long use becomes a habit.
Flora.Lore: Cats will follow whoever carries it. Catfolk consider the joke old.

Flora.Name: St John's wort
Flora.Description: Perennial of about 0.9 m of open woods, hedge banks and dry grassland. Taken against low spirits. Flowers and leaves give yellow, gold, brown and red dyes. It makes the skin burn in sunlight.
Flora.Lore: Gathered at midsummer and hung in the byre against fire and worse.

Flora.Name: Foxglove
Flora.Description: Biennial of about 1.2 m of acid soils in woods and on heaths. The leaves act on the heart. The dose that heals is close to the dose that kills.
Flora.Lore: A physician is someone who knows how much. A poisoner is someone who knows a little more.

Flora.Name: Comfrey
Flora.Description: Fast upright perennial of about 1.2 m of damp meadows, woods and streamsides. Laid on cuts, bruises, sprains and broken bones. Taken inwardly, it harms the liver.
Flora.Lore: "Knitbone" in every language of the Midlands.

Flora.Name: Angelica
Flora.Description: Biennial of about 1.5 m of moist shady places. Stalks, leaves and roots are eaten and the seed flavours drink. A remedy for the digestion and the circulation.
Flora.Lore: Northmen candy the stalks for the winter feast. It is the only sweet thing in the house until the bees wake.

Flora.Name: Gentian and arnica
Flora.Description: Perennials of high mountain pastures. The gentian root is a bitter tonic for the digestion and once flavoured beer. Arnica is laid on bruises and sprains, on unbroken skin only: swallowed, it can kill.
Flora.Lore: Dwarf brewers bitter their ale with gentian. Avalanche rescuers carry arnica.

Flora.Name: Nettle
Flora.Description: Fast perennial of about 1.2 m of hedgerows, woods and rich waste ground. Young leaves are eaten as greens. The stem fibre makes string and cloth. Green and yellow dyes. The sting goes with cooking.
Flora.Lore: Shirts of nettle cloth were what the poor wore through the Ashen Years, when the flax failed.

Flora.Name: Woad
Flora.Description: Biennial of about 1 m of cliffs and cornfields, often on chalk. The leaves give a blue dye and preserve wood.
Flora.Lore: The blue of the north. Northmen sworn guards are painted with it before a fight they do not expect to leave.

Flora.Name: Madder
Flora.Description: Evergreen perennial of about 1 m of hedgerows and neglected ground. The roots give a red dye. The prickly leaves polish metal.
Flora.Lore: Soldiers' red. A realm's madder fields are counted with its armouries.

Flora.Name: Flax
Flora.Description: Annual of about 0.7 m, not known wild. The stem fibre makes cloth, sails, nets and paper. The seed is eaten, and its oil goes into paint and varnish.
Flora.Lore: A Midlander girl spins her own shroud first, so that everything she spins afterwards is profit.

Flora.Name: Hemp
Flora.Description: Annual of about 2.5 m of rich soils near houses. Fibre for cloth and rope. Seed and oil are eaten. It eases pain and sickness and can intoxicate.
Flora.Lore: Every hull that carries Northmen carries a field of hemp in its rigging.

Flora.Name: Ginseng
Flora.Description: Perennial of about 0.8 m of mountain forests. The root is a tonic against weakness, sleeplessness and strain.
Flora.Lore: A root shaped like a man is worth his weight in silver. Canal folk physicians pay Amberblood diggers and ask no questions.

Flora.Name: Monkshood
Flora.Description: Perennial of about 1.5 m of damp shady places and moist meadows. Highly toxic to the nerves: even touching it numbs the skin. The root was used outwardly against pain.
Flora.Lore: Wolfsbane: herders of the north tip their wolf arrows with it and bury the wolf where it falls.

Flora.Name: Deadly nightshade
Flora.Description: Perennial of about 0.9 m of woods, thickets and hedges on limy ground. The whole plant is very poisonous, most of all the root and the ripe berries. It widens the pupils.
Flora.Lore: Courtesans drop it in the eyes to look wide awake, and in the cup to make sure the other does not.

Flora.Name: Hemlock
Flora.Description: Biennial of about 2 m of waste ground and damp places. Very poisonous, the seeds most: death comes by suffocation. Once given as a sedative and against pain.
Flora.Lore: The cup that the old city courts offered a condemned citizen, as a courtesy.

Flora.Name: Rhubarb
Flora.Description: Clumping perennial of up to 3 m of scrub, rocky ground and streamsides at high elevation. The root is a laxative and a tonic for the digestion. The leaves are poisonous.
Flora.Lore: It crosses half the world by caravan, and each hand that carries it doubles the price.

Flora.Name: Glasswort
Flora.Description: Annual of about 0.3 m of coastal sands, mudflats and salt marsh. The young stems are a pot herb. The ash is rich in soda, for soap and glass.
Flora.Lore: Brinefolk soda burners and glassmakers cut it by the cartload at the autumn low tides.

Flora.Name: Clover and lucerne
Flora.Description: Perennials of meadows and pastures, lucerne with a deep taproot. They feed the soil and are dug in as green manure. Leaves and sprouts are eaten. A yellow dye.
Flora.Lore: "Clover in, wheat out" is the whole of Halfling farming as they explain it to others.

Flora.Name: Silphium
Flora.Description: A herb of one dry coast whose juice was prized as medicine and perfume and sold for its weight in silver. It vanished when the land was let for sheep, and the last stalk found was sent to the emperor as a curiosity. Extinct in our world. Its relative the giant fennel is a perennial of 2.5 m of dry hills whose gum is burnt as incense and whose pith is a slow tinder.
Flora.Lore: Here it survives in a few zones. The Saltroad clans that hold them do not say which.

Flora.Name: Dittany
Flora.Description: Perennial of about 0.2 m of shady rocks in dry high mountains, native to one island. Once a wound herb. The leaves flavour drink and make a tea.
Flora.Lore: Wounded goats are said to seek it out, and goatherds to follow the goats.

Flora.Name: Aloe
Flora.Description: Evergreen succulent of 0.6 to 1 m of maritime sands and rocks. The leaf gel is laid on wounds and burns. The sap is a laxative.
Flora.Lore: Every caravan cook grows one in a pot on the lead camel.

Flora.Name: Senna
Flora.Description: Deciduous shrub to 3 m of semi-desert scrub, grassland and riverbanks. Leaves and pods are an old purge.
Flora.Lore: Sold in the night markets of the Duskreaders next to the dates, as its remedy.

Flora.Name: Devil's claw
Flora.Description: Sprawling perennial with fleshy tubers, of veld and waste ground on clay or sand. The bitter root eases pain and swelling. The spiny fruits lame the feet.
Flora.Lore: Sunlander herders dig the root for their own joints and curse the fruit for their cattle's hooves.

Flora.Name: Holy basil
Flora.Description: Aromatic perennial of 0.3 to 1 m with a woody base. A remedy for fevers, colds and the digestion. The stems are cut into prayer beads, and the oil repels insects.
Flora.Lore: A pot of it stands in every Rainkeeper courtyard. The house is not a house until it is planted.

Flora.Name: Ipecac
Flora.Description: Shrub of about 0.5 m of the rain forest understorey. The root brings up vomit and phlegm and is given for coughs and dysentery. An overdose is dangerous.
Flora.Lore: What a Bitterblood antidote maker reaches for first: most poisons are best met coming back up.

Flora.Name: Ginger and turmeric
Flora.Description: Perennial herbs of about 1 m with spreading rhizomes, known only from cultivation. Ginger flavours food and settles the stomach. Turmeric is a spice and a yellow to orange dye for silk and wool.
Flora.Lore: Rainkeeper brides are rubbed yellow with turmeric.

Flora.Name: Thorn apple
Flora.Description: Erect annual to 2 m of waste places and sandy riverbanks. All parts are poisonous and narcotic. Given for asthma and pain and before surgery. The gap between dose and death is small.
Flora.Lore: A Sunlander diviner takes it once, at initiation, and speaks of what he saw for the rest of his life.

Flora.Name: Cloudberry and crowberry
Flora.Description: Low plants of about 0.3 m of cool bogs, moors and mountain tops. Both fruits are eaten raw or cooked and give a purple dye.
Flora.Lore: Cloudberry bogs are owned by families in Northmen law, and trespass in berry time is paid for in silver.

Flora.Name: Bilberry
Flora.Description: Suckering shrub of about 0.2 m of heaths, moors and woods on acid soil. Sweet fruit for eating and preserves. A blue or black dye and an ink from the fruit.
Flora.Lore: Children come home blue to the elbows, and the scribe buys what they did not eat.

Flora.Name: Raspberry and bramble
Flora.Description: Suckering shrub of about 2 m of hedgerows, woodland edges and neglected land. Fruit, shoots and a leaf tea that is given in childbirth. A purple-blue dye.
Flora.Lore: The hedge that feeds the poor. No lord has managed to tax it.

Flora.Name: Salmonberry
Flora.Description: Deciduous shrub of about 1.8 m of moist places in and around woods on the wet coast. Fruit and peeled shoots are eaten. The leaves and root are astringent.
Flora.Lore: It ripens when the first salmon run, and is eaten with them.

Flora.Name: Sea buckthorn
Flora.Description: Deciduous thorny shrub of about 6 m of coasts, dunes and sea cliffs, and inland across Asia. The sour fruit and its oil are a tonic and are laid on burns. Yellow and brown dyes, fuel and charcoal. It holds loose soil.
Flora.Lore: Grass riders feed it to tired horses, and their word for it means "shining horse".

Flora.Name: Hazel
Flora.Description: Deciduous shrub or tree of about 6 m of woods and hedgerows. Nuts and their oil. The rods make baskets. Charcoal.
Flora.Lore: A forked hazel rod finds water and ore in the right hands. Every well-finder owns one, and no two agree on how it is held.

Flora.Name: Apple
Flora.Description: Deciduous tree of about 9 m, not known truly wild. The fruit is eaten raw, cooked and dried. The wood is turned and burnt. The seeds are poisonous in quantity.
Flora.Lore: Halflings keep an orchard behind every burrow and sell cider to people who have never seen a Halfling sober or drunk.

Flora.Name: Sweet chestnut
Flora.Description: Deciduous tree to about 30 m of mountain woods. The nuts are eaten roasted or ground to flour. Good fuel, fence posts and carpentry. The bark tans.
Flora.Lore: The bread tree of hill villages that have no ploughland.

Flora.Name: Walnut
Flora.Description: Rounded deciduous tree of about 20 m. Nuts and oil. Dyes and a tannin. A fine timber and a drying oil for paint.
Flora.Lore: Planted at a son's birth for the furniture of his wedding. Nothing grows under it, and nobody sleeps there twice.

Flora.Name: Olive
Flora.Description: Slow evergreen tree of about 10 m of woods and scrub in dry rocky places. The cured fruit is eaten. The oil is food, medicine, soap, lamp fuel and lubricant. A hard wood for turning.
Flora.Lore: A grove outlives the realm that planted it. Swiftborn pickers were made for the harvest and are still paid by it.

Flora.Name: Fig
Flora.Description: Deciduous tree of about 6 m among rocks and scrub on hot dry soils. The fruit is eaten fresh and dried and loosens the bowels. The latex curdles milk and burns the eyes.
Flora.Lore: The traveller's tree: it fruits twice and asks for nothing. To cut one down by a road is a curse.

Flora.Name: Pomegranate
Flora.Description: Deciduous shrub or small tree of 4 to 10 m on dry limestone soils. The fruit and juice are eaten. Rind and flowers give a red dye, an ink and a tannin. The bark kills tapeworm and can kill the patient.
Flora.Lore: Whoever eats in the house of the dead stays there, the old stories say. Saltroad hosts offer one to seal a debt.

Flora.Name: Almond
Flora.Description: Deciduous tree of about 6 m of thickets and rocky places. The seeds are eaten raw, roasted and ground, and give an oil for soap and the skin. The bitter kind is poisonous.
Flora.Lore: The first blossom of the year. Poisoners prize the bitter tree that looks the same.

Flora.Name: Carob
Flora.Description: Evergreen tree of about 15 m of rocky places near the sea. The sweet pods are eaten or ground and feed stock. The seed gives a flour and a gum.
Flora.Lore: Jewellers weigh gems against its seeds, which are all of one weight, or so the jewellers say.

Flora.Name: Citron
Flora.Description: Evergreen shrub or small tree to 4 m, known only in cultivation. The fruit and its candied peel are eaten. A perfume, and a repellent of moths.
Flora.Lore: A ship that carries them loses no teeth, and Canal folk captains guard the knowledge like a chart.

Flora.Name: Date palm
Flora.Description: Evergreen palm of 25 to 30 m, not known truly wild. The fruit is a staple and a sweetener. Sap, thatch, fibre for rope, baskets and mats, wood and fuel.
Flora.Lore: The Saltroad date gardener counts his palms as a herder counts cattle, and knows each by the taste.

Flora.Name: Prickly pear
Flora.Description: Evergreen cactus to about 5 m of dry, rocky places. The sweet fruit and the cooked pads are eaten. The pads feed stock, and the plant makes a fence. The fine barbed spines stay in the skin. It is the host of the cochineal insect.
Flora.Lore: A hedge that feeds the goats, the children and the dyer.

Flora.Name: Jujube
Flora.Description: Fast, often thorny deciduous tree of about 10 m on dry stony slopes. The fruit is eaten fresh and dried and is a tonic for sleep. Fuel, charcoal and hedging.
Flora.Lore: Travellers who eat it in a strange land are said to forget the way home. The innkeepers who serve it do not deny this.

Flora.Name: Watermelon
Flora.Description: Trailing annual with stems to 4 m of open ground in desert country. The fruit is water and food. The seeds are roasted and pressed for oil.
Flora.Lore: The wild kind is the hunter's well. Duskreaders find the cool fruit in the dark as others find a lamp.

Flora.Name: Shea
Flora.Description: Deciduous tree of 7 to 15 m with a dense spreading crown, of open parkland savanna. The seed fat is shea butter. Timber and charcoal.
Flora.Lore: The women's tree: the nuts and the butter money are theirs by Sunlander custom.

Flora.Name: Tamarind
Flora.Description: Slow tree of 20 to 30 m of low woodland, savanna and riverbanks, often by termite mounds. Pods, leaves and seeds are eaten. Timber, charcoal, a tannin and a leaf dye.
Flora.Lore: The sour pulp polishes brass, and temple lamps are cleaned with nothing else.

Flora.Name: Mango
Flora.Description: Large evergreen of 10 to 45 m with an umbrella crown. Fruit. Timber for building and boats. Bark and leaves dye silk. The sap can raise a rash.
Flora.Lore: A Rainkeeper king is remembered by the mango groves he planted along the roads.

Flora.Name: Banana and plantain
Flora.Description: Evergreen giant herb of about 3 m of moist ravines and slopes. Fruit, flower and stem core are eaten. Fibre for cloth, rugs and paper. The leaves wrap food.
Flora.Lore: The plate, the roof in a shower and the meal are the same plant.

Flora.Name: Coconut
Flora.Description: Single-stemmed palm to 30 m of tropical seashores. The seed gives food, milk and oil. The husk fibre makes mats and rope. Timber, and charcoal from the shell.
Flora.Lore: It floats to a new shore by itself. Shoalfolk claim a beach by planting three.

Flora.Name: Cacao
Flora.Description: Small evergreen tree of about 8 m of the understorey of wet lowland rain forest. The seeds give cocoa and a fat.
Flora.Lore: Boughwalkers drink it bitter and sell it to people who add honey and call it a luxury.

Flora.Name: Kola nut
Flora.Description: Evergreen understorey tree of 9 to 12 m of lowland forest. The seeds are a stimulant, chewed or made into drink. Timber for furniture and boats.
Flora.Lore: Split and shared before any Sunlander bargain. To refuse the half is to refuse the deal.

Flora.Name: Oil palm
Flora.Description: Single-stemmed palm of 20 to 30 m of open forest on wet sandy soils by rivers. Palm oil and palm wine. The leaflets give rope fibre and the shells fuel a furnace.
Flora.Lore: Sunlander smelters fire their furnaces with the shells and oil their iron with the fruit.

Flora.Name: Brazil nut
Flora.Description: Very large evergreen of 25 to 56 m on deep alluvial soil that rarely floods. The seeds are eaten. Durable timber.
Flora.Lore: The fruit falls like a thrown stone. Gatherers work in wide hats and short visits.

Flora.Name: Areca palm
Flora.Description: Single-stemmed palm of 15 to 30 m of the understorey of wet forest. The seed is chewed as a stimulant. A tannin for dyeing. Too much brings vomiting and stupor.
Flora.Lore: Offered to every guest in Rainkeeper country. The red spit on a road tells how far the next town is.

Flora.Name: Sago palm
Flora.Description: Clumping palm of 6 to 25 m of lowland freshwater swamp. The pith of the stem is washed for starch, and a stem dies after it flowers. The leaves thatch.
Flora.Lore: One trunk feeds a family for a month, and Bitterbloods farm nothing else.

Flora.Name: Palmyra palm
Flora.Description: Very tall single-stemmed palm of 20 to 30 m of hot dry monsoon country on sandy and alluvial soil. Sap, fruit and young seeds are food. Timber, fibre and thatch.
Flora.Lore: The leaf is the Rainkeeper scribe's page, scratched with a stylus and rubbed with soot.

Flora.Name: Cottongrass
Flora.Description: Sedge of about 0.6 m of peat bogs, acid meadows and marshes. The white seed hairs make candle wicks, tinder and pillow stuffing. The leaves are woven into mats.
Flora.Lore: When the bog turns white, the reindeer calves have been born and the herders may move.

Flora.Name: Feather grass
Flora.Description: The plumed bunch grass that gives the steppe its silver sheen in the wind. General knowledge no page on it could be opened.
Flora.Lore: Grass riders say the steppe has a pelt, and that it should be stroked the right way: they ride with the wind when they can.

Flora.Name: Tallgrass
Flora.Description: Clump-forming perennial grass about 2 m tall of prairies, open ground and open woods. Forage and hay for horses and cattle.
Flora.Lore: A rider can be lost in it standing. Widegaze build their mounds to see over it.

Flora.Name: Wild barley
Flora.Description: The wild grass from which barley was bred about ten thousand years ago. Barley resists dry heat, grows from the subarctic to the desert edge, and is fodder, malt for beer, and bread and porridge.
Flora.Lore: Gnome seedsmen keep the wild grass in sealed jars beside the tame, in case the tame is lost again.

Flora.Name: Esparto
Flora.Description: Grass of 1 to 1.2 m with clustered wiry stems, of dry sandy soil near southern coasts. Fibre for ropes, sandals, baskets and mats. The leaves make paper. Young plants are forage.
Flora.Lore: The sandals of every Saltroad porter, and the rope of every well.

Flora.Name: Reed and cattail
Flora.Description: Tall perennials of 1.5 to 3.6 m of shallow water and wet ground, found almost worldwide. Reed thatches and makes baskets, paper and string. Cattail gives starchy roots, mats, tinder, rush lights and stuffing.
Flora.Lore: A marsh village owes its lord reeds, not grain, and thatches his hall every seventh year.

Flora.Name: Papyrus
Flora.Description: Clump-forming sedge to 5 m in great stands in swamps, shallow lakes and along streams. Paper, boats, cordage, sandals, mats and huts. Rhizomes and stems are eaten. Herodotus has the marsh people eat the lower stalk baked.
Flora.Lore: The archives of the Old Realms were written on it, and what survives of them survives where it is dry.

Flora.Name: Bamboo
Flora.Description: Fast evergreen giant grass of about 8 m, of woodland and mountain slopes. The young shoots are eaten. Timber, water pipes, weaving and paper.
Flora.Lore: Canal folk scaffolding, water pipes and brush handles. It flowers once in a lifetime, and a famine follows the rats that follow the seed.

Flora.Name: Elephant grass
Flora.Description: Clumping grass with cane-like stems of 3 to 7 m, of damp grassland and forest edges. Forage. Fences, huts and thatch.
Flora.Lore: The grass that hides the elephant and the lion. Sunlander herders burn it at the end of the dry season and walk behind the fire.

Flora.Name: Sorghum
Flora.Description: Vigorous annual grass up to 5 m of the semi-arid tropics. Grain and flour, and a syrup from the sweet stems. Brooms, fencing, mats and roofing. The young or wilted plant is poisonous to stock.
Flora.Lore: Millet and sorghum are the Sunlander grains, and the beer of every funeral.

Flora.Name: Sugar cane
Flora.Description: Large perennial grass with canes of 2 to 3 m and more, known only from cultivation. Sugar, syrup and molasses. The stem is chewed.
Flora.Lore: White sugar is a Rainkeeper secret and a physician's drug everywhere else.

Flora.Name: Wild rice
Flora.Description: Perennial grass to 2 m of swamps, pond and stream edges and ditches, in water to 30 cm. The seed is cooked like rice and is a famine food. It crosses with the crop and is a weed of the paddy.
Flora.Lore: Rainkeeper reservoir keepers weed it out of the paddies and eat it in bad years.

Flora.Name: Hops
Flora.Description: Fast perennial climber of about 7 m of riverbanks and moist thickets. The cones flavour beer and bring sleep. Young shoots are eaten. Stem fibre for cloth and paper. The page read describes the plant from another continent's range.
Flora.Lore: The line between ale lands and beer lands is the hop line, and brewers have fought over it.

Flora.Name: Grape vine
Flora.Description: Fast deciduous climber of about 15 m of riversides and damp woods. The fruit is eaten fresh and dried and made into wine. The leaves are eaten. Seed oil and cream of tartar.
Flora.Lore: The vineyards of the Old Realms went wild in the Ashen Years. The Swiftborn were made to dress them.

Flora.Name: Black pepper
Flora.Description: Woody climber to 10 m with clinging roots. The dried fruit is black and white pepper. A remedy for the digestion and for fever. Pliny knew the long, the white and the black kind and their prices.
Flora.Lore: Counted out by the corn in northern markets, and taken as rent.

Flora.Name: Vanilla
Flora.Description: Climbing orchid with a succulent stem of 5 to 15 m and aerial roots, of warm wet lowland forest. The cured seed pods flavour sweet food and scent perfume.
Flora.Lore: Each flower opens for one morning and is fertilised by hand. Boughwalker fingers are the right length.

Flora.Name: Rattan
Flora.Description: Spiny climbing palm with stems as thick as a finger that pass 30 m. The stems make baskets, furniture, rope and hanging bridges. The shoots are eaten.
Flora.Lore: The Boughwalker high roads are rattan, renewed strand by strand so that no bridge is ever old or new.

Flora.Name: Curare vine
Flora.Description: Woody climber with stems to 30 m into the canopy. The source of an arrow poison that kills by stopping the breath, and only if it enters the blood: swallowed, it does no harm.
Flora.Lore: A hunter tests the brew on a frog and counts its jumps. Three is good poison.

Flora.Name: Yam
Flora.Description: Perennial climber with yearly stems to 15 m and a large tuber, not known wild. The tuber is boiled or baked. Raw, it is toxic.
Flora.Lore: The yam barn shows a Sunlander farmer's standing, and the first tuber of the year is the king's.

Flora.Name: Bottle gourd
Flora.Description: Fast annual climber with stems of about 9 m, not known wild. The young fruit is eaten. The hard dry shell makes bottles, bowls, ladles and instruments.
Flora.Lore: The first pot and the first drum. A hunter calls the jaguar with one.

Flora.Name: Colocynth
Flora.Description: Trailing perennial of sand dunes with a woody root. The dried pulp of the unripe fruit is a violent purge and a poison in excess. The seeds are roasted and give a lamp oil.
Flora.Lore: The bitter apple: it looks like water in the sand and has killed more lost men than thirst.

Flora.Name: Fly agaric
Flora.Description: Mushroom with a red to orange cap set with white warts, of forests and pastures of the temperate and boreal north. Poisonous and hallucinogenic: sickness and confusion, rarely death. Once used to kill flies.
Flora.Lore: Northmen seers eat it dried before they speak for the dead. The reindeer find it first.

Flora.Name: Cep
Flora.Description: Mushroom with pores in place of gills that lives with the roots of spruce, pine, oak and beech. Valued for its nutty taste and meaty flesh.
Flora.Lore: Dwarves and Gnomes grow mushrooms in the dark. This one they have to walk out and find, like everyone else.

Flora.Name: Truffle
Flora.Description: Round fruiting body that grows underground on tree roots in open woodland on chalky soil. A prized food. Pliny describes it as a growth without root in dry sandy ground and rates the southern kind highest.
Flora.Lore: Found with a pig or a dog. Stillfaces, whose nose is as keen as a hound's, need neither.

Flora.Name: Death cap
Flora.Description: Mushroom with a greenish yellow to tan cap of 4 to 16 cm, white gills, a ring and a bulb at the base, near oaks, birches and elms. It causes most deaths by mushroom, and cooking does not make it safe.
Flora.Lore: Bitterbloods eat toadstools at table. A guest who is served the same dish should think about why.

Flora.Name: Fairy ring
Flora.Description: A fungus that grows outward underground in a circle and puts up its mushrooms as a ring that widens each year. Old rings can be hundreds of metres across.
Flora.Lore: Nobody ploughs through one. The Elves say the ring is a door, and do not say to where.

Flora.Name: Ergot
Flora.Description: A fungus of rye, and of sorghum and pearl millet, that replaces the grain with purple-black horns. Bread from such rye brings convulsions, visions, gangrene and death. In small doses it stops bleeding after childbirth.
Flora.Lore: A village that dances and burns in a wet year has eaten the rye wolf's bread.

Flora.Name: Foxfire
Flora.Description: The glow of rotting wood, made by luminous fungi on dead wood in moist forest, most often in the tropics.
Flora.Lore: Lanternkin mark their night paths with foxfire logs.

Flora.Name: Snow algae
Flora.Description: Algae that live on the surface of snow and ice and stain it red.
Flora.Lore: Red snow is the blood of the amarok's last kill. Hoarkin step around it.

Flora.Name: Ice-edge lichens and mosses
Flora.Description: Lichens and mosses are almost the whole plant cover of the icy barrens, with a very few flowering plants in the most sheltered places.
Flora.Lore: The ring of grey on a rock tells a Hoarkin guide how long the ice has been gone from it.

Flora.Name: Reindeer lichen
Flora.Description: Bushy, branched lichen about 8 cm high that covers great areas of tundra and taiga and grows a few millimetres a year. The winter grazing of reindeer, moose and musk ox. A spirit is distilled from it.
Flora.Lore: Grazed ground takes a generation to grow back, so a herding family's round is as long as a life.

Flora.Name: Iceland moss
Flora.Description: Branched bushy lichen about 7 cm high, brown to grey-white, of alpine and northern ground. Soaked, dried and ground, it goes into bread, soups and jellies. Reindeer and stock eat it.
Flora.Lore: The bread of the Ashen Years in the north, and still the bread of the last weeks of winter.

Flora.Name: Beard lichen
Flora.Description: Yellow or greenish hanging lichen of tree branches, in humid mountains up to 1.5 m long. An old remedy for coughs. Some kinds give an orange dye. It burns readily when dry.
Flora.Lore: Old forest wears a beard. Elves judge a wood's age and health by it and settle only under bearded trees.

Flora.Name: Dye lichen
Flora.Description: Lichens of sea rocks that give a purple dye, orchil, when fermented. It dyed silk, wool and parchment and was the cheap everyday purple.
Flora.Lore: The poor man's purple. Sumptuary law forbids it as strictly as the real one, and is obeyed less.

Flora.Name: Peat moss
Flora.Description: Mosses in dense cushions up to 30 cm tall of bogs, swamps and lake shores. The dead cells hold twenty times their weight in water. Dried peat is fuel. The moss dresses wounds and serves as bedding and lamp wick.
Flora.Lore: What sinks in a bog does not rot. The Northmen have found Old Realms soldiers in the peat with their faces on.

Flora.Name: Bracken
Flora.Description: Fern with creeping black rhizomes and fronds that can reach 5 m, one of the most widespread plants and a weed of pasture. The fronds thatch and are fed to animals, though the plant is toxic.
Flora.Lore: See fern seed.

Flora.Name: Kelp
Flora.Description: Large brown seaweeds of cold coasts, with blades of 1 to 3 m and giant kinds of 60 m. A forest for fish. The ash gave potash and iodine.
Flora.Lore: Shoalfolk of the cold branch dive the kelp coasts, greased with seal fat.

Flora.Name: Eelgrass
Flora.Description: Flowering plants with long leaves that grow from rhizomes in shallow, muddy or sandy coastal water. Food and shelter for sea life. The dried leaves packed glass and stuffed cushions. Dugongs graze such beds.
Flora.Lore: Shoalfolk fence the meadows where their dugongs graze and count them as pasture.

Flora.Name: Lotus
Flora.Description: Water plant about 1 m tall with a tuberous rootstock in the mud of large lakes. Roots, young leaves, stems and seeds are eaten. The leaves serve as plates and wrappers. Herodotus has the marsh people bake bread from a lotus.
Flora.Lore: It rises clean out of mud. Every Rainkeeper temple pond grows it.

Flora.Name: Water chestnut
Flora.Description: Floating annual of slow rivers, lakes and ponds. The seed is eaten cooked or ground: raw, it is toxic. An important crop in the east. The seeds are strung as beads.
Flora.Lore: Canal folk grow it in the same water as the fish and the ducks and tax all three.

Flora.Name: Water hyssop
Flora.Description: Creeping perennial herb of estuary mud flats, channel banks and wet fields. A chief remedy for complaints of the nerves. The leaves are eaten.
Flora.Lore: Rainkeeper pupils are dosed with it before the examination of the scribes.

Flora.Name: Taro
Flora.Description: Evergreen perennial of 0.4 to 2 m with a large tuber, of low stream and river banks. Corm, leaves and stems are eaten cooked. Raw, they burn the mouth.
Flora.Lore: The first crop planted on new-cleared wet ground, before anyone trusts it with rice.

Flora.Name: Frost-lotus
Flora.Description: A pale water flower that opens on tundra lakes and rivers for the few days between the thaw and the midges, and whose petals stay frozen in the hand.
Flora.Lore: Hearthbloods, whose blood is at fever heat, pay anything for it: it is the one thing that cools them.

Flora.Name: Glowcap
Flora.Description: A mushroom that glows steadily, bright enough to read by, in limestone country: cave mouths, sinkholes and the roots above them. Foxfire is its faint natural cousin.
Flora.Lore: Gnome and Dwarf halls are lit with it. It dims when someone in the hall lies, the Gnomes claim.

Flora.Name: Elderwood
Flora.Description: A tree of any forest kind that has stood since the Dawn and woken a little. The wood does not rot and remembers the shape it is given.
Flora.Lore: Some elderwoods are Amberbloods who took root. To fell one unasked is murder in their law and a fortune in everyone else's.

Flora.Name: Elven sapflower
Flora.Description: A small golden flower of low woodland whose sap keeps what is steeped in it from spoiling.
Flora.Lore: Elves plant it where one of their own lies. A meadow of it is a graveyard, and its keepers do not sell.

Flora.Name: Dreamleaf
Flora.Description: A broad-leaved shrub of wet tropical highlands, which carry temperate biomes in the generator. The chewed leaf gives true dreams: of what is, not of what will be.
Flora.Lore: A Rainkeeper astrologer who is caught using it is dismissed for cheating.

Flora.Name: Mandrake
Flora.Description: The real plant is a perennial rosette of open woodland, deserted fields and stony places. All parts are poisonous. It was a narcotic and a purge, and it holds hyoscine. Pliny's diggers take care that the wind does not blow in their faces, draw three circles round it with a sword and face west as they pull. The juice was given before cutting to dull the pain.
Flora.Lore: The scream is why a dog is tied to the root, in the tale every digger tells and none has tested.

Flora.Name: Moly
Flora.Description: A herb with a black root and a white flower. Men cannot dig it, only gods. It guards the one who carries it against drugs and spells.
Flora.Lore: Sold in every market by people who could not have dug it.

Flora.Name: Fern seed
Flora.Description: The seed of the fern, which has none. It is said to bloom like gold or fire on Midsummer Eve. Whoever catches it finds buried treasure, and kept among coins it stops them from growing fewer. The fern itself is bracken.
Flora.Lore: Thieves wait in the bracken at midsummer with a white cloth. Guards wait for the thieves.

Flora.Name: Perindens tree
Flora.Description: A tree of the hot east with sweet fruit. Doves live in its branches and its shade, and the dragon, their enemy, fears both the tree and its shadow and keeps to the far side.
Flora.Lore: A village under one sleeps without a watch. It pays for that in doves.

Flora.Name: Vegetable lamb
Flora.Description: A plant of the steppe whose gourd-like fruit opens on a small living lamb, as the old travellers' tale has it.
Flora.Lore: Grass riders say it is cotton, described by someone who had seen neither cotton nor a lamb. They are not always right.

Flora.Name: Singing moss
Flora.Description: A grey moss on wind-scoured rock that hums when the wind crosses the crystal under it.
Flora.Lore: Miners follow the note to the vein, and stop their ears on the way down.

Flora.Name: Mirage lily
Flora.Description: A white flower that opens for one night after rain where star metal has fallen. Its scent shows the walker water that is not there.
Flora.Lore: Duskreaders, who see heat and not pictures, gather it safely and sell it to people who should not buy it.

Flora.Name: Stormthorn
Flora.Description: A thorn tree that lightning seeks. Each strike leaves a bead of glass at its foot, and the tree lives.
Flora.Lore: Herders camp well away from it, and glassmakers camp under it between storms.

Flora.Name: Lantern mangrove
Flora.Description: A mangrove whose breathing roots glow blue-green at the ebb.
Flora.Lore: The Shoalfolk harbour lights. A pilot steers by which trees are lit.

Flora.Name: Snare vine
Flora.Description: A liana that tightens on what struggles in it and slackens on what holds still.
Flora.Lore: Boughwalkers train it across the paths they do not want used. Children learn to hold still before they learn to climb.

Flora.Name: Giant mushrooms
Flora.Description: Mushrooms of tree height that stand where the trees should: pale stalks as thick as an oak, caps as wide as a barn roof, brown, red or violet above and gilled beneath. Under them it is dim, damp and still, the ground is soft with spores, and the gills glow faintly at night. The flesh cuts like cork and dries as hard as wood.
Flora.Lore: A wood of them springs up in one season where the trees fell sick, and no one sees it grow. Gnomes and Dwarves cut the caps for food and the stalks for beams, and count their rings as they would a tree's. Elves will not walk under them: they say the forest is being remembered wrongly.

Fauna.Name: Lemming
Fauna.Description: Stout rodent, 13 to 18 cm, tawny brown, of low treeless tundra meadows. It keeps the same coat in winter and stays active under the snow.
Fauna.Lore: In a lemming year the foxes and owls breed double. The Hoarkin count lemming runs in autumn to judge the winter.

Fauna.Name: Arctic hare
Fauna.Description: Large hare, 3 to 5 kg, white in winter and grey-brown in summer, of tundra and polar coasts. Northern peoples use the fur for clothing and blankets and eat the meat.
Fauna.Lore: Its tracks look three-legged. Children are told that a hare leaving four prints is something else wearing the skin.

Fauna.Name: Ptarmigan
Fauna.Description: Grouse with feathered feet like snowshoes, white in winter with a black tail, barred brown in summer. A popular game bird, and the one tundra bird that does not migrate.
Fauna.Lore: Northmen call a man who stays at his post through the dark a ptarmigan.

Fauna.Name: Snow bunting
Fauna.Description: Small black-and-white bird of rocky slopes that burrows deep into snow to survive the cold.
Fauna.Lore: The first bunting on the ice tells the Hoarkin that the seals will soon pup.

Fauna.Name: Biting swarm
Fauna.Description: Mosquitoes: slim flies with piercing mouthparts. The females take blood and carry fevers, and they are most abundant in the warm humid tropics. The summer clouds over tundra and taiga are general knowledge.
Fauna.Lore: Herds walk into the wind to lose them. A camp is sited by the swarm before it is sited by the water.

Fauna.Name: Red squirrel
Fauna.Description: Tuft-eared squirrel of conifer and broadleaf forest, red to black with a pale belly. Hunted for its fur. Its forgotten caches sprout into trees.
Fauna.Lore: Elves say the squirrels planted the first oak woods and are owed a tithe of nuts.

Fauna.Name: Stoat (ermine)
Fauna.Description: Small weasel-shaped hunter, brown in summer, white in winter with a black tail tip. The white fur trims coats and stoles, and it is an excellent mouser.
Fauna.Lore: Ermine was the fur of the judges of the Old Realms. A court still pays more for a white pelt than a trapper earns in a month.

Fauna.Name: Pika
Fauna.Description: Small short-eared relative of the hare, straw-grey, of steppe and semi-desert. It cuts grass and stacks it to dry. Herders use the hay piles, and the fur once made felt.
Fauna.Lore: Grass riders who take pika hay in a hard winter leave a pinch of salt on the burrow.

Fauna.Name: Bobak marmot
Fauna.Description: Stocky straw-coloured burrowing rodent, about half a metre long, of open steppe. Sentinels whistle the alarm. The pelts made hats and coats, and it was eaten in famines.
Fauna.Lore: An editor's note to Herodotus suggests that the gold-digging ants were marmots. Steppe prospectors sift marmot spoil for gold dust.

Fauna.Name: Jerboa
Fauna.Description: Very small hopping rodent with large three-toed hind feet and a long tufted tail, of sandy and stony desert. Eaten by some people.
Fauna.Lore: Duskreaders, who see warmth in the dark, follow jerboa trails to cool seeps under the sand.

Fauna.Name: Hare and rabbit
Fauna.Description: Brown hare of 3 to 5 kg with long black-tipped ears, of open fields and pastures with hedgerows. Prized game with tasty meat, and a pest of crops and young orchards. It runs at about 60 km/h.
Fauna.Lore: A hare that crosses the plough line before sowing is chased off the field by the whole household.

Fauna.Name: Ground squirrel (souslik)
Fauna.Description: Small yellowish burrowing squirrel of short-grass steppe and pasture. Eaten on a small scale and a pest in vineyards.
Fauna.Lore: Widegaze lookouts read a rider's approach from the sousliks going to ground, long before the dust shows.

Fauna.Name: Locust
Fauna.Description: The desert locust is camouflaged when solitary and black and yellow when it swarms. A destructive migratory pest of dry grassland and desert. One swarm crossing a sea was estimated at 5,000 km².
Fauna.Lore: The last swarms of the Ashen Years ate the thatch off the roofs. Sealed granaries date from then.

Fauna.Name: Honeybee
Fauna.Description: Banded reddish-brown bee of meadows, open woodland and gardens. It pollinates crops and gives honey and wax. Foragers dance to show where food lies.
Fauna.Lore: Halflings keep hives by every burrow and tell the bees of each birth and death in the house.

Fauna.Name: Hedgehog
Fauna.Description: Small round animal with brown-and-white spines, of fields, field edges and hedgerows. It curls into a ball when threatened. Used for food and for pest control.
Fauna.Lore: A hedgehog in the garden is lucky, and a gardener who kills one loses the year's cabbages.

Fauna.Name: Edible dormouse
Fauna.Description: The largest dormouse, grey with a bushy tail, of deciduous and mixed forest. A true hibernator that lives on its fat from autumn to spring. Trapped for fur and meat.
Fauna.Lore: Fattened dormice were a dish of Old Realms banquets. Midlander inns still keep them in clay jars.

Fauna.Name: Woodpecker
Fauna.Description: A large woodpecker, about 46 cm, of conifer and beech woodland. Woodpeckers cut their own nest holes in dead wood.
Fauna.Lore: Pliny reports that a woodpecker reopens a plugged nest hole with a certain herb. Thieves pay well for "woodpecker's herb", said to open any lock.

Fauna.Name: Rat
Fauna.Description: Agile climbing rodent with a tail longer than its body, of coasts, buildings and fields. It damages crops and fruit trees and fouls food, and its fleas spread plague.
Fauna.Lore: Grain towns give their Catfolk wardens meat and fish and count the rats they bring as rent paid.

Fauna.Name: Banana slug
Fauna.Description: Slug up to 25 cm long, mostly yellow with brown spots, of moist dark forest floors under logs. A garden pest.
Fauna.Lore: Its slime numbs the tongue, and children of the wet coast dare each other to lick one.

Fauna.Name: Rough-skinned newt
Fauna.Description: Newt of 13 to 22 cm with grainy dark skin and an orange belly, of forest ponds and streams. One holds enough toxin to kill several people. Threatened, it bends back to show the belly.
Fauna.Lore: Bitterbloods, who eat what poisons others, buy them alive.

Fauna.Name: Leech
Fauna.Description: Flattened dark worm with reddish stripes, of small muddy reed-edged ponds. Long used for bloodletting. It comes to moving shadows.
Fauna.Lore: A barber's leech pond is fenced like a fish pond and inherited like one.

Fauna.Name: Silkworm
Fauna.Description: A fully domesticated moth that is not found in the wild. The caterpillar spins a cocoon of one strand about 915 m long, and silk has been taken from it for thousands of years. It is fed on white mulberry leaves.
Fauna.Lore: Canal folk grow mulberry on the dikes for it. Taking the eggs out of a silk province is a hanging matter.

Fauna.Name: Kermes scale
Fauna.Description: Scale insect whose dried bodies give the oldest known red dye. The dye was once paid as tribute and taken as rent. It lives on the kermes oak.
Fauna.Lore: "Oak blood" pays the rent of many a hill village, gathered by lamplight before the dew dries.

Fauna.Name: Cochineal insect
Fauna.Description: Small grey wingless insect under a white waxy coat, feeding on prickly pear. About 70,000 make one pound of scarlet dye.
Fauna.Lore: Noonfolk estates fence their cactus rows and brush the insects off by hand at noon.

Fauna.Name: Lac insect
Fauna.Description: Scale insect whose resin is shellac, used as wood varnish, sealer and cement. The page read does not name its host trees or its range.
Fauna.Lore: Rainkeeper temples seal their deeds with red lac.

Fauna.Name: Cicada
Fauna.Description: Insect of 2 to 5 cm with clear wings and large eyes, of forests, grasslands and deserts. Used in folk medicine, as a symbol and as food. Some broods emerge in vast numbers every 13 or 17 years.
Fauna.Lore: A brood year is a census year: whoever was born in the last one comes of age.

Fauna.Name: Tortoise
Fauna.Description: Land tortoise of 12 to 23 cm, of forest, scrub and grassland. Kept as a pet and eaten in places.
Fauna.Lore: Halflings carve a child's birth year on a garden tortoise, which outlives the child.

Fauna.Name: Scorpion
Fauna.Description: Large yellowish scorpion of 8 to 11 cm that lives under rocks and in burrows in arid land and comes out at night. One of the most dangerous scorpions.
Fauna.Lore: Saltroad caravans shake out every boot at dawn, and the guide who forgets pays for the camp's water.

Fauna.Name: Scarab
Fauna.Description: Dung beetles are round, dark and 5 to 30 mm long. They shape manure into a ball and bury it, which turns dung into soil. One of them was the sacred scarab of ancient Egypt.
Fauna.Lore: Along the desert river the beetle rolling its ball is the sun crossing the sky, and it is carved on every seal.

Fauna.Name: Termite
Fauna.Description: Soft pale insects that build domed or conical mounds of earth, clay and saliva. They destroy wooden structures and crops, though only one species in ten is a pest.
Fauna.Lore: Sunlander potters dig their clay from old mounds.

Fauna.Name: Tsetse fly
Fauna.Description: Brown fly of 6 to 16 mm, of woodland and sometimes open grassland. It gives sleeping sickness to people and nagana to cattle and horses.
Fauna.Lore: The fly that no mounted army of the Old Realms could pass. Where it lives, wealth is counted in yams and iron, not cattle.

Fauna.Name: Honeyguide
Fauna.Description: Bird of about 20 cm of savanna, scrub and forest edge. It calls and flashes its tail to lead honey badgers and others to hives.
Fauna.Lore: A hunter who follows the bird and leaves it no comb is led to a snake the next time.

Fauna.Name: Quelea (weaver bird)
Fauna.Description: Small weaver bird of the savanna. Colonies nest over several square miles of trees in millions, and it can become an agricultural pest.
Fauna.Lore: Noonfolk children earn their first wage scaring queleas off the millet.

Fauna.Name: Mongoose
Fauna.Description: Small short-legged carnivore with a pointed nose and a long furry tail, grey to brown. The Egyptian kind keeps down rats, mice and snakes and raids chicken yards. Pliny has it coat itself in dried mud to fight the asp.
Fauna.Lore: Rainkeeper houses keep one as others keep a cat.

Fauna.Name: Poison frog
Fauna.Description: Frog of about 47 mm, bright yellow, green or orange, that sits in the open on the rain forest floor. Skin contact can kill. Its poison tips blowgun darts.
Fauna.Lore: Bitterbloods keep them in pens and sell the dart poison by the thorn.

Fauna.Name: Leafcutter ant
Fauna.Description: Ants that carry leaf pieces along trails of over 30 m to underground nests of more than 1,000 chambers, where they grow a fungus on the chewed leaves. They can cut the value of pasture.
Fauna.Lore: Boughwalkers say the ants taught them to tend the forest as a garden.

Fauna.Name: Firefly
Fauna.Description: Soft-bodied beetles of 5 to 25 mm whose flash patterns are signals between the sexes, in most tropical and temperate regions.
Fauna.Lore: Lanternkin call them cousins and will not have them caught in jars.

Fauna.Name: Fiddler crab
Fauna.Description: Small crab whose male waves one enlarged claw, on intertidal mud of marshes and estuaries.
Fauna.Lore: Shoalfolk children learn to count on the waving claws.

Fauna.Name: Mudskipper
Fauna.Description: Fish up to 30 cm with large mobile eyes set close together, of swamps, estuaries and mudflats. It leaves the water to walk and climb, breathing through its gill chambers and skin.
Fauna.Lore: "The fish that could not decide" is a Shoalfolk name for a person of two loyalties.

Fauna.Name: Mud crab
Fauna.Description: Crab with a shell of 25 to 28 cm and a weight of 2 to 3 kg. It burrows in mangroves and soft intertidal mud, the young live in estuaries, and it is commercially important.
Fauna.Lore: A Shoalfolk family owns its crab holes as others own fields.

Fauna.Name: Junglefowl
Fauna.Description: Bird of about 70 cm with gold, red and metallic green plumage, of secondary forest and scrub. Raised for eggs and meat, for cockfighting and for feathers.
Fauna.Lore: Every village cock is said to descend from a pair given by a forest god, and the first egg of the year goes back to the forest.

Fauna.Name: Flying fox
Fauna.Description: Fruit bat with a wingspan of 1.2 to 1.5 m. Several hundred roost in one tree near water. Hunted for food and medicine, and a pest of orchards.
Fauna.Lore: A roost tree is never felled: the bats carry the names of the dead out at dusk and back at dawn.

Fauna.Name: Murex
Fauna.Description: Sea snails whose dye, Tyrian purple, was highly valued in antiquity. Pliny says the dye lies in a small vein in the neck, the fishing is best after the dog star rises, and the finest purple wool cost five times the common kind.
Fauna.Lore: Purple was the colour of the sorcerer-kings. In some realms it is still death to wear it without leave.

Fauna.Name: Pearl oyster
Fauna.Description: Oysters of warm seas that lay nacre around an intruder. Pearls have long been prized as gems. Pliny held that the best came from the eastern ocean and the gulfs of Arabia.
Fauna.Lore: A Shoalfolk family owns its oyster bed and guards it.

Fauna.Name: Ringed seal
Fauna.Description: Small seal of 1.1 to 1.75 m with a dark coat ringed in silver, of ice floes and pack ice. It keeps breathing holes open in the ice. Hunted for food, oil and skins.
Fauna.Lore: The Hoarkin followed the seals out onto the ice. A hunter sits at a breathing hole for a day without moving.

Fauna.Name: Penguin
Fauna.Description: Flightless seabird of 1 to 1.3 m and 25 to 45 kg, black above and white below with yellow ear patches, on polar ice and coasts. It huddles in thousands through the winter.
Fauna.Lore: Hoarkin say the penguins are a people who chose the sea and lost their hands for it.

Fauna.Name: Arctic fox
Fauna.Description: Small fox, white in winter and grey to brown in summer, of coastal and alpine tundra. It stores summer food under stones. The fur is prized, and it takes lambs.
Fauna.Lore: It follows the white bear for scraps. Trappers follow the fox to find the bear.

Fauna.Name: Snowy owl
Fauna.Description: White owl of 63 to 73 cm with yellow eyes, of open tundra, hunting largely by day. It keeps rodents down and robs traplines.
Fauna.Lore: Hearthblood pass wardens take the owl as their badge: it sees the storm first.

Fauna.Name: Sled dog
Fauna.Description: Large, powerful, thick-coated dogs of great endurance that pull sleds over snow and ice with people and supplies, a dozen or more in a fan hitch.
Fauna.Lore: A Hoarkin team is named as one person and inherited as one.

Fauna.Name: Reindeer
Fauna.Description: Deer up to 1.2 m at the shoulder with a hollow-haired coat from dark brown to nearly white. Both sexes carry antlers. It migrates over 5,000 km a year and digs through snow to feed. Herded for thousands of years for meat, fur and antler.
Fauna.Lore: The herd is the calendar of the north: every feast is fixed by where it stands.

Fauna.Name: Eider
Fauna.Description: The largest northern duck, of rocky coasts and offshore islands. The male is black below and white above. Taken for its down, for sport and for food.
Fauna.Lore: Northmen farm the down by building the ducks stone shelters and taking a share from each nest.

Fauna.Name: Wolverine
Fauna.Description: Stocky animal of 9 to 30 kg with brown-black fur and pale shoulder stripes, of boreal forest and tundra. It drives bears and wolves off their kills and raids traps, cabins and food stores. The fur resists cold.
Fauna.Lore: Trappers do not say its name in the forest. They call it "the partner", because it takes half.

Fauna.Name: Moose
Fauna.Description: The largest deer, up to 2.3 m at the shoulder, dark, with huge antlers on the male, of taiga and wetlands near water. Largely solitary. Taken for meat, and captives give milk.
Fauna.Lore: Caesar was told that the elk has no joints, sleeps leaning on a tree, and is caught by sawing the tree. Northmen tell the tale to strangers with a straight face.

Fauna.Name: Beaver
Fauna.Description: Rodent of 13 to 35 kg with a dark coat, of forested lakes, ponds and rivers. Pelts, castoreum and meat are prized. Its dams flood farmland and roads. The bestiary has the hunted beaver bite off the parts wanted for medicine and throw them to the hunter.
Fauna.Lore: A beaver pond is a boundary mark in Northmen law: who drains it moves the border.

Fauna.Name: Sable and marten
Fauna.Description: Marten of about 1 to 2 kg of dense taiga, light to dark brown with a richer winter coat. Fur hunting once cut its numbers.
Fauna.Lore: "Soft gold": the Northmen paid their grain debts of the Ashen Years in sable.

Fauna.Name: Lynx
Fauna.Description: Cat of 18 to 36 kg with a short black-tipped tail, grey to rusty, spotted or plain. A solitary ambush hunter that caches its prey. It kills livestock.
Fauna.Lore: Seen once, it is luck. Seen twice, someone is hunting you.

Fauna.Name: Capercaillie
Fauna.Description: The largest grouse: the cock weighs 4 to 5 kg and is glossy black with red eye combs. It lives in old conifer forest and displays at leks. Taken as game.
Fauna.Lore: The cock is deaf while it sings, and so is a man in love, say the Northmen.

Fauna.Name: Musk deer
Fauna.Description: Small antlerless deer of 15 to 17 kg of mountain taiga. The male has long downward canines and a musk pouch. The musk is valued for perfume and medicine, and hunting for it has made the deer rare.
Fauna.Lore: A pod of musk is worth a horse. Dwarf holds buy it for their dead.

Fauna.Name: Saiga
Fauna.Description: Antelope of 30 to 45 kg with a large head and a mobile swollen nose, yellowish red in summer and grey in winter, of dry steppe and semi-desert. Taken for meat, fur and horn, which is ground for medicine.
Fauna.Lore: Grass rider boys must run one down on horseback before they may marry.

Fauna.Name: Horse
Fauna.Description: Grazer of 227 to 900 kg, of temperate grassland, steppe and savanna, living in herds with a dominance order. Used for food, transport, war and sport. The wild steppe horse is stocky, reddish brown, with a stiff dark mane, and was never tamed.
Fauna.Lore: Children of the Grass riders ride before they walk well, and the theft of a horse is death.

Fauna.Name: Sheep
Fauna.Description: Flocking grazer, white to near black, kept in deserts, grasslands, scrub and mountains for meat, milk, wool and hides. Flocks of up to 1,000 move without a leader. Herodotus tells of a breed whose tails are so long that each rests on a little cart.
Fauna.Lore: The Widegaze keep sheep on open range without fences and watch them from a mound.

Fauna.Name: Wild sheep and ibex
Fauna.Description: The argali is the largest sheep, 60 to 185 kg with corkscrew horns, of steep slopes above 1,000 m. The ibex is a bearded mountain goat taken for food, horn and medicine. The bestiary says the ibex lands on its horns when it falls.
Fauna.Lore: A dwarf who brings down a ram on the heights hangs the horns over the hold gate.

Fauna.Name: Yak
Fauna.Description: Long-haired blackish ox of alpine meadow and steppe with upcurved horns. It gives meat, milk, butter and cheese, hair, pack transport and dung for fuel.
Fauna.Lore: Hearthbloods herd yaks on the high passes and hire them out with their drivers.

Fauna.Name: Bactrian camel
Fauna.Description: Two-humped camel of 300 to 690 kg with a long thick coat, of cold desert and steppe. Used for transport, meat, milk, hides, hair and dung fuel.
Fauna.Lore: Brinefolk salt caravans count distance in camel days and pay tolls in stamped salt.

Fauna.Name: Onager
Fauna.Description: Wild ass of 200 to 260 kg, reddish brown with a white belly and a dark stripe down the back, of desert and steppe within reach of water. Hunted for meat and hide. Herders see it as a rival for water.
Fauna.Lore: No one has broken an onager to the saddle. Orc hearths count the attempt as a rite.

Fauna.Name: Golden eagle
Fauna.Description: Dark brown eagle with a golden nape and a wingspan of about 2 m, of open country from sea level to 3,600 m. Pairs hunt together. It sometimes kills livestock.
Fauna.Lore: Grass rider falconers fly eagles at foxes and wolves. A trained bird is set free after ten winters.

Fauna.Name: Falcon
Fauna.Description: The saker is a brown, streaked falcon of about 50 cm, of open country with cliffs and scattered trees. A persistent hunter that follows prey into brush. It is taken for the bird trade.
Fauna.Lore: A white falcon is a gift between khans and a cause of war when it is refused.

Fauna.Name: Cattle
Fauna.Description: Herd animal of 150 to 1,360 kg, black, white, red or brown, kept on grassland and farmland for milk, meat and leather, for dung, and for ploughing and hauling.
Fauna.Lore: Among Sunlanders cattle are bride-price, blood-price and the measure of a man.

Fauna.Name: Red fox
Fauna.Description: Fox with a coat from yellowish red to deep red-brown and black lower legs, of forest, prairie, farmland and towns: the widest range of any wild dog. Its fur is valuable, and it takes poultry.
Fauna.Lore: In Halfling tales the fox is the tax collector.

Fauna.Name: Red deer
Fauna.Description: Large deer, dark brown in winter and tan in summer with a pale rump. The stag carries antlers up to 1.5 m and bellows in autumn. Taken for food, hide and antler, and a pest of crops.
Fauna.Lore: The stag is the lord's game: most Midlander forests are closed to commoners.

Fauna.Name: Wild boar and pig
Fauna.Description: Boar of 66 to 272 kg, black to red-brown, of forest, shrubland and marsh near water. Sows live in groups. Hunted for sport and food, and it ruins crops. The pig is its domestic form.
Fauna.Lore: Halflings keep a pig by every burrow. Orcs keep them half wild.

Fauna.Name: Goat
Fauna.Description: Bearded, horned browser of about 45 kg kept in nearly all habitats for milk, meat, wool and leather. Gone wild, it grazes land bare. Herodotus and Pliny have the resin ladanum combed from goats' beards.
Fauna.Lore: Dwarves keep goats on the high pastures and make hard cheese. Saltroad nomads weave their tents of goat hair.

Fauna.Name: Donkey and mule
Fauna.Description: Grey ass of 1.1 to 1.4 m at the shoulder with a dark stripe down the back, of desert and mountain country. It carries heavy loads and guards livestock.
Fauna.Lore: A mule knows the mountain road better than the muleteer, and the toll is charged per mule for that reason.

Fauna.Name: Raven
Fauna.Description: Large black bird up to 69 cm with a wedge-shaped tail, of open country from tundra to desert. Highly intelligent. It clears carrion and eats grain.
Fauna.Lore: Soldiers say the ravens know the outcome of a battle the day before, by which camp they roost above.

Fauna.Name: Crane
Fauna.Description: Tall wading bird, larger than a heron, of marshes and plains. Pairs reuse the same nest for years. Pliny says cranes post sentinels at night that hold a stone in one foot, so that it falls and wakes them if they sleep.
Fauna.Lore: The crane with the stone is the badge of sworn sentries.

Fauna.Name: Otter
Fauna.Description: Playful swimmer of about 7 kg of lakes, rivers and coasts, also of peat swamp and rice fields. Its pelt is valuable, and fishers see it as a rival.
Fauna.Lore: Canal folk boatmen train otters to drive fish into the nets.

Fauna.Name: Waterfowl
Fauna.Description: The greylag goose is grey-brown, about 80 cm long, with an orange bill, and lives in marshes, fens, estuaries and farmland. It was domesticated for meat and down. Flocks fly in a V.
Fauna.Lore: Halflings keep geese as watchdogs.

Fauna.Name: Dromedary
Fauna.Description: One-humped camel of 400 to 600 kg, sandy brown, of deserts with long dry seasons. It can drink 100 litres in ten minutes. A beast of burden that also gives milk, meat, wool, leather and dung fuel.
