Fauna.Lore: A caravan of a thousand camels carries salt south. The lead camel has a name and a share of the profit.

Fauna.Name: Gazelle and oryx
Fauna.Description: The dorcas gazelle is pale with brown flank stripes and curved horns, of semi-desert, dunes and wadis. The oryx is larger, cream to grey-brown, with long horns, and travels towards distant rain. Both are hunted for meat and hide.
Fauna.Lore: Duskreaders hunt them at night by the warmth of the ground a herd has lain on.

Fauna.Name: Fennec
Fauna.Description: The smallest fox, 0.8 to 1.5 kg, with very large ears and thick pale fur, of sandy desert. It caches food and remembers the caches.
Fauna.Lore: A fennec den marks water within a day's dig, say the well diggers.

Fauna.Name: Ostrich
Fauna.Description: Flightless bird about 2 m tall, of dry savanna and scrub. The cock is black and white. Taken for hide, feathers and eggs. The shells carry water.
Fauna.Lore: Sunlander title-holders wear the plumes. The eggshell is the traveller's flask.

Fauna.Name: Horned viper
Fauna.Description: Snake of 30 to 60 cm, sand-coloured, with a scale "horn" over each eye. It buries itself in sand with only eyes and nostrils showing. Its bite causes swelling and bleeding. Kept by snake charmers and milked for venom. Herodotus knew small horned snakes that were buried in a temple.
Fauna.Lore: The Duskreaders see them as warm commas on the cold sand and walk around them.

Fauna.Name: Cobra
Fauna.Description: Snake of about 2 m that raises the front third of its body and spreads a marked hood. It lives in forest and farmland, eats rats, and its bite kills many each year.
Fauna.Lore: Rainkeeper granaries tolerate one for the rats and set out milk for it.

Fauna.Name: Wildebeest and zebra
Fauna.Description: The wildebeest is a slate-grey, maned and bearded antelope of open grass and floodplain. The zebra is a black-and-white striped horse led in file by a mare. Both are taken for meat and skins and compete with cattle.
Fauna.Lore: The great herds follow the rains, and the Sunlander herders move their cattle behind them.

Fauna.Name: Giraffe
Fauna.Description: The tallest animal: bulls reach 5.7 m. It has a spotted coat and lives in savanna and open woodland. Taken for meat and hide.
Fauna.Lore: Widegaze say the giraffe is the only beast that has seen as far as they have.

Fauna.Name: Vulture
Fauna.Description: Large carrion birds, many with bare heads, of open country, with keen eyesight and strong beaks. They feed in a strict order.
Fauna.Lore: Where the vultures circle, a caravan has lost a beast or a kingdom a battle. Either is news worth selling.

Fauna.Name: Water buffalo
Fauna.Description: Dark, thin-haired ox with wide horns, of marsh, swamp and river land. It wallows in mud. It gives milk, meat and leather and draws the plough.
Fauna.Lore: The paddy cannot be worked without it. Rainkeepers grow rice in the wet lands, and a village counts its wealth in buffaloes.

Fauna.Name: Peafowl
Fauna.Description: Bird with a bright blue neck. The cock carries a long train of eyespot feathers. It lives in open forest, roosts high in trees, and is kept for its feathers and against pests.
Fauna.Lore: A hundred eyes that never close: the peacock is the bird of the Rainkeeper tax office.

Fauna.Name: Monkeys
Fauna.Description: The langur is a grey, black-faced monkey of about 13 kg, of forest, scrub and towns. It is held sacred, and it raids crops and steals food from houses. The proboscis monkey of the mangrove has a large nose and swims well.
Fauna.Lore: Temple monkeys are fed on feast days and cursed the rest of the year.

Fauna.Name: Tropical deer
Fauna.Description: The chital stands 0.6 to 1 m at the shoulder, with a red-brown coat in rows of white spots. The stag has three-tined antlers. It lives in tropical grassland and along rivers and is hunted.
Fauna.Lore: It grazes under the langurs, which drop fruit and bark at the tiger.

Fauna.Name: Parrot and macaw
Fauna.Description: The scarlet macaw is about 89 cm long, scarlet with yellow and blue wings, and lives in the rain forest canopy. Pairs mate for life. Taken for the cage trade and for feathers.
Fauna.Lore: Boughwalker bird catchers sell birds that speak, and what a bird repeats in a market has started feuds.

Fauna.Name: Sloth
Fauna.Description: Slow tree-dweller of about 4 kg whose coat is green with algae. It sleeps 14 to 16 hours a day in the forest canopy.
Fauna.Lore: To the Swiftborn, who live fast, the sloth is a holy animal or a joke, by temperament.

Fauna.Name: Tapir
Fauna.Description: Dark, heavy browser of 150 to 250 kg with a short trunk, of lowland and swamp forest near rivers. Taken for hide and meat, and trained to pull ploughs.
Fauna.Lore: A forest plough ox for those the tsetse has denied cattle.

Fauna.Name: Dugong
Fauna.Description: Grey-brown sea mammal of 2.4 to 4 m and up to 400 kg that grazes seagrass in shallow sheltered bays. Taken for food and oil, and its tusks for medicine.
Fauna.Lore: Shoalfolk herd them in fenced bays and will not eat a cow that has calved.

Fauna.Name: Monitor lizard
Fauna.Description: Dark lizard, commonly 1.5 m and up to 3 m, of forest rivers and swamps. It climbs trees and dives when threatened. The skin is used for leather, food and medicine.
Fauna.Lore: Bitterblood tanners make a leather of it that rot will not touch.

Fauna.Name: Llama
Fauna.Description: Woolly camel relative of about 1.2 m and 140 kg, of high plateaus up to 4,000 m. A pack animal that gives wool and guards sheep. In the generator it stands on tropical highlands, which carry temperate biomes.
Fauna.Lore: The highland road has no wheels. Everything a mountain kingdom owns has been on a llama's back.

Fauna.Name: Salmon
Fauna.Description: Silver-sided fish of 2 to 9 kg that lives at sea and returns to its home stream to spawn. A prized food fish.
Fauna.Lore: The run is counted at the first weir, and the count sets the year's river tolls.

Fauna.Name: Cod and herring
Fauna.Description: Cod is a green-brown fish up to 2 m of the shelf down to 600 m, a major fishery and the source of cod liver oil. Herring is a small silver fish in schools several miles long, eaten for centuries.
Fauna.Lore: Northmen are herring fishers. A bad herring year empties the fjords of young men.

Fauna.Name: Sturgeon and eel
Fauna.Description: The sturgeon is a long-snouted fish with rows of bony plates that runs up rivers to spawn and is caught for its roe. The eel is a snake-shaped fish of rivers and coasts, a popular food.
Fauna.Lore: Sturgeon is the lord's fish on most rivers. Eels pay the rent of the mill.

Fauna.Name: Tuna
Fauna.Description: Fish of 0.5 to 2 m and up to 680 kg, metallic blue above and silver below, of coastal and open water down to 1,000 m. A food fish and the object of a large fishery.
Fauna.Lore: Coast towns build watchtowers for the tuna run before they build walls.

Fauna.Name: Polar bear
Fauna.Description: Bear of 300 to 800 kg in the male, with translucent fur that looks white over black skin, of pack ice and polar coasts. It waits at the breathing holes of seals. Dangerous to people. Taken for food and medicine.
Fauna.Lore: The Hoarkin hunter and the bear sit at the same holes. Each leaves the other the hole he came to first.

Fauna.Name: Walrus
Fauna.Description: Sea beast of 1,200 to 1,500 kg and about 3.2 m with thick grey-brown skin and long tusks, of polar ice and coasts. Bulls fight with the tusks. Taken for food, oil, ivory and hide.
Fauna.Lore: Northmen paid for grain with walrus ivory in the Ashen Years. Hoarkin carve it small and patiently.

Fauna.Name: Narwhal
Fauna.Description: Whale of 4 to 5 m, mottled blue-grey, of deep polar water. The male often carries one straight tusk up to 3 m long. Pods join in herds of hundreds. Taken for food, lamp oil and the tusk.
Fauna.Lore: South of the ice the tusk is sold as the horn of the unicorn, and no northern trader corrects the buyer.

Fauna.Name: Whale
Fauna.Description: The bowhead is 14 to 18 m long and up to 100 tonnes, black, with the largest baleen of any whale, of cold polar water. It gives meat, baleen and blubber. The bestiary whale opens its mouth and breathes out a sweet scent that draws small fish in.
Fauna.Lore: One whale lights a Northmen fjord for a winter. The harpooner's share is fixed by the oldest law they have.

Fauna.Name: Musk ox
Fauna.Description: Barrel-shaped, short-legged ox with a shaggy outer coat and a fine underwool, of tundra north of the tree line. Bulls butt heads in the rut. The underwool is valuable for garments.
Fauna.Lore: Hearthbloods comb the shed wool off the willows and sell it for its weight in silver.

Fauna.Name: Woolly mammoth
Fauna.Description: Elephant of 3 to 3.7 m and 6 to 8 tonnes with long dark outer hair, a dense undercoat and thick fat, of cold steppe-tundra. Extinct in our world. Its ivory has been exported from the far north since medieval times.
Fauna.Lore: The Ashen Years killed the southern herds. The last walk the tundra edge, and the Hoarkin name each one.

Fauna.Name: Grey wolf
Fauna.Description: The largest wild dog, about 55 kg in the male, white in the far north and grey, brown or black elsewhere. It lives in packs with a strict order. It kills livestock, though losses are often overstated. The bestiary has the she-wolf whelp only in May, when it thunders.
Fauna.Lore: Every herding people has a wolf oath. The Grass riders swear by it, the Midlanders against it.

Fauna.Name: Brown bear
Fauna.Description: Bear of 80 to over 600 kg, usually dark brown, of tundra, forest and mountain. It dens for a deep winter sleep. Considered dangerous, though attacks are rare. Taken for hide and body parts. The bestiary has the mother lick her shapeless cubs into form.
Fauna.Lore: Amberbloods hold that the bear is the oldest person in the forest and is not to be named aloud.

Fauna.Name: Tiger
Fauna.Description: Great cat with a red-orange coat and black stripes, of forest, rain forest, scrub and marsh. It swims rivers several kilometres wide. It injures people and rarely becomes a man-eater. Its body parts are traded.
Fauna.Lore: Rainkeeper kings hunt it from elephants. A village that loses three people to one tiger is excused the year's tax.

Fauna.Name: Snow leopard
Fauna.Description: Pale grey to cream cat of 1 to 1.3 m with dark rosettes, a long tail and large paws, of steep rocky ground in high mountains. Active at dawn and dusk. It kills livestock and is not known to attack people.
Fauna.Lore: Dwarves call it the ghost of the scree. A hold that finds its tracks at the gate expects a death.

Fauna.Name: Bison
Fauna.Description: Wild ox about 2.9 m long and 800 to 1,000 kg, golden to dark brown, of broadleaf and mixed forest with meadows and clearings. It damages crops.
Fauna.Lore: The Grass riders of the west follow bison as their cousins follow horses.

Fauna.Name: Aurochs
Fauna.Description: Wild ox about 1.8 m at the shoulder, black, with forward-curving horns, the likely ancestor of cattle. Extinct in our world since 1627. Caesar's uri are a little smaller than an elephant, spare neither man nor beast, are taken in pits, and cannot be tamed. Their horns are rimmed with silver as cups.
Fauna.Lore: A young Midlander lord shows the horns in the hall before he is thought fit to lead, as Caesar says of the Germans.

Fauna.Name: Cougar
Fauna.Description: Large slender cat, yellowish to grey-brown, of forest, scrub, desert and mountain. It caches large prey and drags it far. It threatens livestock and now and then attacks people.
Fauna.Lore: The cat nobody sees. Catfolk leave a share of a kill where its tracks cross theirs.

Fauna.Name: Lion
Fauna.Description: Tawny cat. The male is maned and weighs about 189 kg. It lives in prides on plains, savanna and scrub. The lionesses raise cubs together. It attacks people and livestock.
Fauna.Lore: Sunlander herders pay Catfolk to watch the herd at dusk, when the lions come.

Fauna.Name: Leopard
Fauna.Description: Cat of 17 to 65 kg, tawny with black rosettes, from desert to rain forest. A solitary night hunter that caches its kills. It takes livestock, and an injured one may hunt people.
Fauna.Lore: The leopard skin is the cloak of Sunlander title-holders. It may not be bought, only earned.

Fauna.Name: Cheetah
Fauna.Description: Slim long-legged cat of 21 to 72 kg, pale with small black spots, of grassland and desert. It was kept as a hunting animal in antiquity. Herders see it as a pest.
Fauna.Lore: Saltroad princes course gazelle with hooded cheetahs carried on the saddle.

Fauna.Name: Hyena
Fauna.Description: Sandy to grey spotted hunter with a massive neck. The females are heavier and rule the clan. It takes livestock and attacks people. Pliny and the bestiary say it mimics the human voice to call victims out and digs up graves.
Fauna.Lore: Noonfolk bury their dead under stones for the reason the bestiary gives.

Fauna.Name: African elephant
Fauna.Description: The largest land animal: bulls weigh 4.5 to 6 tonnes. Grey creased skin and ivory tusks. Matriarchal herds in savanna, woodland and rain forest. Taken for meat and ivory. It wrecks crops and kills people in raids.
Fauna.Lore: Sunlander hunters' brotherhoods take one bull a year and bury the tusks' worth in gold with the hunt master.

Fauna.Name: Asian elephant
Fauna.Description: Elephant of 3.5 to 6 tonnes of which only the male is tusked, of forest, scrub and grassland. It hauls timber and serves in ritual. A bull in musth is highly aggressive. It kills people and ruins crops.
Fauna.Lore: Rainkeeper kings ride to war on elephants and keep an elephant corps.

Fauna.Name: Rhinoceros
Fauna.Description: Grey hairless browser of 800 to 1,400 kg with two horns and a grasping upper lip, of grassland, scrub and forest edge. It charges. The horn is sold as medicine and for dagger hilts.
Fauna.Lore: A cup of the horn is said to sweat when poison is poured in it. Kings buy the cup and keep the taster.

Fauna.Name: Hippopotamus
Fauna.Description: River beast of 1.3 to 3.2 tonnes with slate-grey skin, of shallow lakes, rivers and swamps. Attacks are sometimes fatal. Taken for meat, tusks and hide, which makes shields and whips. Herodotus calls it the river horse and says its dried hide makes spear shafts.
Fauna.Lore: River traders fear it more than the crocodile: it upsets the boat, and the crocodile only waits.

Fauna.Name: Wild buffalo
Fauna.Description: Very large dark ox with heavy horns in both sexes. Bulls pass 835 kg. It keeps near water in savanna and forest. Taken for meat. It raids crops and gives its diseases to cattle.
Fauna.Lore: The beast that waits for the hunter who wounded it. A buffalo's horns on a hut mean the owner is not to be argued with.

Fauna.Name: Crocodile
Fauna.Description: Reptile of 4 to 4.5 m and about 410 kg of lakes, rivers, swamps and brackish water. It kills several hundred people a year and is hunted for meat and skin. The saltwater kind reaches 6 to 7 m. Herodotus has it sacred in one town and eaten in the next, and caught on a hook baited with pork.
Fauna.Lore: Along the desert river a temple keeps a tame one, adorned and fed, and embalms it when it dies, as Herodotus tells.

Fauna.Name: Python
Fauna.Description: Snake of about 4.8 m, yellowish to brown with black diamonds, of rain forest, wetland and swamp. It kills by constriction. Hunted for skin and meat. It has killed people.
Fauna.Lore: Bitterbloods keep them for the skins and say a python fed at the new moon never bites.

Fauna.Name: Jaguar
Fauna.Description: Cat of 68 to 136 kg, pale yellow to red-brown with black rosettes, often all black, of dense lowland forest, swamp and riverside. It kills livestock and injures people. Hunters call it with hollow gourds.
Fauna.Lore: The black jaguar is the night with teeth. Boughwalkers do not come down while one calls.

Fauna.Name: Bull shark
Fauna.Description: Shark about 2.4 m long, grey above and white below, of warm coasts, estuaries, rivers and lakes: it tolerates fresh water. It can injure people. Taken for meat, skin, fins and liver oil.
Fauna.Lore: Shoalfolk divers carry a bone knife for it and hope not to learn if it works.

Fauna.Name: Komodo dragon
Fauna.Description: Lizard of over 3 m and up to 165 kg, dull brown-grey, of dry island forest and tall-grass lowland. It attacks livestock and now and then people. The males wrestle upright.
Fauna.Lore: Sailors who land for water on the wrong island bring back the tale of the small dragon. Nobody inland believes them.

Fauna.Name: Amarok
Fauna.Description: A great lone beast of the north that roars and hunts by land and lake. In the tale a man kills its young and hides in a cave. The amarok, which sees what is hidden, takes his companion's soul, and he falls dead.
Fauna.Lore: Hoarkin do not hunt alone at night. They say the amarok takes only those who do.

Fauna.Name: Snow wasset
Fauna.Description: A winter predator of the far northern logging camps, known from the tales of the lumberjacks. It sleeps the summer away and hunts under the snow in winter.
Fauna.Lore: Trappers blame it for every sprung and empty trap.

Fauna.Name: Rime drake
Fauna.Description: A wingless white drake that dens in glacier caves of the polar and subpolar mountains. Its breath is a freezing wind.
Fauna.Lore: Hearthbloods say the windcrystal is its breath, frozen in the rock. Miners listen for it before they dig.

Fauna.Name: Griffin
Fauna.Description: A beast said to guard the gold of the far north, from which one-eyed men steal it. Herodotus does not believe the tale. Pliny gives the griffin long ears and a hooked bill and calls it a fable.
Fauna.Lore: Grass riders trade for "griffin claws" that are the horns of some old beast. Dwarves know which.

Fauna.Name: Gold-digging ant
Fauna.Description: Ants larger than foxes and smaller than dogs that throw up sand full of gold from their burrows in a sandy desert. Men take the sand at the hottest hour, when the ants are below, and flee on camels.
Fauna.Lore: Saltroad folk sell maps to the ant hills. Nobody who has one has come back rich. Some have not come back.

Fauna.Name: Steppe pegasus
Fauna.Description: Pliny lists "pegasi", birds with the heads of horses, among the fables of the open north. Here: a great crane-legged bird with a horse's head that runs with the wild herds.
Fauna.Lore: A Grass rider who rides one, once, becomes khan. The tale does not say what happens to those who try.

Fauna.Name: Bonnacon
Fauna.Description: A wild ox with a horse's mane and horns curled back so far that they cannot wound. In flight it throws out dung that burns over a great distance.
Fauna.Lore: Its hide is the best in the grassland. The first tanner to bring one in was not thanked by his street.

Fauna.Name: Rye wolf
Fauna.Description: The spirit of the corn as a wolf. When wind moves the standing grain, peasants say that the wolf goes through the corn. Children are kept out of the fields by it, and it sits in the last sheaf, which the reapers shun.
Fauna.Lore: Since the Ashen Years no Midlander cuts the last sheaf without leaving bread for the wolf.

Fauna.Name: Unicorn
Fauna.Description: A beast with the body of a horse, the head of a stag, the feet of an elephant and one black horn. It can be killed and never taken alive.
Fauna.Lore: Every court has a horn. Most are narwhal tusks. The one true horn in a region is the reason for its oldest feud.

Fauna.Name: Hercynian stag
Fauna.Description: An ox in the shape of a stag with a single horn between the ears, taller and straighter than any known horn and branching at the top like a palm.
Fauna.Lore: Elves hold that each great forest has one and dies with it.

Fauna.Name: Werewolf
Fauna.Description: A person who becomes a wolf. Pliny tells of a man who lived as a wolf for nine years, and does not believe it.
Fauna.Lore: It began in the Ashen Years, the tales say, with the first family that ate what it should not have.

Fauna.Name: Will-o'-the-wisp
Fauna.Description: A goblin fire that dances over marshy ground and leads the late traveller into bogs and pools. It waits when he stops and moves when he follows. Draining the bogs starves it.
Fauna.Lore: The peat under it burns with a cold blue flame, and a mage pays for it by the basket.

Fauna.Name: Water horse
Fauna.Description: A horse-shaped thing that haunts a lake. Yeats tells of a farmer who dragged his lake with nets and then tried to pump it dry to be rid of one.
Fauna.Lore: It stands saddled by the ford at dusk. Seven children can sit on its back, and there is room for one more.

Fauna.Name: Hercinia
Fauna.Description: Birds of a great northern forest whose feathers shine like fire in the night. Pliny has nothing more to tell of them.
Fauna.Lore: A feather lights a path for one night. Charcoal burners follow the flock home and sell the feathers they find to the lost.

Fauna.Name: Squonk
Fauna.Description: A shy creature of the hemlock woods in the tales of the lumberjacks. It has an ill-fitting warty skin, weeps as it goes and dissolves into tears when it is caught.
Fauna.Lore: A sack that held a squonk holds salt water in the morning. Brinefolk find this very funny.

Fauna.Name: Wapaloosie
Fauna.Description: A small tree-climber of the wet coast forests in the tales of the lumberjacks. It climbs the tallest trunks to eat shelf fungus.
Fauna.Lore: Mittens of its skin climb the tent pole by themselves, the loggers say.

Fauna.Name: Salamander
Fauna.Description: The real fire salamander is 15 to 25 cm long, black with yellow or orange spots, lives in shady woodland near streams, and sprays a toxin. Pliny's is spotted like stars, comes out only in great rain, and is so cold that it puts out fire. The bestiary gives it the strongest of poisons: it taints every apple on a tree it climbs.
Fauna.Lore: Smiths keep one in the quench trough, or say they do.

Fauna.Name: Caladrius
Fauna.Description: A white bird that knows whether a sick man will live. If he will, it looks him in the face, takes the sickness into itself and flies towards the sun, which burns it away. If not, it turns its head aside.
Fauna.Lore: A court that owns one hides it. The price of a healer falls when the bird is known to have looked away.

Fauna.Name: Basilisk
Fauna.Description: A small serpent with a pale star-like mark on its head. Other snakes flee its hiss, and its touch and breath kill plants. Only the weasel can kill it. The bestiary adds that its glance kills a man and burns a bird out of the air.
Fauna.Lore: Dead ground in a green valley is a basilisk's doing. Duskreaders hunt it blindfold, by its cold.

Fauna.Name: Amphisbaena
Fauna.Description: A serpent with a second head on its tail that runs either way with its body in a hoop. Its eyes glow like lamps, and it is the first snake out in spring.
Fauna.Lore: Its skin, wound on a staff, is the well digger's charm: it finds the way down and the way back.

Fauna.Name: Phoenix
Fauna.Description: A bird like an eagle, red and gold, that comes once in five hundred years carrying its dead father in an egg of myrrh. Pliny has it build a nest of cinnamon and frankincense and die on it, and the new bird rise from the remains. One at most in a region.
Fauna.Lore: Nobody has seen it. Every incense merchant has a cousin who has.

Fauna.Name: Winged serpent
Fauna.Description: Small snakes of many colours with bat-like wings that guard the frankincense trees and are driven off only with the smoke of storax. They fly towards the river land in spring and are killed by the ibis. The bestiary's kind outruns horses and kills before the bite is felt.
Fauna.Lore: The price of incense is the price of the smoke that buys a day among the trees.

Fauna.Name: Cactus cat
Fauna.Description: A cat of the cactus country in the tales of the lumberjacks. It has a thorny coat and slashes cactus to drink the fermented sap.
Fauna.Lore: It sings on the nights it is drunk. Caravan guards are forbidden to join in.

Fauna.Name: Roperite
Fauna.Description: A runner of the dry foothill scrub in the tales of the lumberjacks. It snares hares with a rope-like beak.
Fauna.Lore: Shepherds find their dogs hobbled at dawn and know what passed.

Fauna.Name: Hill drake
Fauna.Description: A wingless dragon the size of a cart ox that dens in dry sandstone hills and hunts by ambush. It is the small remnant of the great dragons whose bones lie in the same rock.
Fauna.Lore: Dwarves mine dragonbone only after buying the hill from its drake, with a goat a week.

Fauna.Name: Catoblepas
Fauna.Description: A sluggish beast whose head is too heavy to lift, so that it hangs to the ground. Anyone who meets its eyes dies.
Fauna.Lore: Herders water their cattle at noon, when it sleeps. Noonfolk are hired to stand watch.

Fauna.Name: Manticore
Fauna.Description: A beast with a man's face, a lion's body, a tail that stings like a scorpion's, three rows of teeth and a hunger for human flesh. Pliny has it from Ctesias.
Fauna.Lore: It calls travellers by name from the scrub in a voice like a flute. The right answer is to keep walking.

Fauna.Name: Leucrocuta
Fauna.Description: A beast the size of an ass with a lion's body, a badger's head and one ridge of bone for teeth, that copies human speech. The bestiary makes it the young of a hyena and a lioness.
Fauna.Lore: It learns the names of a camp by listening at night. Sunlander herders answer only to a name they chose that day.

Fauna.Name: Yale
Fauna.Description: A black beast as large as a horse with an elephant's tail, a boar's jaws and long horns that it can swing at will: it fights with one and keeps the other folded back.
Fauna.Lore: A pair of yale horns is the best bow a Sunlander smith can mount, and the hardest to match.

Fauna.Name: Dragon
Fauna.Description: A crested serpent of the hot lands whose strength is in its tail. It lies on the paths of elephants, knots itself round their legs and strangles them, and the two often die together. One at most in a region.
Fauna.Lore: Pliny says the red pigment cinnabar is the blood of a dragon crushed under a dying elephant. Painters pay for it as if that were true.

Fauna.Name: Roc
Fauna.Description: A bird like an eagle and of enormous size, of the islands of the southern sea. In Marco Polo's account it seizes an elephant in its talons, carries it up and drops it to break it read in a search excerpt of Yule's edition only.
Fauna.Lore: Shoalfolk pilots mark its islands on no chart and steer by where the charts are blank.

Fauna.Name: Cinnamon bird
Fauna.Description: A great bird that builds its nest of cinnamon sticks on a crag. The gatherers lay out joints of ox and ass. The birds carry them up, the nests break under the weight, and the sticks fall. Pliny has the nests shot down with leaded arrows, and calls all such tales lies told to raise the price.
Fauna.Lore: The spice guilds keep the tale alive, as Pliny guessed. Now and then a real nest is found, and that keeps it alive too.

Fauna.Name: Scitalis
Fauna.Description: A serpent whose back glitters with so many colours that the onlooker stands dazed. It is slow and takes those it has stunned. It runs so hot that it sheds its skin even in winter.
Fauna.Lore: Boughwalker painters grind the shed skin for a colour that only they can see.

Fauna.Name: Javelin snake
Fauna.Description: A flying serpent that throws itself from a tree onto whatever passes below and kills it.
Fauna.Lore: Forest porters carry their loads on their heads for this reason, they say, and not for comfort.

Fauna.Name: Hydrus
Fauna.Description: A water snake of the great river. Pliny tells of the small enemy of the crocodile that slips into its open mouth and gnaws out through the belly. Here the two are one creature.
Fauna.Lore: Fishers free a hydrus from the net with an apology. The crocodile is everyone's enemy.

Fauna.Name: Storm crane
Fauna.Description: A tall grey bird that follows thunderheads over open plains and nests where lightning has fused the soil to glass.
Fauna.Lore: Widegaze see the flock a day before the storm and move the herds.

Fauna.Name: Canopy spinner
Fauna.Description: A spider the size of a dog that webs the gaps between the tallest trees and takes birds and monkeys.
Fauna.Lore: Boughwalkers cut the old webs for rope bridges and leave the spinner a parrot.

Fauna.Name: Moon oyster
Fauna.Description: A giant shell of warm shallow water that opens only under a full moon and closes on whatever reaches in.
Fauna.Lore: A Shoalfolk diver who brings up a moonpearl may name the price of the family's reef.

Fauna.Name: Serra
Fauna.Description: A sea monster with huge wings that races a ship under sail for three or four miles, tires, folds its wings and is carried back to the deep.
Fauna.Lore: Sailors bet on the race. The serra has never won, and they say that is why the sea is still crossed.

Fauna.Name: Stay-ship
Fauna.Description: The real sharksucker is a slim fish up to 1 m that rides on sharks and whales by a sucker on its head, and is used as living bait on a line. Pliny's echeneis clings to a keel and holds the ship back.
Fauna.Lore: A becalmed captain has the hull scraped before he has the crew flogged.

Resources.Name: Grain
Resources.Description: The cereals a land is sown with: fields of standing corn that turn from green to gold, cut with sickle and scythe and threshed on the barn floor. The bread, the porridge and the ale of most people.
Resources.Lore: Every calendar is a grain calendar, and every tax began as a share of the threshing floor. A people is known by its bread: the Catfolk, who cannot eat grain, are trusted to guard it.

Variants.Name: bread wheat
Variants.Description: Tall golden wheat with plump beardless ears, grown on good ploughland. Its flour makes the white loaf that rises.
Variants.Lore: White bread is for the lord's table. Midlanders reckon a man's standing by the colour of his loaf.

Variants.Name: durum wheat
Variants.Description: Hard wheat of dry sunny land, with long dark beards on the ear and amber, glassy grains. Ground for flat bread, groats and paste.
Variants.Lore: The Saltroad folk roll it into grains by hand and steam it, and carry it dried across the desert.

Variants.Name: barley
Variants.Description: A low pale-gold grain with long silky beards that nod in the wind. It takes cold, drought and poor soil, and is malted for ale and boiled for porridge.
Variants.Lore: The first grain to be sown and the first to be brewed. Dwarves keep seven years of it behind the gate.

Variants.Name: rye
Variants.Description: A tall, thin, grey-green grain of cold and sandy land, with slender bearded ears. It gives a dark, heavy, sour bread.
Variants.Lore: The bread of the north and of the poor. In a wet year a black spur grows in the ear, and a village that eats it burns and dances.

Variants.Name: oats
Variants.Description: A grain with loose, drooping heads of small husked seeds, grown in cool wet land. Food for horses, and porridge and flat cakes for people.
Variants.Lore: Fed to horses in the south and to people in the north, as southerners like to point out. Hearthbloods eat it by the pot, twice a day.

Variants.Name: paddy rice
Variants.Description: Bright green rice standing in flooded, banked fields that mirror the sky, on valley floors and hillside terraces. The ears droop gold at harvest.
Variants.Lore: The Canal folk built an empire to keep the banks mended. The Rainkeepers catch a season's rain in ten thousand reservoirs for it.

Variants.Name: maize
Variants.Description: Stalks taller than a person with broad leaves and thick cobs of yellow, white or red kernels wrapped in husks.
Variants.Lore: It must be planted by hand, seed by seed. The peoples who grow it say the first humans were made of its dough.

Variants.Name: sorghum
Variants.Description: A grain of hot dry land, taller than a person, with a heavy head of round red or white seeds at the top of a cane-like stalk.
Variants.Lore: The Sunlanders brew it into a thick, sour beer, and a day's work is paid with a pot of it.

Variants.Name: pearl millet
Variants.Description: A grain of the driest farmland: tall stalks that end in a dense spike like a bulrush, set with small pearl-grey seeds.
Variants.Lore: It grows where nothing else will, at the edge of the sand. The Saltroad folk call it the grain that asks for nothing.

Variants.Name: finger millet
Variants.Description: A short millet of tropical hills, whose head spreads like the fingers of a hand, curled inward and set with tiny red-brown seeds.
Variants.Lore: It keeps in the granary for ten years. A hill village that has it does not fear one bad monsoon.

Variants.Name: proso millet
Variants.Description: A quick millet of the steppe, knee to waist high, with drooping bushy heads of small round golden seeds. It ripens in a short summer.
Variants.Lore: The Grass riders sow it, ride away and come back to reap it. It is the only farming they admit to.

Variants.Name: buckwheat
Variants.Description: A low plant with red stems, heart-shaped leaves and white flowers thick with bees, grown on poor cold soil. The dark three-cornered seeds are ground for cakes and porridge.
Variants.Lore: The crop of new clearings and bad land. Its honey is dark and strong, and the Northmen like it so.

Variants.Name: fonio
Variants.Description: A fine grass grown on poor sandy soil in the savanna, with seeds as small as sand. It ripens before any other grain, in the hungry weeks.
Variants.Lore: The Sunlanders say the world was made from a grain of it. It is served to chiefs and to guests.

Variants.Name: teff
Variants.Description: A delicate highland grass with feathery heads and seeds smaller than a pinhead, white or red-brown. Ground for a sour, spongy flat bread.
Variants.Lore: A lost handful sows a field. Highland peoples carried it in a fold of cloth through the Ashen Years.

Variants.Name: quinoa
Variants.Description: A leafy plant of high cold plateaus, waist high, with great seed heads of red, purple, yellow and white. The small round seeds are boiled like grain.
Variants.Lore: The mother grain of the high plateaus. The first furrow of the year is opened by the ruler, with a spade of gold.

Resources.Name: Produce
Resources.Description: The food of garden and field that is not grain: roots, tubers, beans, peas and greens, grown in plots near the house and carried to market in baskets.
Resources.Lore: What kept the poor alive when the grain failed. Halflings came through the Ashen Years on their cellars of roots and beans, and shared them.

Variants.Name: potato
Variants.Description: A low leafy plant grown in earthed-up ridges on cool hills, with white or purple flowers. The brown tubers are dug from the soil in autumn.
Variants.Lore: Armies trample a wheat field, and leave a potato field alone because they do not know what is under it.

Variants.Name: cassava
Variants.Description: A woody tropical shrub, taller than a person, with hand-shaped leaves. Its long brown roots are white inside, and are grated and pressed to take out the poison.
Variants.Lore: Badly prepared, it kills. The Bitterbloods eat it raw and think nothing of it.

Variants.Name: sweet potato
Variants.Description: A creeping vine with heart-shaped leaves that covers the ground in warm lands. Its swollen roots are red-skinned with orange or white flesh.
Variants.Lore: It grows on poor land in a famine year, and the Canal folk credit it with a doubling of their numbers.

Variants.Name: greater yam
Variants.Description: A climbing vine grown on poles from mounds of earth in wet tropical land. Its rough brown tubers can be as long as an arm.
Variants.Lore: A man shows his best yams at the harvest feast and is ranked by them. The yam is a man's crop, and the other roots are women's.

Variants.Name: taro
Variants.Description: A plant of wet ground and pond fields, with huge heart-shaped leaves on long stalks. The grey corm at its foot is boiled or pounded.
Variants.Lore: On the islands it is the elder brother of the people, and no one quarrels while the bowl is open.

Variants.Name: banana and plantain
Variants.Description: Tall soft-stemmed plants with great tattered leaves, grown beside the house in hot wet land. Each bears one hanging bunch of green or yellow fruit.
Variants.Lore: A grove is planted at a birth. Its beer is the drink of every bargain in the wet highlands.

Variants.Name: sago palm
Variants.Description: A palm of tropical swamps, felled just before it flowers. Its trunk is split and the pith is washed to a white starch.
Variants.Lore: One palm feeds a family for a month. The Shoalfolk say a people with sago has no need of a field.

Variants.Name: faba bean
Variants.Description: An upright bean with grey-green leaves and white flowers marked with black, grown in cool lands. The fat pods hold broad flat beans.
Variants.Lore: The dead are said to live in beans, and some sects will not eat them. A bean baked in a cake makes a king for a night.

Variants.Name: pea
Variants.Description: A climbing plant with curling tendrils, grown on sticks in fields and gardens of cool lands. The peas are dried and boiled to pottage.
Variants.Lore: Pease pottage is the daily dish of the Midlander poor, hot or cold, and nine days old in the rhyme.

Variants.Name: lentil
Variants.Description: A low, fine-leaved plant of dry lands, with small pods that hold two flat round seeds each: brown, green or red.
Variants.Lore: The food of mourners, and of a birthright sold for a bowl of it. The Saltroad folk eat it every day.

Variants.Name: chickpea
Variants.Description: A low bushy plant of dry warm land with feathery leaves and puffed pods, each with one or two round beaked seeds.
Variants.Lore: Roasted and sold in paper twists at every market of the dry south. Caravans carry it because it does not spoil.

Variants.Name: common bean
Variants.Description: A bean of warm lands, bushy or climbing up poles and maize stalks, with long pods of kidney-shaped seeds in many colours.
Variants.Lore: Planted with maize and squash as three sisters: the maize holds the bean up, and the bean feeds the soil.

Variants.Name: cowpea
Variants.Description: A trailing bean of hot dry land with long thin pods and small pale seeds with a black eye.
Variants.Lore: The Sunlanders eat the black-eyed bean at the new year, for luck, and plant it between the millet.

Variants.Name: cabbage and kale
Variants.Description: Leafy plants of cool gardens: round heads of cabbage and tall curled kale, blue-green and standing through the winter.
Variants.Lore: The winter green of the north. Northmen ferment it in barrels and take it to sea against the sailors' sickness.

Variants.Name: onion and alliums
Variants.Description: Onions, leeks and garlic in neat garden rows: hollow green leaves above, bulbs below, hung in plaits to dry.
Variants.Lore: Garlic keeps off the evil eye and things that walk at night. The builders of the Old Realms were paid in onions.

Variants.Name: carrot and root vegetables
Variants.Description: Carrots, turnips, parsnips and beets: roots of white, purple, yellow and red, pulled from garden beds and kept in sand through the winter.
Variants.Lore: The turnip is the food of honest poverty in every tale. Halflings grow them to a size that wins prizes.

Variants.Name: melons
Variants.Description: Trailing vines on warm sandy soil and river banks, with melons, gourds and watermelons lying heavy on the ground.
Variants.Lore: The Saltroad folk count a slice of melon in the desert among the proofs of a kind god.

Variants.Name: enset
Variants.Description: A plant like a giant banana grown round highland houses in the tropics. It bears no fruit worth eating: the pulp of its stem and root is buried to ferment and baked as bread.
Variants.Lore: A highland house with enset round it has never known famine. It is called the tree against hunger.

Resources.Name: Orchard
Resources.Description: Trees, vines and oil plants that stand for years: orchards, vineyards, groves and nut woods, grown for fruit, nuts, oil and wine and sold more than eaten at home.
Resources.Lore: A tree planted is a claim on the land for a lifetime. Armies cut orchards down to punish a people for a generation, and every law calls it a crime.

Variants.Name: olive
Variants.Description: A grey-green, twisted tree of dry sunny hills that lives for centuries. Its small bitter fruits are pressed for oil.
Variants.Lore: The oil lights the lamps, anoints kings and feeds the poor. A branch of it means peace in every land that grows it.

Variants.Name: grape
Variants.Description: Vines trained on stakes, trees or trellises on sunny slopes, with broad lobed leaves and hanging bunches of green or purple grapes.
Variants.Lore: Wine is the blood of the god in half the temples. Elves keep vintages older than the kingdoms that buy them.

Variants.Name: date palm
Variants.Description: A tall palm of desert oases, with its foot in water and its head in fire. Heavy clusters of brown, sweet dates hang under the crown.
Variants.Lore: The Saltroad folk greet a guest with dates and milk. They say the palm was made from what was left of the clay of the first man.

Variants.Name: fig
Variants.Description: A low, spreading tree of warm dry land, with smooth grey bark and large lobed leaves. The soft purple or green fruits are dried on mats.
Variants.Lore: To sit under one's own vine and fig tree is the whole of peace. The tree is never seen to flower, and people wonder at it.

Variants.Name: pomegranate
Variants.Description: A thorny shrub or small tree with scarlet flowers. Its round, leathery red fruit is crowned like a small king and full of juicy red seeds.
Variants.Lore: The fruit of the dead and of marriage. Six seeds of it kept a goddess underground for half the year.

Variants.Name: almond
Variants.Description: A small tree of dry hills that blossoms pink and white before any other. The nuts lie in a hard pitted shell inside a grey-green velvet hull.
Variants.Lore: The first blossom of the year, and so the tree of watchfulness. Sugared almonds are given at weddings.

Variants.Name: pistachio
Variants.Description: A small, tough tree of hot dry hills, with clusters of reddish fruit whose shells split open on a green kernel.
Variants.Lore: Lovers meet under the trees at night to hear the shells crack open, which is good luck.

Variants.Name: apple
Variants.Description: A round-headed tree of cool lands, with pink-white blossom in spring and red, green or yellow apples in autumn.
Variants.Lore: Every forbidden fruit and every prize of beauty is an apple in the telling. Halflings wassail the trees in midwinter.

Variants.Name: pear
Variants.Description: A tall, upright tree of cool lands with white blossom and green or russet pears. It lives longer than the apple.
Variants.Lore: Plant pears for your heirs, the saying goes. Perry is the drink of the western Midlander shires.

Variants.Name: peach and stone fruit
Variants.Description: Small trees of warm sheltered gardens: peach, apricot, plum and cherry, with pink and white blossom and soft fruit around a stone.
Variants.Lore: The Canal folk hold the peach to be the fruit of long life, and paint it on the birthday gifts of the old.

Variants.Name: citrus
Variants.Description: Evergreen trees with dark glossy leaves, scented white flowers and bright fruit: oranges, lemons and citrons, grown in walled, watered gardens.
Variants.Lore: A golden fruit in a walled garden is a king's boast. Sailors have learnt to carry lemons, and not why.

Variants.Name: walnut
Variants.Description: A large spreading tree with smooth grey bark. The nut ripens in a green husk that stains the hands brown.
Variants.Lore: Nothing grows in its shade. The nut is shaped like a brain, so it is prescribed for the head.

Variants.Name: sweet chestnut
Variants.Description: A large tree of warm hill country with long toothed leaves. The brown nuts ripen in prickly green burrs and are the bread of the mountains.
Variants.Lore: Hill people who have never seen a wheat field live on its flour. The lowlanders call them chestnut eaters, and mean it badly.

Variants.Name: hazel
Variants.Description: A shrub of many stems in woods and hedges, with yellow catkins in late winter and small round nuts in leafy cups.
Variants.Lore: The tree of wisdom and of the dowser's rod. A good nut year is a good year for babies, the Midlanders say.

Variants.Name: coconut
Variants.Description: A tall leaning palm of tropical shores, with a crown of feathered fronds and clusters of large green and brown nuts.
Variants.Lore: The Shoalfolk call it the tree of a hundred uses and plant one for each child. A drifting nut founds an island.

Variants.Name: oil palm
Variants.Description: A stout palm of wet tropical land, with dense bunches of orange-red fruit at the base of the fronds. The fruit is boiled for a red oil.
Variants.Lore: The red oil is in every Sunlander pot, and its wine in every cup. The tapper climbs with a rope round the trunk and his waist.

Variants.Name: mango
Variants.Description: A great, dense, dark-leaved shade tree of the tropics, hung in season with oval green, yellow and red fruit on long stalks.
Variants.Lore: Rainkeeper villages meet under the mango tree. Its leaves are hung over the door for a wedding.

Variants.Name: cashew
Variants.Description: A low, spreading tropical tree. Each nut hangs in a grey kidney-shaped shell under a swollen red or yellow false fruit.
Variants.Lore: The shell burns the hands that crack it. The work is given to those who have no other.

Variants.Name: shea
Variants.Description: A gnarled tree of the dry savanna, left standing in the fields. Its plum-like green fruit holds a nut that is boiled and churned to a pale butter.
Variants.Lore: The butter is women's gold among the Sunlanders: gathered, churned and sold by women, and the men have no say in the money.

Variants.Name: baobab
Variants.Description: A savanna tree with a vast, swollen grey trunk and short bare branches like roots in the air. Its velvety pods hold a sour white pulp.
Variants.Lore: A god pulled it up and planted it upside down, in anger. Sunlanders bury their praise-singers in its hollow trunk.

Variants.Name: tamarind
Variants.Description: A big tropical shade tree with feathery leaves and brown, brittle pods filled with a sticky, sour-sweet pulp.
Variants.Lore: Spirits live in it, and no one sleeps under one. Its pulp polishes brass and sours every dish of the monsoon lands.

Variants.Name: breadfruit
Variants.Description: A tall tree of tropical islands with large, deeply cut glossy leaves and round green fruit the size of a head, baked like bread.
Variants.Lore: One tree feeds a household for life, and so the islanders have time to sing.

Variants.Name: Brazil nut
Variants.Description: A giant of the rain forest, far taller than the trees around it. Its fruit is a woody ball like a cannonball, packed with three-sided nuts.
Variants.Lore: It cannot be planted in an orchard: it fruits only in the deep forest. The Boughwalkers gather it, and stand clear when the balls fall.

Variants.Name: avocado
Variants.Description: A leafy tree of warm highlands with pear-shaped, dark green fruit: buttery flesh around one large stone.
Variants.Lore: The highland peoples call it by the word for a part of a man, and keep girls indoors at the harvest.

Variants.Name: sunflower
Variants.Description: A field crop taller than a person, with one great yellow flower head that follows the sun. The seeds are pressed for oil.
Variants.Lore: It turns its face to the sun all day. The Noonfolk plant it at their doors as a kindred thing.

Variants.Name: rapeseed
Variants.Description: A field crop of cool lands that flowers in sheets of bright yellow in spring. Its small black seeds are pressed for lamp oil.
Variants.Lore: Its oil lights the lamps of the north where the olive will not grow. It smokes, and the north is used to that.

Variants.Name: sesame
Variants.Description: An upright plant of hot dry fields with pale bell flowers and seed capsules that burst open when ripe. The tiny seeds give a fine oil.
Variants.Lore: The pods open at a touch, and so a door in a tale opens at its name. The oil does not go rancid on a long road.

Variants.Name: groundnut
Variants.Description: A low plant of warm sandy soil whose flowers bend down and push into the ground. The nuts ripen there, in pale wrinkled pods.
Variants.Lore: It hides its fruit in the earth. The Sunlanders grind it into a stew, and travellers ask for it by name.

Variants.Name: soybean
Variants.Description: A bushy, hairy bean plant of warm temperate fields, with short pods of round yellow beans, pressed for oil and made into curd and sauce.
Variants.Lore: The Canal folk make of it a milk, a curd and a black sauce, and call it the meat of the fields.

Resources.Name: Livestock
Resources.Description: The animals kept for meat, milk, wool and hides: herds and flocks on pasture, moor and stubble, with their herders and dogs.
Resources.Lore: Wealth that walks: the oldest word for money is the word for cattle. Herders and farmers have been at law over trampled corn since the Dawn.

Variants.Name: yak
Variants.Description: A shaggy, long-haired ox of high cold plateaus, black or brown, with wide horns and a bushy tail. It gives milk, wool, meat and dung for the fire.
Variants.Lore: Hearthbloods live on its butter, stirred into salt tea, and burn its dung. A herd is a hall's whole wealth.

Variants.Name: goats
Variants.Description: Lean, agile animals with horns and beards, in every colour, that browse thorn and rock where nothing else can live.
Variants.Lore: The poor man's cow. Dwarves keep them on the high pastures above the hold, and the goat is the devil's beast in the lowlands.

Variants.Name: alpine summer pasture
Variants.Description: High green meadows above the tree line, grazed by cattle and sheep in the summer months only, with stone huts where the cheese is made.
Variants.Lore: The herds go up with bells and garlands in spring and come down with the cheese in autumn. The right to the high grass is the oldest law of a valley.

Variants.Name: herded reindeer
Variants.Description: Half-tame reindeer kept in great herds on tundra and in northern forest, followed by their herders through the year.
Variants.Lore: The herd is the people. A child is given a calf at birth, and its descendants are the child's dowry.

Variants.Name: sheep
Variants.Description: Woolly flocks, white, grey and black, on hill pasture, heath and stubble. Kept for wool first, and for milk and mutton.
Variants.Lore: Wool built the Midlander towns, and the great lords evict their tenants to make room for it. The sheep, it is said, eat men.

Variants.Name: cattle
Variants.Description: Horned cows and oxen, red, black and dun, smaller than modern beasts. They pull the plough and give milk, meat and hides.
Variants.Lore: Sunlanders count wealth, marriage and blood-price in cattle. The old epics of every people are about a cattle raid.

Variants.Name: pigs
Variants.Description: Lean, bristly, long-snouted pigs, dark and half wild, that feed in the woods on acorns and beechnuts and in the streets on refuse.
Variants.Lore: The peasant's meat, killed at the first frost and salted for the winter. Some faiths forbid it, and are known by that.

Variants.Name: water buffalo
Variants.Description: A heavy, dark grey beast with wide swept-back horns that wallows in mud and pulls the plough through flooded rice fields.
Variants.Lore: The tractor of the paddy. Canal folk children ride it home in the evening, and a family that loses it sells a field.

Variants.Name: poultry
Variants.Description: Hens, ducks and geese that scratch about the yard and the pond, kept for eggs, meat and feathers.
Variants.Lore: The hen is the wife's, and the egg money with it. A cock crows on the temple tower against the dark.

Resources.Name: Fish
Resources.Description: The catch of sea, river and lake: fish and shellfish taken with net, line, trap and spear, and eaten fresh, salted, smoked or dried.
Resources.Lore: The food of fast days and of the poor of every coast. A catch spoils in a day, so the salter grows rich on the fisher's luck.

Variants.Name: cod banks
Variants.Description: Shallow banks in cold seas where great grey-green cod gather in their thousands. They are caught on long lines and dried on racks until hard as wood.
Variants.Lore: The Northmen found the banks and told no one for a century. Dried cod is the only coin some coasts have ever used.

Variants.Name: herring
Variants.Description: Vast silver shoals of small fish in cold seas, netted from fleets of open boats and packed in barrels of salt.
Variants.Lore: The silver of the sea. Whole leagues of towns have risen on the shoals, and fallen when the shoals moved away.

Variants.Name: sardine and anchovy
Variants.Description: Small silver fish of warm seas that shoal near the surface, netted at night by the light of torches.
Variants.Lore: The Old Realms rotted them into a sauce and shipped it in jars to every province. The shards still smell.

Variants.Name: reef fish and shellfish
Variants.Description: Bright-coloured fish, clams and conches from coral reefs and warm lagoons, taken with spears, traps and by hand.
Variants.Lore: The reef is the Shoalfolk's field, parcelled by family. A reef may be closed for a season by planting a marked pole on it.

Variants.Name: tuna and large pelagics
Variants.Description: Great, fast, blue-backed fish of the open sea, as heavy as a person, taken in trap nets on their yearly run past the headlands.
Variants.Lore: A whole village rows out for the kill and the sea turns red. The chief of the trap is called by a king's title.

Variants.Name: crabs, lobsters and shrimp
Variants.Description: Armoured, clawed creatures of rocky and muddy shores, caught in baited wicker pots and push nets.
Variants.Lore: Fed to servants and prisoners on the cold coasts, who have it written into their terms that it shall not be every day.

Variants.Name: salmon runs
Variants.Description: Big silver fish that swim up cold rivers from the sea each year and leap the falls. They are speared and trapped at weirs.
Variants.Lore: The salmon of knowledge swims in every tale of the west. The first fish of the run is put back, with thanks.

Variants.Name: oysters and mussels
Variants.Description: Beds of shellfish on rocks and mud flats between the tides: rough grey oysters and blue-black mussels, gathered at low water.
Variants.Lore: The food of the poor, eaten by the hundred. The shell heaps behind the Shoalfolk villages are hills.

Variants.Name: sturgeon
Variants.Description: A huge, ancient river fish, longer than a person, with a long snout and rows of bony plates. Its meat and its black roe go to lords' tables.
Variants.Lore: A royal fish: wherever it is caught it belongs to the ruler. Its roe is salted for courts, and the fishers eat the rest.

Variants.Name: river fish
Variants.Description: Pike, carp, perch and bream of slow rivers, taken with nets, traps and weirs, and kept alive in ponds.
Variants.Lore: The monks keep carp ponds for the fast days. The pike in the pond is said to be as old as the abbey.

Variants.Name: eels
Variants.Description: Long, slippery, snake-like fish of rivers and marshes, trapped in wicker pots at mills and weirs and smoked or salted.
Variants.Lore: No one has seen an eel's eggs. The learned say they are born of mud, and the trappers let them say it.

Variants.Name: lake fish
Variants.Description: Trout, whitefish and perch of clear lakes, netted from small boats and through holes in the ice in winter.
Variants.Lore: The Hoarkin and the Northmen fish through the ice in winter. A hole is owned for the season, and marked with a branch.

Resources.Name: Wild food & game
Resources.Description: What the wild land gives without sowing: game, wildfowl, berries, nuts, mushrooms and herbs, taken by hunters and foragers.
Resources.Lore: Free to all in the old law, and the lord's in the new. The forest feeds a village in a bad year, and hangs a man for it in a good one.

Variants.Name: edible seaweed and kelp
Variants.Description: Brown, red and green weed gathered from the rocks at low tide and dried on the shore, for food, for fodder and for the fields.
Variants.Lore: Famine food on the Northern coasts, and daily food on the eastern ones. The Shoalfolk grow it on ropes.

Variants.Name: wild sheep and ibex
Variants.Description: Sure-footed mountain animals with great curved horns that keep to cliffs and high ledges. Hunted for meat, hide and horn.
Variants.Lore: The stones in an ibex's stomach are sold against poison. Hearthblood boys must bring one down alone to be counted as men.

Variants.Name: waterfowl
Variants.Description: Ducks, geese and swans that gather on marshes, lakes and river mouths in great noisy flocks, taken with nets and decoys.
Variants.Lore: The geese go over in autumn and the north reads the winter from how high they fly. The swan is the lord's alone.

Variants.Name: lotus
Variants.Description: A water plant of warm ponds and slow rivers with round leaves and large pink flowers held above the water. Its seeds and long roots are eaten.
Variants.Lore: It rises clean from the mud, and the Rainkeepers set their gods upon it. Those who eat the fruit in the tales forget their homes.

Variants.Name: seals
Variants.Description: Sleek, grey, spotted sea animals that lie on rocks and ice at the shore. Hunted for meat, blubber and oil.
Variants.Lore: The Hoarkin live on the seal: meat, oil for the lamp and a skin for the boat. The seal people of the tales shed that skin on the shore.

Variants.Name: caribou
Variants.Description: Wild reindeer that cross tundra and northern forest in herds of thousands. They are hunted at river crossings.
Variants.Lore: The herds cross where they have always crossed, and the hunters wait there. In the year they do not come, the people starve.

Variants.Name: cloudberry and crowberry
Variants.Description: Low plants of bog and tundra: the cloudberry with one amber berry on a stalk, the crowberry a mat with small black ones.
Variants.Lore: The gold of the bogs. Northmen have a law on cloudberries, and the picking places are a family secret.

Variants.Name: deer and elk
Variants.Description: The big game of northern forests: red deer with branching antlers and the tall, long-legged elk with its broad shovels.
Variants.Lore: The Northmen hunt the elk on skis in the deep snow. Its hoof is carried against the falling sickness.

Variants.Name: bilberry and blueberry
Variants.Description: Low shrubs that carpet the floor of pine and birch woods, covered in late summer with small blue-black berries that stain the mouth.
Variants.Lore: A blue mouth gives away the child who was sent for a full basket. The berries are the right of all in the northern woods.

Variants.Name: forest mushrooms
Variants.Description: The mushrooms of the forest floor in autumn: brown ceps, yellow chanterelles and many more, gathered into baskets and dried on strings.
Variants.Lore: Each family has its places and does not share them. Bitterbloods are asked to the first meal of the season, to eat first.

Variants.Name: deer
Variants.Description: Red, fallow and roe deer of woods and their edges: the lord's game and the poacher's.
Variants.Lore: The lord's game. A hart with a cross between its antlers has converted more than one huntsman in the legends.

Variants.Name: wild boar
Variants.Description: A dark, bristly wild pig with tusks that roots in oak and beech woods. A dangerous quarry, hunted with spear and hounds.
Variants.Lore: The beast of the midwinter feast, carried in with an apple in its mouth. A boar's tusks on a helmet are an Orc chief's mark.

Variants.Name: acorns
Variants.Description: The nuts of the oak, in their small cups, that cover the wood floor in autumn. Pigs are fattened on them, and people eat them leached in hungry years.
Variants.Lore: The right to fatten pigs on them is counted in the lord's rolls. The Orcs grind and eat them, and outlasted the Ashen Years on it.

Variants.Name: raspberry and bramble
Variants.Description: Thorny, arching canes at wood edges and in clearings, with red raspberries and black bramble berries.
Variants.Lore: Brambles are not picked after the first frost: the devil has spat on them. They are the fruit of everyone who has no garden.

Variants.Name: bison and wild cattle
Variants.Description: Huge, shaggy, humped wild oxen of grassland and open forest, in herds that shake the ground.
Variants.Lore: The Grass riders drove them over cliffs before they had horses. A horn of the great wild ox is a king's drinking cup.

Variants.Name: hares and rabbits
Variants.Description: Long-eared grazers of field and heath: the hare alone in the open, rabbits in warrens of burrows. Snared and coursed with dogs.
Variants.Lore: Witches go about as hares, and a hare crossing the road turns a traveller back. The warren is the lord's, and the rabbit the poacher's.

Variants.Name: antelope and gazelle
Variants.Description: Slender, swift, horned grazers of dry plains, fawn and white, in leaping herds.
Variants.Lore: The Saltroad poets compare every beloved to a gazelle. It is hunted with hawks and swift hounds, from horseback.

Variants.Name: upland game birds
Variants.Description: Grouse, partridge, pheasant and quail of moor, heath and field edge, taken with nets, snares and hawks.
Variants.Lore: Quail fall on the desert in their thousands, tired from the crossing, and are taken by hand. A partridge is a lord's dish.

Variants.Name: wild herbs
Variants.Description: The green herbs of the kitchen that grow wild: garlic leaf, sorrel, nettle, mint and cress, gathered in spring.
Variants.Lore: The first green of spring, after a winter of salt meat. Nine herbs go into the pot on the first warm day.

Resources.Name: Timber
Resources.Description: Wood for building, ships, tools and fuel: standing forest and the logs taken from it, felled with the axe and hauled by ox and river.
Resources.Lore: The Old Realms cut forests for fleets and furnaces, and the Elves have not forgiven it. Every people has a law on which tree may fall, and breaks it for a ship.

Variants.Name: larch
Variants.Description: A conifer of cold mountains and the far north that sheds its soft needles gold in autumn. Its hard, reddish wood resists rot.
Variants.Lore: A city of the lagoons stands on larch piles driven into the mud, and they have not rotted in a thousand years.

Variants.Name: spruce
Variants.Description: A dark, spire-shaped conifer with drooping boughs and long hanging cones, in dense northern forests. Light, straight wood for masts, boards and instruments.
Variants.Lore: Gnomes buy the slow-grown spruce of the high valleys for the bellies of their instruments, and tap each trunk to hear it first.

Variants.Name: Scots pine
Variants.Description: A tall pine with orange-red upper bark and a flat blue-green crown, on sand and rock. It gives straight timber, tar and pitch.
Variants.Lore: The Northmen's tree: it gives the mast, the plank and the tar. A lone pine marks a grave or a meeting place.

Variants.Name: fir
Variants.Description: A tall, regular conifer of mountain forests, with flat needles, silver below, and cones that stand upright. Long beams for roofs.
Variants.Lore: The ridge beam of a great hall is one fir, drawn from the mountain by forty oxen. A small one is brought indoors at midwinter.

Variants.Name: beech
Variants.Description: A tall tree with a smooth grey trunk like a pillar and a dense canopy that shades the ground bare. Pale hard wood for tools, furniture and fuel.
Variants.Lore: The first books were beech boards, and the word for a book is the word for the tree. Its mast fattens the pigs.

Variants.Name: oak
Variants.Description: A massive, broad-crowned tree with a rugged trunk and lobed leaves. The strongest and most lasting timber, for ships, frames and barrels.
Variants.Lore: The Old Realms planted oaks in rows for ships they never built. Lightning seeks it, and so it is the thunder god's.

Variants.Name: lime
Variants.Description: A tall tree with heart-shaped leaves and sweet-scented flowers. Its soft pale wood is the carver's, and its inner bark makes rope.
Variants.Lore: The village court sits under the lime tree, since no one can lie in its shade. Every holy image of the north is carved from it.

Variants.Name: cedar
Variants.Description: A great mountain conifer with wide, flat tiers of dark branches. The red, scented wood does not rot and roofs temples and palaces.
Variants.Lore: Kings have sent armies for it since the Dawn, and the mountains where it grew are bare. What stands is guarded by priests.

Variants.Name: ash
Variants.Description: A tall, open tree with feathered leaves and black winter buds. Tough, springy pale wood for spear shafts, handles and wheels.
Variants.Lore: The world hangs on an ash tree in the Northmen's telling. Every spear and every axe handle is cut from it.

Variants.Name: elm
Variants.Description: A tall tree of valleys and hedgerows with a lopsided leaf. Its wood does not split and lasts under water: wheel hubs, pipes and piles.
Variants.Lore: The coffin tree, and the water pipe under the street. It drops a bough without warning, and is not trusted.

Variants.Name: giant conifers
Variants.Description: Trees of the wet western coasts, taller than any tower, with red, fibrous trunks wider than a house and no branch for the first fifty paces.
Variants.Lore: One tree builds a village. The Amberbloods say the oldest of them were people once, and can name some.

Variants.Name: juniper
Variants.Description: A small, twisted evergreen of dry slopes, with blue berries and prickly needles. Scented red wood for posts, chests and smoking meat.
Variants.Lore: Burnt at the turn of the year to smoke out sickness and spirits. Its berries go into the strong drink of the north.

Variants.Name: cypress
Variants.Description: A narrow, dark, flame-shaped evergreen of warm dry lands. Scented, lasting wood for doors, chests and coffins.
Variants.Lore: Planted on graves in the south, since it never sprouts again once cut. Temple doors of it have lasted eleven centuries.

Variants.Name: Mediterranean pines
Variants.Description: Pines of warm coasts: umbrella-shaped stone pines and wind-leaning coast pines, on red earth above a blue sea. Ship timber, resin and pine nuts.
Variants.Lore: The pine cone is the sign of the wine god and tops his staff. Resin from these trees flavours the wine and seals the jars.

Variants.Name: cork oak
Variants.Description: An evergreen oak of warm dry hills. Its thick, spongy bark is stripped every ten years and leaves the trunk red-brown.
Variants.Lore: The tree may be stripped once in nine years, and the year is painted on the trunk. To strip it sooner is theft from one's own son.

Variants.Name: teak
Variants.Description: A tall tree of the monsoon forest with huge rough leaves that fall in the dry season. Its golden-brown, oily wood is the best there is for ships.
Variants.Lore: The Rainkeepers haul it with elephants and float it for two years to the sea. A teak ship outlives three of oak.

Variants.Name: sal
Variants.Description: A tall, straight tree that stands in pure forests in the monsoon lands. Hard, heavy brown wood for beams and posts, and a resin burnt as incense.
Variants.Lore: The Rainkeepers hold it holy: a teacher of theirs was born under one and died between two.

Variants.Name: Spanish cedar
Variants.Description: A tall tree of the tropical forest with light, red-brown, scented wood that insects leave alone. Easy to work, for chests and boats.
Variants.Lore: Chests of it keep moths from cloth, and the scent tells a buyer the wood is true.

Variants.Name: rosewood
Variants.Description: A tropical tree with dark wood streaked purple and black that smells of roses when cut. For fine furniture and instruments.
Variants.Lore: Court furniture and the finest instruments. Its export is the ruler's alone, and a log of it is weighed like spice.

Variants.Name: mahogany
Variants.Description: A giant of the tropical forest with a buttressed trunk. Its red-brown wood works smooth and takes a deep polish.
Variants.Lore: One tree is worth a house, so the cutters search the forest for a year to find it.

Variants.Name: iroko
Variants.Description: A great tree of the tropical forest and its edge, with golden wood that darkens to brown and resists rot and insects.
Variants.Lore: A spirit lives in it, and a Sunlander woodcutter asks its leave. Furniture made of it is heard to groan at night.

Variants.Name: ebony
Variants.Description: A small tree of dry tropical forest whose heartwood is jet black and so heavy that it sinks in water.
Variants.Lore: Sold by weight, like metal. Black thrones and the black keys of instruments, and it turns a poisoned cup, they say.

Variants.Name: African mahogany
Variants.Description: A tall tree of the wet tropical forest and river banks, with pinkish wood that darkens to red-brown. Canoes are hollowed from single trunks.
Variants.Lore: The Sunlanders hollow war canoes for sixty paddlers from one trunk, and carve the prow before the tree is dry.

Variants.Name: thorn-scrub wood
Variants.Description: Small, hard, crooked thorn trees with flat crowns, in dry bush. Wood for posts, fences, tool handles and charcoal.
Variants.Lore: The cattle fold of every dry country is a ring of cut thorn. The wood is so hard that it is shaped green or not at all.

Variants.Name: mangrove timber
Variants.Description: Trees that stand on stilt roots in tidal mud. Dense red wood that does not rot in salt water: poles, piles and a bark for tanning.
Variants.Lore: The Shoalfolk build on mangrove stilts that outlast the house. The poles are shipped to the treeless coasts as rafters.

Variants.Name: poplar
Variants.Description: A fast, tall, straight tree along rivers and the canals of dry lands. Light, soft wood for roof poles and boards.
Variants.Lore: The Saltroad folk plant a row at a son's birth, to be the roof beams of his house.

Variants.Name: willow and poplar
Variants.Description: The trees of river banks and wet meadows: pollarded willows with a head of shoots for baskets and hurdles, and poplars for light boards.
Variants.Lore: The willow weeps, and is the tree of the forsaken. Cut back every few years, it gives the baskets of the whole country.

Variants.Name: driftwood
Variants.Description: Bleached logs thrown up by the sea on treeless northern coasts: the only timber there is, grey-white and smooth.
Variants.Lore: The Hoarkin own no tree, and hold that the sea sends each log to someone. The finder marks it, and no one touches it.

Resources.Name: Stone
Resources.Description: Stone to build and carve with, broken from quarries and cliffs or gathered from the fields: grey, white, red or black, by the rock under the land.
Resources.Lore: Wood is for the living and stone for the gods, the dead and the lord. A city is the colour of its nearest quarry.

Variants.Name: granite
Variants.Description: A hard, speckled stone, grey or pink, with glittering grains. It lies in rounded tors and great blocks, is slow to cut and lasts for ever.
Variants.Lore: Dwarves cut their halls in it and call the softer stones summer rock. A granite cross outlasts the faith that raised it.

Variants.Name: slate
Variants.Description: A fine, dark, blue-grey stone that splits into thin flat sheets, quarried from hillsides for roofs and floors.
Variants.Lore: A roof of it lasts a century, and the schoolchild writes on a piece of it. The slate valleys speak a tongue of their own.

Variants.Name: marble
Variants.Description: A white or veined stone that takes a polish and glows in the light, cut in great blocks from mountain quarries for temples and statues.
Variants.Lore: The Old Realms faced whole cities with it. Later peoples burnt the statues for lime, and build their walls from the temples.

Variants.Name: whetstone
Variants.Description: A fine, gritty, grey stone cut into bars for sharpening blades. A good quarry is known across many lands.
Variants.Lore: The Northmen traded whetstones across the sea, and a king was buried with one as a sceptre. A reaper is no better than his stone.

Variants.Name: basalt
Variants.Description: A dark, heavy, fine-grained stone of old lava, often standing in six-sided columns. For walls, paving and querns.
Variants.Lore: The six-sided columns are a road built by giants, as anyone living near them will explain.

Variants.Name: pumice and pozzolana
Variants.Description: The light stuff of volcanoes: grey pumice full of holes, which floats on water, and a fine ash that makes mortar set under water.
Variants.Lore: The harbour moles of the Old Realms were poured with this ash and have stood in the sea ever since. No one now knows the mixture.

Variants.Name: obsidian
Variants.Description: Black volcanic glass that breaks with a curved, shining face and an edge sharper than steel. For blades, mirrors and ornaments.
Variants.Lore: Seers look into a polished mirror of it. A blade of it cuts cleaner than steel, and the Flinchless surgeons keep one.

Variants.Name: millstone and quern stone
Variants.Description: A hard, rough, gritty rock that keeps its bite. Cut into round stones for mills and hand querns.
Variants.Lore: The lord breaks the hand querns of his tenants, so that they must pay at his mill. Old ones are found buried under floors.

Variants.Name: soapstone
Variants.Description: A soft, grey-green stone that feels greasy and can be cut with a knife. It does not crack in fire: pots, lamps and moulds.
Variants.Lore: The Hoarkin carve their blubber lamps of it. A pot of it holds its heat for an hour off the fire.

Variants.Name: chalk
Variants.Description: A soft, white stone that lies in rolling downs and shows in white sea cliffs. Burnt for lime, and cut for inner walls.
Variants.Lore: Giants and white horses are cut into the chalk hills, and scoured every seven years with a fair. No one knows who cut the first.

Variants.Name: limestone
Variants.Description: A pale grey or cream stone in level beds, easy to cut and carve. The common stone of walls, towers and temples, and burnt for lime.
Variants.Lore: The stone of the great temples, soft from the quarry and hard in the air. It is full of shells from a sea no one remembers.

Variants.Name: flint and chert
Variants.Description: Hard, glassy nodules, grey and black inside a white rind, found in chalk. Knapped to a sharp edge, struck for fire, and set in walls.
Variants.Lore: The thunderstones turned up by the plough are flint arrowheads from the Dawn. They are kept under the roof against lightning.

Variants.Name: sandstone
Variants.Description: A stone of bound sand, in red, yellow, brown and grey, that cuts freely into blocks and weathers into ledges and cliffs.
Variants.Lore: Whole cities of the dry lands are cut into red cliffs of it: tombs, temples and cisterns, with no stone laid on another.

Variants.Name: field stone and boulders
Variants.Description: Loose stones and rounded boulders cleared from the fields and stream beds, piled into dry walls and rough foundations.
Variants.Lore: The fields grow stones, the farmers say: a new crop every spring. The walls are the work of thirty generations.

Variants.Name: gypsum and alabaster
Variants.Description: A soft, white stone: gypsum, burnt for plaster, and its fine, translucent form, alabaster, carved into figures and thin window panes.
Variants.Lore: The effigies on the tombs of lords are alabaster, and so are the lamps of the Saltroad temples, which glow through the stone.

Resources.Name: Clay
Resources.Description: Earth that can be shaped: clay for pots, bricks and tiles, and loam for the walls of houses, dug from pits on low ground.
Resources.Lore: The first people were made of it, in most tellings. A potter's shards outlast the kingdom that used the pots.

Variants.Name: adobe and mud-brick earth
Variants.Description: Earth of dry lands mixed with straw and water, shaped in moulds and dried in the sun into pale brown bricks.
Variants.Lore: A mud town is rebuilt on its own ruins until it stands on a hill of them. The Saltroad folk replaster the temple each year as a festival.

Variants.Name: brick and pottery clay
Variants.Description: Sticky grey, red or yellow clay dug from pits in river valleys, that fires hard and red in the kiln.
Variants.Lore: The Old Realms stamped each brick with the name of the ruler. The bricks are still in use, in other people's walls.

Variants.Name: wattle and daub
Variants.Description: Clay mixed with straw and dung and smeared over a weave of hazel rods between the timbers of a house.
Variants.Lore: A house a family can build in a week with what lies within a mile. Daubing day ends with a dance on the floor to tread it flat.

Variants.Name: rammed earth and cob
Variants.Description: Damp earth with gravel and straw, rammed between boards or built up by hand into thick walls with rounded corners.
Variants.Lore: The long walls of the Canal folk are rammed earth. A cob house wants a good hat and good boots, the builders say: a roof and a stone footing.

Variants.Name: kaolin
Variants.Description: A pure, white, soft clay from rotted granite that fires white and fine: the earth of the best ware.
Variants.Lore: The white ware of the Canal folk is made from it, and for centuries no one else knew how. It is named for a hill of theirs.

Resources.Name: Crystal
Resources.Description: The clear stuff of glass and lenses: rock crystal from the mountains and pure white sand from shores and rivers.
Resources.Lore: Clear things hold light, and what holds light may hold more. Mages, glassmakers and Gnomes pay for the same sand and the same stones.

Variants.Name: rock crystal
Variants.Description: Clear, six-sided spears of quartz, like ice that does not melt, found in clefts of high rock. Cut for lenses, vessels and jewels.
Variants.Lore: Held to be ice frozen so hard that it cannot melt. A ball of it is the seer's glass, and a king's sceptre is tipped with it.

Variants.Name: glass sand
Variants.Description: Fine, white sand, free of iron, from beaches, dunes and river bars. Melted with ash or soda into glass.
Variants.Lore: Glass was found, the story goes, by sailors who propped their cooking pot on blocks of soda on a beach. The Brinefolk tell it of themselves.

Resources.Name: Fibre
Resources.Description: Plants and threads that are spun and twisted: fibre for cloth, rope, sacks and nets, grown in fields or gathered wild.
Resources.Lore: A people is clothed in what grows near it, and the rich in what does not. The spindle is in every woman's hand from the Dawn onward.

Variants.Name: flax
Variants.Description: A slender, knee-high plant with sky-blue flowers, grown in cool damp fields. Its stems are soaked, beaten and combed to pale fibre for linen.
Variants.Lore: The priests of the old temples wore nothing but linen. Northmen bury a woman with her flax comb.

Variants.Name: hemp
Variants.Description: A plant taller than a person with jagged, hand-shaped leaves. Its coarse, strong fibre goes to rope, sailcloth and sacks.
Variants.Lore: The rope of every ship and every gallows. The Grass riders throw its seed on hot stones in a closed tent, and howl with pleasure.

Variants.Name: cotton
Variants.Description: A bushy plant of hot lands with yellow flowers and pods that burst into balls of white fluff, picked by hand.
Variants.Lore: The first travellers said it was the wool of a lamb that grew on a stalk. The Rainkeepers weave it so fine that a length passes through a ring.

Variants.Name: jute
Variants.Description: A reed-like plant twice the height of a person, grown in hot, flooded river plains. A golden-brown fibre for sacks and cord.
