Variants.Lore: The golden fibre of the delta. Every sack on every quay is made of it, and the sack is worth nothing, so no one steals it.

Variants.Name: ramie
Variants.Description: A tall nettle without stings from warm wet lands. A white, lustrous fibre, stronger than flax, for fine cloth.
Variants.Lore: The Canal folk wrap their dead in it and wear it in summer. It is whiter and older than their silk.

Variants.Name: kenaf
Variants.Description: A tall, cane-like plant of hot lands, with hollyhock flowers and a coarse fibre like jute.
Variants.Lore: Ropes, sacks and the caulking of boats in the hot lands. The Sunlanders eat its leaves and twist its bark.

Variants.Name: sisal and agave
Variants.Description: Rosettes of stiff, sword-shaped, spine-tipped leaves on dry ground. The leaves are scraped for a hard, pale fibre for rope.
Variants.Lore: The plant flowers once, after many years, and dies. The highland peoples brew its sap and say a goddess lives in it.

Variants.Name: abaca
Variants.Description: A plant like a banana, of wet tropical islands. The fibre of its leaf stalks makes ship's rope that does not rot in sea water.
Variants.Lore: The Shoalfolk moor their houses with it. Northmen captains who have used it once will pay any price for a second cable.

Variants.Name: esparto grass
Variants.Description: A tough, wiry grass that grows in grey tussocks on dry hills. Plaited into rope, baskets, mats and sandals.
Variants.Lore: The miners of the dry hills wear sandals of it and carry ore in baskets of it. A pair lasts a week.

Variants.Name: silk
Variants.Description: The thread of the silkworm, a pale caterpillar fed on mulberry leaves in trays indoors. The cocoons are white and gold, the thread fine and shining.
Variants.Lore: A princess of the Canal folk carried the eggs out in her headdress, and the secret with them. The road it is traded along is named for it.

Variants.Name: kapok
Variants.Description: A giant tropical tree with a spiny trunk and great buttresses. Its pods are stuffed with a silky floss, for pillows and padding.
Variants.Lore: The tree joins the earth to the sky, in the forest peoples' telling. The Boughwalkers build in its crown.

Variants.Name: New Zealand flax
Variants.Description: A plant of wet ground on far southern coasts, with stiff, sword-shaped leaves as tall as a person, scraped for a strong fibre.
Variants.Lore: The cloaks woven of it show a wearer's rank by their border. The plant is cut so that the child leaf and its parents are left.

Variants.Name: nettle and lime-bast
Variants.Description: The poor land's fibres: thread from the stems of stinging nettles and cord from the inner bark of the lime tree.
Variants.Lore: Shirts of nettle are worn where flax fails. A sister in the tale weaves seven of them in silence to free her brothers.

Resources.Name: Fuel
Resources.Description: What is burnt for heat and for work: wood, charcoal, peat, dung and coal, stacked at every door and forge.
Resources.Lore: A town is as large as the wood within a day's carting. Smelters, salters and glassmakers eat forests, and move on when they are gone.

Variants.Name: charcoal
Variants.Description: Black, light, ringing lumps of wood burnt slowly without air in a turf-covered mound in the forest. The fuel of the smith and the smelter.
Variants.Lore: Without the charcoal burner no iron is made. A forge town counts its forest in years of charcoal left.

Variants.Name: firewood
Variants.Description: Split logs and bundled faggots from coppice and forest, stacked to dry against the wall of every house.
Variants.Lore: A villager may take dead wood by hook or by crook, and no more. A winter is measured in cords.

Variants.Name: peat
Variants.Description: Dark brown, fibrous earth cut in bricks from bogs and stacked to dry. It burns slowly, with a thick sweet smoke.
Variants.Lore: The fire of a peat house is never let out: it is carried from the mother's hearth to the bride's. It gives the northern drink its taste.

Variants.Name: turf and sod
Variants.Description: Slabs of grass and roots cut from heath and moor, dried and burnt where there is neither wood nor peat.
Variants.Lore: The Northmen build with it as well as burn it: a hall of turf is green in summer and grazed by the goat.

Variants.Name: dung fuel
Variants.Description: Cakes of dried animal dung, slapped on walls to dry and stacked in heaps. The fire of treeless plains.
Variants.Lore: Gathering it is the work of the daughters of the Grass riders. The stack beside the tent is the measure of a careful house.

Variants.Name: coal
Variants.Description: Black, shining stone that burns, dug from seams in hillsides and shallow pits. A hot fire with a foul smoke.
Variants.Lore: Sea coal, washed out of the cliffs. Smiths wanted it and the towns banned its smoke, and the Dwarves burnt it all along.

Variants.Name: lignite
Variants.Description: Brown, crumbly, woody coal from shallow pits in low ground. A smoky, weak fire.
Variants.Lore: The poor man's coal. A town that burns it can be smelt before it is seen.

Variants.Name: oil and naphtha seeps
Variants.Description: Black, stinking oil that wells from the ground into pools and tar pits, and burns. Skimmed for lamps, caulking and fire weapons.
Variants.Lore: Fires that have burnt at the seeps since the Dawn have temples built over them. The fire that burns on water is a state secret of the sea cities.

Resources.Name: Salt
Resources.Description: The one thing every house must buy: white salt from sea pans, desert lakes, mines and brine springs, traded in blocks and sacks.
Resources.Lore: Oaths are sworn on it, wages were paid in it, and rulers tax it because no one can do without. The Brinefolk hold the great flats in trust and weep the stuff themselves.

Variants.Name: solar sea salt
Variants.Description: Shallow, banked pans on a flat, hot shore, where sea water dries in the sun to a white crust that is raked into gleaming heaps.
Variants.Lore: The grey salt of the pans is for the fish barrels, and the white flower that floats on top is for the table.

Variants.Name: lake and playa salt
Variants.Description: The white, cracked crust of a dried salt lake in the desert, blinding in the sun, cut into slabs and carried off by caravan.
Variants.Lore: The Brinefolk say the flats are their sea, asleep. The Saltroad caravans carry the slabs south and trade them weight for weight against gold.

Variants.Name: natron and soda
Variants.Description: A white and grey crust at the edge of desert lakes: a bitter salt for glass, soap, bleaching and the embalming of the dead.
Variants.Lore: The Brinefolk embalm with it and blow glass with it. The priests of the old temples washed their mouths with it before they spoke to the god.

Variants.Name: rock salt
Variants.Description: Beds of grey, pink and white salt deep in the ground, cut out in blocks in glittering galleries.
Variants.Lore: The miners carve chapels and saints from the salt. A lost wedding ring was found in the first block cut, in the founding tale.

Variants.Name: brine springs
Variants.Description: Springs and wells of salt water inland, whose brine is boiled dry in pans over wood fires. A salt town grows round each.
Variants.Lore: The Canal folk drill for brine with bamboo, a thousand paces down, and pay the empire's army out of the salt tax.

Resources.Name: Iron ore
Resources.Description: The red, brown and black stone that iron is smelted from, dug from bogs, pits and mountain veins.
Resources.Lore: The Sunlanders smelted it first. Iron is the metal of the plough and the sword, and things of the old magic are said not to bear its touch.

Variants.Name: bog iron
Variants.Description: Rusty brown lumps and crusts that form in bogs and wet meadows, dug from under the turf with a spade. Poor ore, found everywhere in the north.
Variants.Lore: The bog gives it back: a place dug out can be dug again in a generation. Northmen farmers smelt their own in the autumn.

Variants.Name: lateritic iron and ironstone
Variants.Description: Hard, red-brown, pebbly crust on the red earth of hot lands, broken up and smelted in clay furnaces.
Variants.Lore: The ore of the first Sunlander smelters. The old furnace sites are holy, and a smith's family guards each.

Variants.Name: banded iron formation
Variants.Description: Ancient rock in thin stripes of red, black and steel grey: a rich ore that lies in whole ridges.
Variants.Lore: Whole mountains of it. The Dwarves say the stripes are the years of the world before anyone counted them.

Variants.Name: magnetite skarn iron
Variants.Description: Heavy, black ore in mountain rock that pulls at iron. The richest ore, mined from veins and pockets.
Variants.Lore: A sliver of it, floated, points north. Sailors tell of a mountain of it in the far sea that pulls the nails out of ships.

Variants.Name: black sands
Variants.Description: Heavy, black, glittering sand in streaks on beaches below dark cliffs, gathered and washed for the iron in it.
Variants.Lore: The eastern swordsmiths make their best steel from it, washing a hillside into the river for a single blade.

Resources.Name: Copper ore
Resources.Description: Green-stained rock and brassy ore that copper is smelted from, for bronze, brass, pots and coin.
Resources.Lore: The metal of the Dawn, before iron. Bronze still makes the bells, the statues and the cauldrons, and the Dwarves count a hold's age by its copper workings.

Variants.Name: porphyry copper
Variants.Description: Speckled mountain rock stained green and rusty at the surface, with fine grains of brassy ore through a whole hillside.
Variants.Lore: A whole mountain of poor ore. The Dwarves take a hill down from the top, over ten generations, and call it one working.

Variants.Name: malachite and azurite
Variants.Description: Bright green and deep blue crusts and bands in the rock: copper ore that is also ground for paint and cut for ornament.
Variants.Lore: Ground for the green of painted eyes and the blue of painted skies. The miners knew copper by these colours before they knew how to smelt it.

Variants.Name: red-bed copper
Variants.Description: Green and blue stains and nodules in beds of red sandstone and shale. A thin ore that spreads wide.
Variants.Lore: The works of the Midlander shale lands made a banking family rich enough to buy an emperor.

Variants.Name: massive-sulfide copper
Variants.Description: Heavy, brassy-yellow bodies of ore in dark green rock, under a cap of rusty red and yellow earth.
Variants.Lore: An island of the middle sea gave the metal its name. The red caps of the hills there were mined before the Old Realms.

Variants.Name: native copper
Variants.Description: Pure red metal found as lumps and sheets in dark lava rock, green on the outside. It can be hammered without smelting.
Variants.Lore: The lake peoples hammered it cold before anyone had a furnace. A lump too big to move was left with offerings on it.

Resources.Name: Tin
Resources.Description: The rare, heavy, dark stone that white tin is smelted from: the metal that makes copper into bronze, and pewter for the table.
Resources.Lore: A little tin makes copper into bronze, and it lies in few places. The Old Realms sent fleets to the edge of the world for it.

Variants.Name: tin lode
Variants.Description: Veins of heavy, dark brown, shining tin stone in granite, followed underground with pick and fire.
Variants.Lore: The mines run out under the sea, and the tinners hear the boulders roll above their heads. They have a parliament and a court of their own.

Variants.Name: stream tin
Variants.Description: Heavy black pebbles and sand of tin stone in the gravel of valley floors below granite hills, washed out with running water.
Variants.Lore: The tin islands at the world's edge, which the Old Realms sought and the traders kept off the maps.

Resources.Name: Silver & lead
Resources.Description: The grey ores of silver and lead, which lie together: silver for coin and plate, lead for roofs, pipes and windows.
Resources.Lore: Silver is the coin of every market and the first thing a ruler debases. A silver strike makes a town in a year, and a ghost town in thirty.

Variants.Name: silver
Variants.Description: Veins of dull grey ore, and sometimes wires of the bright metal itself, in mountain rock. Mined deep, by many hands, for coin and plate.
Variants.Lore: A mine in the mountains paid for the fleet that saved a city, and another for the ruin of an empire. Silver turns black at poison, they say.

Variants.Name: lead-zinc in carbonates
Variants.Description: Heavy, lead-grey, shining cubes of ore in pockets and veins of limestone hills. Smelted for lead, with a little silver in it.
Variants.Lore: The lead of roofs, pipes and coffins. The Old Realms piped their water in it and went mad, the Gnomes maintain.

Variants.Name: calamine
Variants.Description: An earthy, yellow-brown and white ore in limestone, which is heated with copper to make golden brass.
Variants.Lore: It turns copper to gold, or near enough for a candlestick. The brass founders long thought it only a dye for the metal.

Variants.Name: lead-zinc skarns and veins
Variants.Description: Veins of grey lead ore and dark, resinous zinc ore in volcanic mountains, with white quartz and a little silver.
Variants.Lore: The miners cursed the false ore that would not smelt, and named it for the goblins of the mine.

Resources.Name: Gold
Resources.Description: The yellow metal that does not tarnish, found in white quartz veins and in river sand. Worth more than anything else that is dug.
Resources.Lore: It buys kings, and cannot be eaten. The Sunlanders are rich in it, the Saltroad folk carry it, and the Dwarves write down where every ounce went.

Variants.Name: lode gold
Variants.Description: Specks and threads of yellow gold in veins of milky white quartz, in old hard rock. Mined, crushed and washed.
Variants.Lore: Dwarves follow a quartz vein for generations and record each ounce. Men come for a season and leave their bones.

Variants.Name: epithermal and hot-spring gold-silver
Variants.Description: Rich, banded veins of quartz with gold and silver, in volcanic mountains near hot springs and steaming ground.
Variants.Lore: Found where the ground steams. The miners say the fire under the mountain cooks the gold, and hurry.

Variants.Name: placer gold
Variants.Description: Flakes, grains and now and then a nugget of gold in the sand and gravel of rivers, washed out with a pan or a fleece.
Variants.Lore: The fleece laid in a stream to catch the dust is the golden fleece of the tale. A Sunlander king's stool is covered in it.

Variants.Name: beach gold
Variants.Description: Fine gold dust in the dark sand of a beach near a river mouth, sorted by the waves and washed out by hand.
Variants.Lore: A storm lays it bare and the next one buries it. A whole town can spring up on a beach and be gone in two winters.

Resources.Name: Gems & pearls
Resources.Description: Precious stones and the treasures of the sea: gems dug from rock and gravel, pearls and coral brought up by divers. Small, bright and worth a life.
Resources.Lore: A fortune that fits in the mouth. Each stone has a virtue in the books, and a history of the hands it was cut from.

Variants.Name: pearl oyster
Variants.Description: Rough-shelled oysters on the floor of warm seas, lined with mother-of-pearl. One in many holds a round, lustrous pearl.
Variants.Lore: A pearl is a drop of dew or a tear that the oyster swallowed. The Shoalfolk price a reef by its divers' lives.

Variants.Name: precious red coral
Variants.Description: A small, branching, blood-red tree of stone that grows on rock deep under the sea. Polished into beads and charms.
Variants.Lore: The blood of a monster's cut head, hardened in the sea. Hung on children against the evil eye, from the middle sea to the high plateaus.

Variants.Name: diamond
Variants.Description: A small, greasy-looking pebble found in river gravels, harder than anything else. Cut, it blazes with white fire.
Variants.Lore: It cannot be cut, the old books say, except with a goat's blood. The valley where it lies is guarded by snakes, and reached by throwing meat to the eagles.

Variants.Name: topaz, beryl and tourmaline
Variants.Description: Clear, six-sided crystals in pockets of granite: golden topaz, sea-green beryl, pink and green tourmaline.
Variants.Lore: Gnomes ground the first reading lenses from clear beryl, and the word for spectacles remembers it.

Variants.Name: garnet
Variants.Description: Deep red, many-sided crystals the size of a pea or a nut, studded in grey mountain rock.
Variants.Lore: The red stones in the sword hilts of the Northmen kings came half across the world. A garnet lights the way of a traveller at night.

Variants.Name: emerald
Variants.Description: A six-sided crystal of deep, clear green, rare and often flawed, in veins of dark mountain rock.
Variants.Lore: A serpent that looks on it goes blind. A queen of the south owned the only mines and gave the stones carved with her face.

Variants.Name: amethyst and agate
Variants.Description: The gems of old lava: hollow stones lined with purple amethyst crystals, and agates banded in rings of many colours.
Variants.Lore: The amethyst keeps its wearer sober, and so is set in a bishop's ring and a drinking cup.

Variants.Name: ruby and sapphire
Variants.Description: The hardest gems but one: blood-red ruby and deep blue sapphire, found as small barrel-shaped crystals in marble and in the gravels below it.
Variants.Lore: Rainkeeper kings take the title lord of the rubies and keep every large stone by law. A sapphire is the stone of an oath.

Variants.Name: jade
Variants.Description: A tough, smooth stone, green to white, found as boulders in mountain rivers. Carved into blades, ornaments and ritual things.
Variants.Lore: The Canal folk hold it above gold: it is virtue made visible. A prince is buried in a suit of it, to keep the body whole.

Variants.Name: lapis lazuli
Variants.Description: A deep blue stone flecked with gold, from a few high mountain mines. Cut for inlay and ground for the costliest blue paint.
Variants.Lore: It comes from one valley at the roof of the world. The painter's contract says how much of it the patron will pay for.

Variants.Name: turquoise
Variants.Description: An opaque, sky-blue to green stone in thin veins in desert rock, often webbed with brown.
Variants.Lore: The Saltroad folk set it on the bridle against a fall. It pales when its owner sickens, and they watch it.

Variants.Name: opal
Variants.Description: A milky stone that flashes with moving fire in every colour as it is turned, in seams in desert sandstone.
Variants.Lore: Every stone in one, and so the luck of all of them, or the ill luck. Thieves prize it: it is said to hide the wearer.

Variants.Name: amber
Variants.Description: Golden, clear, warm, light lumps of ancient resin, washed up on cold shores, sometimes with an insect inside.
Variants.Lore: The tears of sisters who wept for a brother and became trees. The Amberbloods say it is the blood of their oldest dead, and buy back what they can.

Variants.Name: jet
Variants.Description: A black, light stone of fossil wood from sea cliffs, that polishes to a deep shine. For beads and mourning jewels.
Variants.Lore: The stone of mourning. Burnt, it drives off snakes, and it is the one black thing a widow may wear.

Variants.Name: freshwater pearl mussel
Variants.Description: Dark, long-lived mussels in the gravel of cold, clean rivers. One in a thousand holds a small pearl.
Variants.Lore: The pearl fishers open a thousand shells for one pearl. The best of a river goes to the crown by old right.

Resources.Name: Spices
Resources.Description: Scented and burning things from hot, far lands: seeds, barks, buds and gums, dried, carried across the world and sold by the ounce.
Resources.Lore: The lightest cargo and the dearest. Those who grow them and those who eat them have never met, and the merchants in between mean to keep it so.

Variants.Name: black pepper
Variants.Description: A climbing vine of hot wet forest, grown up trees and poles, with hanging strings of green berries that dry black and wrinkled.
Variants.Lore: A city was once ransomed for three thousand pounds of it. Rents are paid in peppercorns still, where no one wants them collected.

Variants.Name: clove
Variants.Description: An evergreen tree of small tropical islands. Its pink flower buds are picked before they open and dried to dark brown nails.
Variants.Lore: A tree is planted for each child, and the child's fate is read from it. The Canal folk court required a clove in the mouth of anyone who spoke to the emperor.

Variants.Name: nutmeg and mace
Variants.Description: A tropical island tree with a fruit like an apricot, which splits to show a brown nut wrapped in a scarlet lace: the nutmeg and the mace.
Variants.Lore: It grows on a handful of islands, and wars have been fought for each of them. Carried in a pocket against the plague.

Variants.Name: cinnamon
Variants.Description: A small evergreen tree of wet tropical land. Its inner bark is peeled and dried into curled, brown, scented quills.
Variants.Lore: The spicers said that great birds build their nests of it on cliffs, and it must be brought down with baits of meat. It kept the price up.

Variants.Name: cardamom
Variants.Description: A tall, leafy plant of the forest floor in wet tropical hills. Its small green pods of black, scented seeds grow at the foot of the plant.
Variants.Lore: The Saltroad folk put it in the coffee they pour for a guest, and the amount is the measure of the welcome.

Variants.Name: ginger
Variants.Description: A reed-like plant of hot wet land, grown for its knobbly, pale, hot-tasting root.
Variants.Lore: A pound of it bought a sheep. Midlander fairs sell it baked into bread in the shape of a man.

Variants.Name: turmeric
Variants.Description: A broad-leaved plant of hot wet land. Its root is bright orange inside and is dried and ground to a yellow powder, spice and dye.
Variants.Lore: The Rainkeepers rub a bride yellow with it before the wedding, and tie a root of it round her neck.

Variants.Name: vanilla
Variants.Description: A climbing orchid of wet tropical forest with long green pods, which are cured until black, oily and sweet-scented.
Variants.Lore: The flower opens for one morning and must be fertilised by hand. A stolen pod is known by the grower's mark pricked into it.

Variants.Name: chili pepper
Variants.Description: A small bush of warm lands hung with glossy pods, green, red and yellow, that burn the mouth.
Variants.Lore: Burnt in the fire, its smoke was a punishment for children and a weapon of war.

Variants.Name: myrrh
Variants.Description: A low, thorny tree of hot, stony desert. Cuts in its bark bleed a red-brown, bitter, scented gum, for incense, medicine and the dead.
Variants.Lore: The Brinefolk embalm with it. It is the gift for a death, as frankincense is the gift for a god.

Variants.Name: frankincense
Variants.Description: A small, gnarled tree with papery bark on bare desert cliffs. Its milky sap dries into pale tears that are burnt in temples.
Variants.Lore: The trees belong to families and may be cut only by those who are clean. Winged serpents guard them, the Saltroad merchants insist.

Variants.Name: gum arabic
Variants.Description: A thorny acacia of dry savanna. Its bark oozes amber balls of clear gum, for ink, paint, sweets and medicine.
Variants.Lore: Every scribe's ink and every illuminator's colour is bound with it. The caravans bring it north in goatskins.

Variants.Name: sandalwood
Variants.Description: A small tree of dry tropical forest that grows on the roots of others. Its yellow heartwood keeps a sweet scent for decades.
Variants.Lore: The Rainkeepers burn their dead on it if they can afford to, and mark the forehead with its paste. Every tree belongs to the king.

Variants.Name: rubber latex
Variants.Description: A tall tree of the rain forest that bleeds a white milk when cut. The milk is smoked into dark, springy, waterproof balls.
Variants.Lore: The forest peoples make a ball of it for a game that is played for the players' lives. Nobody else has found a use for it.

Resources.Name: Stimulants & sugar
Resources.Description: Sweet things and things that wake, calm or cheer: sugar, honey, and the leaves, beans and nuts that are brewed, chewed and smoked.
Resources.Lore: Small comforts that a people will not give up once it has them. Rulers have learnt that they can be taxed harder than bread.

Variants.Name: sugar cane
Variants.Description: A giant grass of hot wet land, twice the height of a person, with thick jointed stems full of sweet juice. Crushed and boiled down to brown loaves.
Variants.Lore: The reed that gives honey without bees. It came west as a medicine, and the apothecaries sold it by the ounce.

Variants.Name: palm sugar and toddy
Variants.Description: Palms whose cut flower stalks drip sap into pots hung in the crown. The sap is boiled to brown sugar or left to ferment into a milky wine.
Variants.Lore: The tapper climbs forty palms twice a day. The sap is sweet at dawn and strong by evening, and no one drinks it at noon.

Variants.Name: tea
Variants.Description: An evergreen shrub of misty, wet hills, kept waist high in rows. The young leaves are picked, rolled and dried.
Variants.Lore: A leaf fell into a Canal folk emperor's boiling water. The empire pays for the horses of the Grass riders in bricks of it.

Variants.Name: coffee
Variants.Description: A glossy-leaved shrub of tropical highlands, grown under shade trees, with white flowers and red berries. The two seeds in each are roasted.
Variants.Lore: A goatherd saw his goats dance after eating the berries. The scholars of the Saltroad folk took it up to stay awake, and the rulers ban the houses where it is drunk.

Variants.Name: cacao
Variants.Description: A small tree of the rain forest's shade, with large ribbed pods, yellow and red, that grow straight from the trunk. The seeds are fermented and ground into a bitter drink.
Variants.Lore: The beans are money: a rabbit costs ten. The drink is for lords and warriors, bitter, with chili.

Variants.Name: kola nut
Variants.Description: A tree of the wet tropical forest with knobbly pods of pink and white nuts, chewed to keep off hunger and sleep and offered to guests.
Variants.Lore: The Sunlanders say that he who brings kola brings life. No oath, visit or bargain begins without one being broken and shared.

Variants.Name: betel nut
Variants.Description: A slim, tall palm of hot wet coasts with bunches of orange nuts, sliced and chewed with a leaf and lime. It stains the mouth red.
Variants.Lore: A Rainkeeper host offers it before anything is said. Red teeth are the mark of a grown person, and white ones belong to dogs.

Variants.Name: coca
Variants.Description: A shrub of warm mountain valleys with small, thin, bright green leaves, chewed with lime against hunger, cold and thin air.
Variants.Lore: The runners of the mountain roads measure distance in the mouthfuls chewed. The leaf is read by diviners.

Variants.Name: tobacco
Variants.Description: A tall plant with huge, sticky leaves and pink trumpet flowers. The leaves are hung to cure brown and are smoked, chewed or snuffed.
Variants.Lore: Halflings grow the best leaf and settle disputes over a pipe. Elsewhere the smoke carries prayers upward.

Variants.Name: honey and beeswax
Variants.Description: The stores of the bee, from straw skeps, log hives and wild nests: golden honey in the comb, and yellow wax for candles and seals.
Variants.Lore: The bees must be told of a death in the house. The temple takes the wax and the hall takes the mead.

Resources.Name: Furs & ivory
Resources.Description: The costly spoils of wild beasts: fine winter furs, ivory tusks, plumes and musk, brought from forest, ice and savanna by trappers and hunters.
Resources.Lore: The law says who may wear which fur, and the forest is emptied to keep the law supplied. Northern peoples pay their tribute in pelts.

Variants.Name: seals
Variants.Description: The skins of seals from cold coasts: short, dense fur, silver-grey and spotted, that sheds water. For boots, cloaks and boat covers.
Variants.Lore: The Hoarkin dress in it from the skin out. The seal people of the tales take off the same coat to walk on land.

Variants.Name: whales
Variants.Description: The great beasts of cold seas, hunted from open boats. They give oil for lamps, springy baleen and bone as long as a roof beam.
Variants.Lore: A whale on the shore belongs to the ruler: the head to the king and the tail to the queen. The oil lights the cities.

Variants.Name: beaver
Variants.Description: A stout brown water animal with a flat, scaly tail, that dams streams with felled trees. Its dense underfur makes the best felt.
Variants.Lore: Its felt makes the hats of every man of standing, and the animal is gone from the settled lands on that account.

Variants.Name: sable and marten
Variants.Description: Slender, quick hunters of the northern forest, with dark brown, silky fur and a pale throat. The fur of princes.
Variants.Lore: The soft gold of the north. The forest peoples pay their tribute in it, and a coat is a king's gift to a king.

Variants.Name: squirrel
Variants.Description: The winter coat of the northern squirrel: blue-grey on the back and white on the belly, sewn by the thousand into the linings of robes.
Variants.Lore: The grey and white of it is drawn on shields as a pattern of its own. A noble robe takes two thousand bellies.

Variants.Name: ermine
Variants.Description: The stoat in its winter coat: pure white with a black tail tip. Worn by rulers and judges.
Variants.Lore: It dies rather than soil its coat, the bestiaries say. It was the fur of the judges of the Old Realms.

Variants.Name: walrus
Variants.Description: A huge, wrinkled, whiskered sea beast of the ice edge, with two long ivory tusks and a hide thick enough for ship's rope.
Variants.Lore: The Hoarkin carve its tooth through the dark of the year. The gaming pieces of the Northmen kings are made of it.

Variants.Name: fox and Arctic fox
Variants.Description: The red fox of wood and field, and the white and blue-grey fox of the tundra, taken in winter for their thick fur.
Variants.Lore: The trickster of every people's tales. The Hoarkin trade the white pelts south and wonder at what is paid.

Variants.Name: narwhal tusk
Variants.Description: A straight, spiralled ivory tusk, longer than a person, from a small whale of icy seas. Sold in the south as the horn of a unicorn.
Variants.Lore: The horn of the unicorn. A cup of it sweats at poison, and kings have paid its weight in gold twenty times over.

Variants.Name: bear
Variants.Description: Great brown and black bears of forest and mountain, and the white bear of the ice. Taken for the pelt, the fat and the claws.
Variants.Lore: No northern people says its name aloud: it is the honey eater, the old one in the fur coat. After a kill they ask its pardon.

Variants.Name: elephant ivory
Variants.Description: The long, curved, creamy-white tusks of the elephant. Carved into combs, caskets, thrones and holy images.
Variants.Lore: Among the Sunlanders one tusk of every elephant killed is the king's. The altars of his fathers stand on carved tusks.

Variants.Name: ostrich
Variants.Description: A flightless bird of dry plains, taller than a person, that runs faster than a horse. Great soft plumes, black and white, and eggs like ivory bowls.
Variants.Lore: A feather of it is the sign of truth, since its vanes are equal on both sides. The eggs hang in temples.

Variants.Name: big cats
Variants.Description: Lions, leopards and tigers: tawny, spotted and striped pelts, with teeth and claws, worn by kings and warriors.
Variants.Lore: Only a chief may sit on a leopard skin. The Catfolk will not trade in the pelts, and do not explain.

Variants.Name: exotic feathers
Variants.Description: The bright plumage of tropical birds: scarlet, blue, green and gold, traded in bundles for crowns, cloaks and fans.
Variants.Lore: The forest peoples pay their tribute in feathers, and a cloak of them takes ten thousand birds. The birds are plucked and let go.

Variants.Name: musk deer
Variants.Description: A small, hornless deer of cold mountain forest with long fangs. The male carries a pod of musk, the costliest of all scents.
Variants.Lore: The Stillfaces, who speak by scent, pay more for musk than any court. A grain of it scents a room for forty years.

Resources.Name: Dyes
Resources.Description: The plants, insects and shells that colour cloth: blue, red, yellow and purple, steeped in vats that stain the dyer's arms.
Resources.Lore: Colour is rank: the law keeps purple for the ruler and scarlet for the great. A dye town guards its vats as a mint guards its dies.

Variants.Name: woad
Variants.Description: A plant with yellow flowers and blue-green leaves, which are crushed, balled and fermented into a blue dye. The vats stink.
Variants.Lore: The old Midlander tribes painted themselves blue with it to fight. No woad vat is allowed within a mile of a palace, for the smell.

Variants.Name: madder
Variants.Description: A sprawling, scratchy plant with whorled leaves. Its long red roots are dug in the third year, dried and ground for a strong red.
Variants.Lore: The red of soldiers' coats. Fed on it, an animal's bones turn red, and the dyers' own do too.

Variants.Name: weld
Variants.Description: A tall, slender plant with a spike of pale yellow-green flowers. Boiled whole, it gives the clearest yellow.
Variants.Lore: Over woad it gives the green of the greenwood, the outlaw's colour.

Variants.Name: indigo
Variants.Description: A bushy tropical plant with small leaves and pink flowers. The leaves are steeped and beaten in vats until a deep blue mud settles, and that is dried into cakes.
Variants.Lore: Sunlander dyers are women, and the pits are theirs. The blue rubs off on the skin, and the desert riders wear that as a mark of wealth.

Variants.Name: safflower
Variants.Description: A thistle-like plant with orange-yellow flowers. The petals give a yellow and a pink-red dye, and the seeds an oil.
Variants.Lore: The red of the cords that tie the Canal folk's documents. Sold to the unwary as saffron.

Variants.Name: henna
Variants.Description: A shrub of hot dry lands with small leaves that are dried and ground to a green powder. It stains hair, skin and nails red-brown.
Variants.Lore: The night of the henna comes before the wedding. A bride does no work until the pattern has worn from her hands.

Variants.Name: annatto
Variants.Description: A tropical shrub with spiky red pods full of seeds coated in an orange-red paste, used to colour food, cloth and skin.
Variants.Lore: The forest peoples paint the body with it against insects, spirits and the sun. Strangers took them for a red-skinned race.

Variants.Name: red dyewoods
Variants.Description: Tropical trees whose dense heartwood is deep red. It is shipped in logs and rasped to chips that give reds and purples.
Variants.Lore: A country across the ocean is named after the wood. The logs come as ballast and are rasped by prisoners.

Variants.Name: lac
Variants.Description: The crust that tiny insects leave on the twigs of certain trees in the monsoon lands. It is scraped off for a crimson dye and a hard, clear lacquer.
Variants.Lore: The seals on a Rainkeeper letter are lac, and so is the shine on the wood. It is counted by the hundred thousand insects.

Variants.Name: cochineal
Variants.Description: A small scale insect that lives on prickly-pear cactus under a white fluff. Dried and crushed, it gives the richest crimson.
Variants.Lore: The traders swore it was a seed, and guarded the cactus fields for two centuries. Seventy thousand insects make a pound.

Variants.Name: lichen dyes
Variants.Description: Grey and orange crusts scraped from rock and bark in cold wet lands, and steeped for weeks to give purple, red and brown.
Variants.Lore: The island weavers scrape the rocks and steep the crust in stale urine. The cloth keeps the smell for life, and they miss it abroad.

Variants.Name: murex
Variants.Description: Spiny sea snails gathered from rocky shores. Each gives one drop of a dye that turns purple in the sun: the colour of rulers.
Variants.Lore: The purple of rulers, worth its weight in silver. A dye town can be smelt across the bay, and its shell heaps are hills.

Variants.Name: kermes
Variants.Description: Small red-brown scale insects, like berries, on the twigs of a low evergreen oak of dry hills. Dried, they give the scarlet of fine cloth.
Variants.Lore: The scarlet of a cardinal and a judge. It was long taken for a berry, and it gave its name to crimson.

Resources.Name: Horses & pack animals
Resources.Description: The animals that carry and pull: horses, donkeys, camels and stranger beasts, with saddle, pack and harness. They are what moves an army and a caravan.
Resources.Lore: A people's reach is the reach of its beasts. The Grass riders have the horse, the Saltroad folk the camel, and the Rainkeepers the elephant, and each despises walking.

Variants.Name: sled dogs
Variants.Description: Thick-coated, wolf-like dogs with curled tails, that pull sleds over snow and ice in teams and sleep in the open.
Variants.Lore: A Hoarkin driver owes the lead dog a share of every kill. In a famine the dogs are eaten last, and the lead dog never.

Variants.Name: reindeer
Variants.Description: Tame reindeer of the far north, broken to pull a sled and carry a pack or a rider. Both sexes bear antlers.
Variants.Lore: The only deer that can be ridden. The herders geld the sled animals with their teeth, and will not use a knife.

Variants.Name: donkeys and mules
Variants.Description: Small, long-eared, patient beasts, grey and brown, that carry a pack over stony tracks where no cart can go.
Variants.Lore: The mule has no pride of ancestry and no hope of posterity, and carries the world's goods regardless. A priest rides one for humility.

Variants.Name: dromedary camel
Variants.Description: The one-humped, long-legged, sand-coloured camel of hot deserts. It carries a heavy load for days without water.
Variants.Lore: The Saltroad folk say it knows the hundredth name of the god and will not tell, which is why it looks as it does.

Variants.Name: Bactrian camel
Variants.Description: The two-humped, shaggy, dark brown camel of cold deserts and high steppe. It bears frost and thirst alike.
Variants.Lore: It smells a sandstorm before it comes and buries its nose. The caravans of the cold deserts stop when the old camels kneel.

Variants.Name: llama and alpaca-like camelids
Variants.Description: Woolly, long-necked, humpless beasts of high mountains, in many colours. They carry small loads in long trains and give fine wool.
Variants.Lore: It lies down under an unfair load and spits at the one who loaded it. The mountain roads were built to its step, with stairs.

Variants.Name: elephants
Variants.Description: Tamed elephants, grey and huge, with a driver on the neck. They haul timber, carry a tower of fighters and bear kings in procession.
Variants.Lore: The Rainkeepers give a driver to one elephant for life. A white one is too holy to work, and its keep can ruin the courtier it is given to.

Variants.Name: horses
Variants.Description: Riding, war and draught horses, from shaggy steppe ponies to tall chargers. The wealth of every lord and rider.
Variants.Lore: The Grass riders are in the saddle before they walk, and a man on foot is no man. The Midlander knight is named for his horse.

Resources.Name: Reagents
Resources.Description: The salts, metals and earths of the dyer, the tanner, the glassmaker and the alchemist: scraped from volcanoes, caves and dry lake beds.
Resources.Lore: The dull stuffs that every craft rests on. Alum has caused more wars than gold, and the alchemists get the blame for the smell.

Variants.Name: alum
Variants.Description: A white, sour-tasting salt in crusts and veins on volcanic ground. It fixes dye to cloth, tans white leather and stops bleeding.
Variants.Lore: No cloth takes a dye without it. The temple once held the only mine and banned trade with any other.

Variants.Name: sulphur
Variants.Description: Bright yellow, brittle crystals round steaming vents on volcanoes. It burns with a blue flame and a choking smell.
Variants.Lore: Brimstone: the smell of the lower world. It is burnt to cleanse a house after sickness, and it bleaches wool.

Variants.Name: quicksilver
Variants.Description: A liquid, silver metal that runs in heavy beads, roasted from a blood-red stone, cinnabar. The alchemist's first matter, and a poison.
Variants.Lore: The alchemists hold every metal to be born of it and sulphur. A Canal folk emperor drank it to live for ever, and is buried among rivers of it.

Variants.Name: alum shale and vitriol
Variants.Description: Dark, crumbling shale that is heaped, burnt and washed for alum, and for green and blue vitriol: the makings of ink, dye and acid.
Variants.Lore: The black ink of every charter is made of vitriol and oak galls. It eats the page through in five hundred years.

Variants.Name: saltpetre
Variants.Description: White needle crystals scraped from the crust of dry lake beds in the desert. It makes flame burn fierce, and cures meat.
Variants.Lore: The Canal folk call it the snow of their land and make fire flowers of it. Mages and artificers quarrel over who may buy it.

Variants.Name: borax
Variants.Description: A soft, white crystal from the shores of dry desert lakes. It helps gold and silver flow in the goldsmith's fire, and glazes pots.
Variants.Lore: It comes down from the high lakes on the backs of sheep, a small bag on each. Goldsmiths will not work without it.

Variants.Name: cave saltpetre
Variants.Description: White, fluffy crusts on the walls and floors of dry limestone caves where bats roost, scraped off and boiled clean.
Variants.Lore: The ruler's saltpetre men may dig in any cellar, stable or dovecote, and no one may refuse them.

Resources.Name: Herbs
Resources.Description: The plants of the healer, the brewer and the alchemist, not of the kitchen: roots, leaves, barks and flowers, gathered wild and dried in bunches.
Resources.Lore: Every plant is a medicine or a poison, and the dose decides. The village healer and the Bitterblood apothecary know the same herbs by different names.

Variants.Name: gentian
Variants.Description: A mountain plant with deep blue or yellow trumpet flowers. Its thick, bitter root is dug for the stomach.
Variants.Lore: Named for a king who found its use. Mountain folk distil the root, and a glass of it settles any dinner.

Variants.Name: arnica
Variants.Description: A mountain-meadow plant with yellow daisy flowers on a hairy stalk. A salve for bruises and sprains.
Variants.Lore: Mountain herders smoke the leaf. It is called fall-herb, and every Hearthblood pass warden carries the salve.

Variants.Name: roseroot
Variants.Description: A fleshy, grey-green plant of cold cliffs with yellow flower heads. Its thick root smells of roses when cut, and is chewed against weariness.
Variants.Lore: Northmen took it to sea for strength. A bunch of it is given to a couple at their wedding, with a wish for children.

Variants.Name: Iceland moss
Variants.Description: A brown, leathery, curled lichen of the tundra and the heath. Boiled into a jelly for coughs, and as food in famine.
Variants.Lore: Ground into the bread of the far north in hungry years. The Hoarkin stew it with seal broth.

Variants.Name: bog myrtle
Variants.Description: A low shrub of cold bogs with scented, grey-green leaves. It flavours ale and keeps off midges.
Variants.Lore: The ale of the north was brewed with it before hops came, and the old folk say it was the stronger and the merrier.

Variants.Name: Labrador tea
Variants.Description: A low evergreen shrub of northern bogs, with narrow leaves rusty-woolly beneath and white flowers. Brewed as a strong tea.
Variants.Lore: Brewed strong, it makes the head swim. The tanners of the north use it, and the housewives lay it among the clothes against moths.

Variants.Name: yarrow
Variants.Description: A meadow herb with feathery leaves and flat heads of small white flowers. Laid on wounds to stop the blood.
Variants.Lore: The soldier's woundwort: a hero taught its use to his men. The Canal folk cast its stalks to read the future.

Variants.Name: wormwood
Variants.Description: A silver-grey, bitter, strongly scented shrub of dry steppe. It drives out worms and flavours strong drink.
Variants.Lore: It sprang up in the track of the serpent leaving the garden. The green spirit made with it drives poets mad.

Variants.Name: liquorice
Variants.Description: A bushy plant of dry river plains with feathery leaves. Its long roots are sweet, and are chewed for coughs.
Variants.Lore: The Old Realms' soldiers chewed it on the march against thirst. Found in the tomb of a king, in jars.

Variants.Name: ephedra
Variants.Description: A leafless, broom-like shrub of green jointed twigs with red berries, on desert slopes. Brewed for the chest and to stay awake.
Variants.Lore: The Canal folk physicians have brewed it for five thousand years. The Grass riders drink it before a long ride.

Variants.Name: chamomile
Variants.Description: A low, feathery plant of fields and waysides with small white daisies that smell of apples. Brewed to calm.
Variants.Lore: The plants' physician: a sick shrub recovers with it planted near. The more it is trodden, the more it spreads.

Variants.Name: sage
Variants.Description: A low, woody shrub of dry sunny hills, with soft, grey, wrinkled leaves and violet flowers. For the kitchen and the sickroom.
Variants.Lore: Why should a man die who has sage in his garden, the physicians' school asks. It thrives where the wife rules, by the proverb.

Variants.Name: thyme and rosemary
Variants.Description: Low, woody, scented shrubs of dry stony hills: thyme in small cushions with pink flowers, rosemary with dark needles and pale blue flowers.
Variants.Lore: Rosemary is for remembrance, worn at weddings and thrown into graves. Thyme gives courage, and ladies embroider it on a knight's scarf.

Variants.Name: poppy
Variants.Description: A tall poppy with grey-green leaves and white or purple flowers. Its green seed head is scratched to bleed a milk that dries brown: it kills pain and brings sleep.
Variants.Lore: The gift of the god of sleep. The physicians bless it and the temple warns of it, and both are right.

Variants.Name: hops
Variants.Description: A climbing vine grown up tall poles, with green, papery cones that give ale its bitterness and keep it.
Variants.Lore: The brewers of unhopped ale called it a wicked weed and had it banned. The hopped beer kept longer, and won.

Variants.Name: valerian
Variants.Description: A tall plant of damp meadows with pale pink flower heads. Its strong-smelling root brings sleep, and draws cats.
Variants.Lore: The ratcatcher's secret: rats follow it, as cats do. All-heal, by its other name.

Variants.Name: St John's wort
Variants.Description: A wayside plant with yellow, star-like flowers that bleed red when crushed. An oil for wounds and a tea for a heavy heart.
Variants.Lore: Gathered on midsummer morning and hung over the door, it keeps out witches, lightning and melancholy.

Variants.Name: foxglove
Variants.Description: A tall spire of purple, spotted bells at the edge of woods. A medicine for the heart in a small dose, a poison in a larger.
Variants.Lore: The gloves of the good folk, who gave them to the fox to soften his step. The village herbalist knew its use on the heart long before the physicians.

Variants.Name: comfrey
Variants.Description: A coarse, hairy plant of damp ground with drooping purple bells. Its root and leaves are bound on broken bones.
Variants.Lore: Knitbone. The Flinchless surgeons and the village bonesetter both pack a break with it.

Variants.Name: angelica
Variants.Description: A plant taller than a person, with hollow stems and great round heads of greenish flowers, in wet ground. Candied, and taken against plague.
Variants.Lore: An angel showed it to a monk in a plague year. The Northmen have had a law since their beginning against stealing it from a garden.

Variants.Name: aloe
Variants.Description: A rosette of thick, fleshy, spiny-edged leaves on dry ground. They hold a clear gel for burns and a bitter yellow sap that purges.
Variants.Lore: A conqueror was told to take an island for the sake of its aloes, to heal his soldiers. Hung over a Saltroad door, it lives on air.

Variants.Name: senna
Variants.Description: A low desert shrub with yellow flowers and flat pods. Leaves and pods are brewed as a purge.
Variants.Lore: The Saltroad physicians brought it into medicine. Every caravan carries it, and children dread it.

Variants.Name: devil's claw
Variants.Description: A creeping plant of dry sandy savanna with pink trumpet flowers and a fruit of hooked claws. Its tubers ease aching joints.
Variants.Lore: The hooked fruit catches in a beast's hoof to be carried. The hunters of the dry savanna dig the root in secret places.

Variants.Name: neem
Variants.Description: A large, evergreen shade tree of dry tropical land. Its bitter leaves, bark and oil clean teeth, heal the skin and drive off insects.
Variants.Lore: The village pharmacy of the Rainkeepers. A twig of it is the toothbrush of a whole people, and its leaves are strewn where there is pox.

Variants.Name: holy basil
Variants.Description: A small, hairy, scented bush with purple-tinged leaves, grown in a pot by the door and at shrines. Brewed against fever.
Variants.Lore: A goddess in the form of a plant. Rainkeeper houses are built around the pot it grows in, and it is watered at dawn.

Variants.Name: fever bark
Variants.Description: A tree of wet tropical mountain forest. Its bitter, red-brown bark is stripped, dried and ground against the shaking fever.
Variants.Lore: The mountain people saw a sick puma drink from a pool under the tree. The Bitterbloods gather it and sell the cure for the shaking fever.

Variants.Name: ipecac
Variants.Description: A small shrub of the rain forest floor. Its thin, ringed roots bring on vomiting and cure the bloody flux.
Variants.Lore: The forest healers call it the roadside sick-making plant, and sell the secret dearly.

Variants.Name: arrow-poison vine
Variants.Description: A thick, woody vine that climbs to the canopy of the rain forest. Its bark is boiled down to a black paste that stills the muscles.
Variants.Lore: Each forest family has its own recipe, and the Bitterbloods the best. The strength is told in trees: how many a monkey can leap before it falls.

Variants.Name: water hyssop
Variants.Description: A small, creeping, fleshy herb with pale flowers, on the mud of warm marshes and mangrove edges. Taken to sharpen the memory.
Variants.Lore: Rainkeeper pupils are given it to learn the long texts by heart. It is offered to the god who made the world.

Resources.Name: Arcane materials
Resources.Description: Things that hold magic: strange metals, glowing crystals, old bones and plants that should not be, found only where the Supernatural is strong. Rare, costly, and sought by mages, alchemists and artificers.
Resources.Lore: The sorcerer-kings of the Old Realms built their power on these and mined out what they found. What is left lies where the world is still strange, and a college, a crown and a cabal will each pay to hear of a new find.

Variants.Name: star metal
Variants.Description: Iron that fell from the sky: black, pitted, heavy lumps with a melted crust, lying in sand or on ice round an old crater. Cut, it shows a silver, criss-cross grain. It is forged cold, and a blade of it turns magic aside.
Variants.Lore: A king's dagger of it was laid in his tomb when iron was still unknown. The Grass riders do not touch a fallen star for a year, and then only the smith may.

Variants.Name: truesilver
Variants.Description: A white metal, lighter than steel and harder, that never tarnishes. It runs as bright threads through the granite of high mountains, and melts only in the hottest forge. Drawn into wire, it sings.
Variants.Lore: The Dwarves say the sorcerer-kings mined the last great veins and that what is found now is crumbs. They do not say where the crumbs are.

Variants.Name: mana crystal
Variants.Description: Clear crystals with a slow inner glow, violet to blue, that line hollow stones in wet volcanic ground. They hold magic as a jar holds water, and are cut as the focus stones of mages.
Variants.Lore: A college of mages buys every stone it hears of, and counts the unsold ones as a threat. The crystals dim in the hand of someone dying.

Variants.Name: dragonbone
Variants.Description: The stone bones of the great dragons, weathering out of dry sandstone hills: ribs like ship's timbers, dark and heavy, with a dull red sheen. Lighter and tougher than steel when worked.
Variants.Lore: Dwarves mine it only after buying the hill from its drake, with a goat a week. The Midlanders show a rib of it in a church as the bone of a giant.

Variants.Name: glowcap fungi
Variants.Description: A mushroom that glows steadily, bright enough to read by, in limestone country: cave mouths, sinkholes and the roots above them. Foxfire is its faint natural cousin.
Variants.Lore: Gnome and Dwarf halls are lit with it. It dims when someone in the hall lies, the Gnomes claim.

Variants.Name: moonpearls
Variants.Description: Large pearls of a pale blue-white that shine with their own light in the dark, as the full moon does. They grow in the moon oyster, a giant shell of warm shallow seas that opens only under a full moon. Used for scrying.
Variants.Lore: A Shoalfolk diver who brings up a moonpearl may name the price of the family's reef. Lanternkin envoys wear one, and it is said to dim at a lie.

Variants.Name: frost-lotus
Variants.Description: A pale water flower that opens on tundra lakes and rivers for the few days between the thaw and the midges, and whose petals stay frozen in the hand.
Variants.Lore: Hearthbloods, whose blood is at fever heat, pay anything for it: it is the one thing that cools them.

Variants.Name: windcrystal
Variants.Description: A pale, blue-white crystal, like frozen breath, that grows on the highest and coldest peaks and hums when the wind crosses it. A piece of it weighs less than nothing and tugs upward in the hand.
Variants.Lore: Hearthbloods say it is the breath of the frost drake, frozen in the rock. Miners listen for the drake before they dig.

Variants.Name: sunstone
Variants.Description: A warm, amber-gold stone found in the hottest sands of the desert. It drinks the heat of the day and gives it back through the night, glowing like an ember.
Variants.Lore: The Saltroad caravans carry one in the bedding for the desert night. It is found in the ash of a phoenix, the incense merchants say, and each has a cousin who saw it.

Variants.Name: elderwood
Variants.Description: A tree of any forest kind that has stood since the Dawn and woken a little. The wood does not rot and remembers the shape it is given.
Variants.Lore: Some elderwoods are Amberbloods who took root. To fell one unasked is murder in their law and a fortune in everyone else's.

Variants.Name: sap of Elanor
Variants.Description: A small golden flower of low woodland whose sap keeps what is steeped in it from spoiling.
Variants.Lore: Elves plant it where one of their own lies. A meadow of it is a graveyard, and its keepers do not sell.

Variants.Name: dreamleaf
Variants.Description: A broad-leaved shrub of wet tropical highlands, which carry temperate biomes in the generator. The chewed leaf gives true dreams: of what is, not of what will be.
Variants.Lore: A Rainkeeper astrologer who is caught using it is dismissed for cheating.

Variants.Name: ghostlight peat
Variants.Description: Black peat from bogs where pale lights dance at night. A brick of it burns with a cold, blue, smokeless flame that gives light and no heat, and draws no beast.
Variants.Lore: The lights over the bog are the lanterns of the drowned. A mage pays for the peat by the basket, and the peat cutters cross themselves and take the money.

Variants.Name: stormglass
Variants.Description: Twisted tubes and beads of grey-green glass, made where lightning strikes the open plain. A faint light flickers inside them, and brightens before a storm.
Variants.Lore: The Widegaze see the grey birds gather a day before the storm and know where the glass will be. Herders bury a bead of it under the threshold of the winter fold.

Biomes.Name: Ice & snow
Biomes.Description: Ice caps and polar barrens: the high Arctic, Greenland, the Antarctic coast.
Biomes.Lore: The Hoarkin gave up their own warmth to live here, and sleep through the dark half of the year. Everyone else holds that the ice is where the world was left unfinished.

Biomes.Name: Tundra
Biomes.Description: Arctic tundra, and alpine tundra above the tree line.
Biomes.Lore: A land with no trees to hide in and no night in summer. The herders follow the reindeer across it, and the dead of the Dawn lie whole in its frozen ground.

Biomes.Name: Cold steppe
Biomes.Description: The Mongolian and Kazakh steppe, the high plateau steppe, Patagonia.
Biomes.Lore: The sea of grass. The Grass riders hold that it belongs to no one and that walls are an insult to it. Every few generations it empties itself onto the settled lands.

Biomes.Name: Boreal forest
Biomes.Description: The taiga of Siberia, Scandinavia and Canada.
Biomes.Lore: The Northmen farm its edge and do not go far in. It is a week of the same tree in every direction, and what lives in the middle has no dealings with people.

Biomes.Name: Cold desert
Biomes.Description: The Gobi, the Taklamakan, the Great Basin.
Biomes.Lore: The caravans cross it from well to well, and a well is worth a kingdom. Buried cities of the Old Realms show in the sand after a storm, and are gone after the next.

Biomes.Name: Temperate grassland
Biomes.Description: Prairie, the Pontic steppe, the pampas. Most of it is farmland where people live.
Biomes.Lore: The bread land. Most of it is under the plough, and every army that ever marched came across it. The barrows of forgotten kings are the only hills.

Biomes.Name: Woodland & shrubland
Biomes.Description: Mediterranean woodland and scrub, chaparral. At its cool end an open oak, pine and juniper woodland.
Biomes.Lore: The land of the olive, the vine and the goat. The Old Realms were richest here and cut the forest for their fleets. The goats have seen to it that it did not come back.

Biomes.Name: Temperate mixed forest
Biomes.Description: The conifer and hardwood forests of the Baltic, New England and Manchuria.
Biomes.Lore: Half cleared and half not: the Midlanders call the cleared half the kingdom and the rest the wood. Charcoal burners, outlaws and hermits live in the rest.

Biomes.Name: Temperate broadleaf forest
Biomes.Description: The oak and beech forests of western Europe, and the broadleaf forests of eastern China and Japan.
Biomes.Lore: The old forest of the Elves, who garden it and are losing it, an acre at a time, to the plough. The oldest oaks were saplings in the Dawn.

Biomes.Name: Temperate rain forest
Biomes.Description: The Pacific Northwest, Valdivia, New Zealand, the Atlantic oakwoods.
Biomes.Lore: It rains two days in three and moss covers whatever stands still. The Amberbloods end their lives here, standing as trees, and the groves are counted as graveyards.

Biomes.Name: Hot desert
Biomes.Description: The Sahara, Arabia, the Sonoran desert.
Biomes.Lore: The Duskreaders cross it by night and the Saltroad folk from well to well. The sorcerer-kings are said to have made it, out of a land that had displeased them.

Biomes.Name: Thorn scrub
Biomes.Description: The Sahel, the Horn of Africa, the Caatinga, the Chaco, the Indian thorn forest.
Biomes.Lore: Everything here has a thorn or a sting, and every tree is someone's. The herders fold their cattle in rings of cut thorn, and the lions test them nightly.

Biomes.Name: Savanna
Biomes.Lore: The long grass of the Sunlanders, their cattle and their kings. It burns each dry season and is green a week after the rain, and the herds of game follow the green.

Biomes.Name: Tropical dry forest
Biomes.Description: The monsoon forests of India and Indochina (teak and sal), the dry forests of Central America.
Biomes.Lore: The Rainkeepers' land of two seasons: half the year the trees are bare and the reservoirs sink, and then the monsoon breaks and everything is forgiven.

Biomes.Name: Tropical rain forest
Biomes.Description: The Amazon, the Congo, the Malay archipelago.
Biomes.Lore: The Boughwalkers live in its crown and seldom touch the ground. Below, it is dusk at noon. Outsiders die of its fevers, and so it has never been conquered.

Biomes.Name: Mangrove
Biomes.Description: The Sundarbans and other mangrove coasts.
Biomes.Lore: Neither land nor sea, and under the law of neither. The Shoalfolk live on stilts at its edge, and the Bitterbloods fled into it to be let alone.

Biomes.Name: Volcano
Biomes.Description: A lone fire mountain: a steep, dark cone with a smoking crater, black lava fields and grey ash on its flanks, and hot springs and yellow sulphur vents at its foot. Little grows on it but birch, heather and fireweed. Etna, Hekla, Fuji.
Biomes.Lore: Every people says a smith or a dragon lives under it, and the Dwarves do not contradict either. The soil at its foot is the richest there is, so it is farmed between its tempers.

ElevationTypes.Name: Ocean
ElevationTypes.Description: Open salt water to the horizon: grey-green swell, white surf on the shore, gulls and a far sail. No one lives on it, but ships cross it and fishers work its edge.
ElevationTypes.Lore: The Northmen call it the whale road and the Shoalfolk call it home. To everyone else it is the edge of the world, and what comes over it is trade or raiders.

ElevationTypes.Name: Flat Land
ElevationTypes.Description: Level land under a wide sky, with a far, straight horizon: plains, river flats and marsh. Rivers wind slowly across it, roads run straight, and a tower is seen from a day away.
ElevationTypes.Lore: There is nowhere to hide and nothing to stop an army or a flood. The people of the plain build mounds, dikes and walls, and watch the horizon.

ElevationTypes.Name: Lowland
ElevationTypes.Description: Gently rolling country of low rises and broad, shallow valleys, easy to plough and to cross. Fields, hedges and woods cover the swells, and a village lies in every hollow.
ElevationTypes.Lore: The settled land, where the Old Realms laid their roads and the kingdoms of the Scattered Age hold their courts. Every field has a name and an owner.

ElevationTypes.Name: Hills
ElevationTypes.Description: Steep, rounded heights and narrow valleys with quick streams. Pasture and wood on the slopes, rock showing at the crests, winding roads, and a fort or a tower on many a hilltop.
ElevationTypes.Lore: The hill people keep sheep, feuds and their own counsel. The plains have always called them thieves, and have always hired them as soldiers.

ElevationTypes.Name: Mountains
ElevationTypes.Description: High ranges of bare rock, with snow on the peaks, cliffs, scree and deep gorges. Forest clings to the lower slopes, torrents fall white to the valleys, and the few roads cross by high passes.
ElevationTypes.Lore: The gods live on the peaks and the Dwarves under them. A pass is a kingdom's gate, and the peoples of the heights have never been ruled for long.

FactionTypes.Name: Family
FactionTypes.Description: Bound by blood and marriage: a house and its household.
FactionTypes.Lore: The oldest bond, and the one that outlasts every other. A house remembers a slight for five generations and a kindness for two.

FactionTypes.Name: Race
FactionTypes.Description: Bound by a people: one race, its clans and its customs.
FactionTypes.Lore: A people looks after its own first. In the Ashen Years each of them learnt who would open a gate to it, and none has forgotten.

FactionTypes.Name: Vocation
FactionTypes.Description: Bound by work: a trade, its masters and its monopoly.
FactionTypes.Lore: A trade is a brotherhood with secrets, dues and a feast day. Its masters decide who may work, and call that protecting the craft.

FactionTypes.Name: Belief
FactionTypes.Description: Bound by a faith: a temple, an order, a sect.
FactionTypes.Lore: A faith holds what the crown cannot reach: the conscience, the calendar and the dead. It is also the largest landlord in most kingdoms.

FactionTypes.Name: Magic
FactionTypes.Description: Bound by the arcane: a college, a circle, a cabal.
FactionTypes.Lore: The sorcerer-kings ruled the Old Realms and broke them. Every bond of mages since has been watched for the same ambition, usually with reason.

FactionTypes.Name: Place
FactionTypes.Description: Bound by a home: a town or a valley that rules itself.
FactionTypes.Lore: Town air makes free, the saying goes: a year and a day inside the walls, and no lord may claim you. Those who share a wall or a valley defend it together.

FactionForms.Name: Crown
FactionForms.Lore: Each kingdom is sure that it is the heir of an Old Realm. A crown reaches as far as its court can ride, and is disputed at every death.

FactionForms.Name: House
FactionForms.Description: A rival house in opposition, or a great house under the ruler.
FactionForms.Lore: A great house keeps its own hall, its own colours and its own list of wrongs. It serves the crown until the day it sees a better claim, which is often its own.

FactionForms.Name: Horde
FactionForms.Description: A herding people of open land.
FactionForms.Lore: The herding peoples are a scatter of camps until one khan is raised over all. Then they are a single army, and the settled lands learn its name.

FactionForms.Name: Clan
FactionForms.Lore: Everyone in it is kin, and the chief is the first among cousins. He rules by the consent of the elders, and they remind him of it.

FactionForms.Name: Hold
FactionForms.Description: A people in rough land with ore.
FactionForms.Lore: A gate, a granary and a ledger. The hold keeps seven years of grain and every contract it ever signed, and has never yet opened to a siege.

FactionForms.Name: Enclave
FactionForms.Description: A people that lives under the ruler of another.
FactionForms.Lore: A people living by its own law inside another's land, by an old grant. It pays for the grant in each reign, and keeps the parchment safe.

FactionForms.Name: Merchant republic
FactionForms.Description: Rule by the guilds of the trading towns.
FactionForms.Lore: Ruled by those with ships and warehouses, who elect one of themselves and watch him closely. It fights its wars with hired soldiers and its ledgers.

FactionForms.Name: Guild
FactionForms.Description: A guild of one trade, in opposition or under the ruler.
FactionForms.Lore: The masters of one trade, sworn together. They fix the price, the wage and the number of shops, bury their dead and feast their saint.

FactionForms.Name: Temple state
FactionForms.Lore: The god is the ruler and the high priest the steward. The tithe is the tax, the temple granary is the treasury, and heresy is treason.

FactionForms.Name: Sect
FactionForms.Description: A faith of the poor against the ruler.
FactionForms.Lore: It begins with a preacher and the poor. The temple calls it heresy and the crown calls it rebellion, and it thinks little of either.

FactionForms.Name: Order
FactionForms.Description: A faith with a rule of its own, in opposition or under the ruler.
FactionForms.Lore: Sworn men and women under a rule and a master, with houses in many lands. An order answers to its own head and outlives the kings who gave it land.

FactionForms.Name: Magocracy
FactionForms.Lore: The sorcerer-kings come again, its neighbours say. The mages answer that those who understand the world should govern it, as they said the last time.

FactionForms.Name: Cabal
FactionForms.Lore: Mages who took no oath to a college or broke the one they took. They meet masked, and want what the sorcerer-kings had.

FactionForms.Name: Circle
FactionForms.Lore: The licensed mages of a realm, sworn to the ruler and to each other. They police their own, which is the price of being left alone.

FactionForms.Name: Free city
FactionForms.Description: Towns that rule themselves, as the ruler or against it.
FactionForms.Lore: It owes no lord anything but a yearly gift. The citizens man the walls themselves, ring the great bell in danger, and shut the gates on princes.

FactionForms.Name: Commune
FactionForms.Description: Free farmers that rule themselves, as the ruler or against it.
FactionForms.Lore: Farmers who swore an oath together and kept it. They meet under a tree, vote by raised hands, and have beaten armies of knights with pikes.

FactionForms.Name: Chartered town
FactionForms.Description: A town with a charter of its own under the ruler.
FactionForms.Lore: Its freedoms are written in a charter kept in a chest with three locks. Each new ruler confirms it, for a fee.

SettlementKinds.Name: Town
SettlementKinds.Description: A small market place: a square with a well, a temple, an inn, a row of workshops and a weekly market, behind a ditch and a palisade or a low wall. Fields and gardens begin at the last house.
SettlementKinds.Lore: A town is where the country comes on market day. Everyone knows whose daughter you are, and the lord's bailiff lives in the big house by the square.

SettlementKinds.Name: City
SettlementKinds.Description: A large walled place: stone walls with towers and gates, crowded streets of tall, narrow houses, guild halls, a great temple, markets for every trade, and a castle or a palace. Its smoke is seen from far off, and suburbs spill out along the roads.
SettlementKinds.Lore: A city eats more people than are born in it, and fills up again from the villages. They come because behind its walls no one asks who their father was.

SettlementTiers.Name: Countryside
SettlementTiers.Description: The land outside the towns: villages, hamlets and lone farms among fields, pasture and wood, with a mill on the stream, a small shrine and a manor house. Where most people live, and where nearly all of them work the land.
SettlementTiers.Lore: Nine people in ten live here and are born, wed and buried within sight of one tower. The year is the plough, the scythe and the feast days.

SettlementTiers.Name: Town
SettlementTiers.Description: The life of a small market town: a few streets of craftsmen and shopkeepers round a market square, where the country comes to sell and buy. Everyone knows everyone, and a guild is a dozen masters.
SettlementTiers.Lore: A townsman is a farmer's grandson with a trade. The guild, the market cross and the council of twelve are the whole of public life.

SettlementTiers.Name: City
SettlementTiers.Description: The life of a city: whole streets given to one trade, great merchants and their warehouses, schools, courts and temples, and crowds of labourers, servants, beggars and thieves. Here are the rare crafts that a town cannot feed.
SettlementTiers.Lore: A city has a stranger in every street and a guild for every craft, the thieves and the beggars included. What is new begins here, and what is banned is sold here.

SettlementTiers.Name: Capital
SettlementTiers.Description: The seat of a ruler: a city with a court. A palace or a citadel above the roofs, the halls of the officials, the mint and the treasury, the houses of the great families, envoys from other lands, and the finest craftsmen there are, who work for the court.
SettlementTiers.Lore: Where the court sits, everything is for sale and everyone is a petitioner. The capital lives on the taxes of the realm, and is the first place to riot.
